“Stressed Out”, Andrej Lišakov, Unsplash.com, Unsplash+ License

The post What is Healthy and Unhealthy Stress? appeared first on Tacoma Christian Counseling.

item.title: Have I Just Had a Traumatic Experience? Signs and Ways to Recover from Trauma
item.description:
Words are some of the most precious gifts the Lord has given us. Using our words, we can describe ourselves, our experiences, and the world around us. When we name something, it allows us to understand it better. In fact, the Bible talks directly about the power of words in Proverbs 18:21: “The tongue has the power of life and death.”

The same goes when you have a traumatic experience. Understanding what trauma is and naming your trauma appropriately can help you begin recovering from the effects of a devastating experience.

We live in a world that is broken and fallen (Genesis 3). This doesn’t mean there’s nothing good in the world. On the contrary, there is much to celebrate. However, amid the beauty, there is also pain, even in something as beautiful and creative as childbirth or a romantic relationship. Pain, hardship, and loss touch us all in one way or another as we make our way through life. Traumatic experiences are part of the fabric of the world we live in.

Understanding and Naming Trauma After a Traumatic Experience

After you’ve gone through something, you may be the sort of person who pauses, reflects, and asks, “What was that?” Perhaps it’s a painful breakup or divorce, or maybe you were involved in a bad traffic accident, and you’re still trying to put the pieces back together. Some people have been the victims of crime, and they struggle to make sense of their feelings after the fact.

After certain difficult experiences, you may be prompted to ask whether you’ve just gone through a traumatic event. You may even want to know how you’d know if something you’ve been through has traumatized you. Beyond that, you might also be asking how to find healing in Christ so that the experience doesn’t have a hold on you, and it doesn’t have the final say in who you are and how you live your life.

Trauma can be understood as the psychological and emotional response a person has to an experience that they find disturbing or deeply distressing. These kinds of experiences tend to overwhelm an individual’s ability to cope with them.

It’s a bit like when a circuit is overloaded and it trips, shutting down. To talk about trauma is mainly to talk about how our bodies and minds experience and try to make sense of what just happened.

While trauma is less about the event itself and more about how that event is processed, certain events tend to overwhelm our ability to cope with them. Though we are wired differently and don’t all have the same level of resilience or ability to cope, there are certain kinds of events that most people would find overwhelming. These include witnessing violence or experiencing physical, emotional, or sexual abuse.

Other examples of experiences that could result in trauma are natural disasters like a tsunami, earthquake, or wildfire. Being caught in a serious accident or having a sudden and serious health crisis can also be the cause of trauma. Various situations where you may have felt either powerless, unsafe, or threatened may lie at the root of trauma as well.

Trauma is not only the result of situations where you find yourself in physical danger. Trauma can be experienced by the sudden loss of a loved one, if you experience deep betrayal, or if you are abandoned by a loved one.

These and other kinds of experiences can contribute to trauma. It is important to remember that even though two people experience the exact same event, they won’t necessarily develop trauma. Trauma and being traumatized depend on how the individual experiences the moment, and that includes how it impacts one’s sense of meaning, control, and their sense of safety as well.

The Signs of Trauma to Look Out for

If you’ve gone through some things and you’re wondering if the experience has traumatized you, there are several signs of trauma that you can keep an eye out for. Trauma manifests in various ways, on the heels of the event, but also over time. There are some signs to consider as you reflect on your experience. These include:

Physical and behavioral signs of trauma Physical symptoms such as stomach pains, headaches, or unexplained muscle tension. These also include struggling to sleep or having recurring nightmares. Behaviors such as avoiding reminders of the experience or social withdrawal are also signs of trauma. Lastly, feeling on edge and struggling to concentrate also point to trauma.

Emotional and mental signs Feelings such as anxiety, panic, or a lingering sense of dread are suggestive of anxiety. Other emotions such as shock, numbness, and intense fear are also signs of trauma. Trauma and the ensuing loss of a sense of safety could result in irritability, mood swings, or anger. Additionally, you may feel disconnected or emotionally detached from your loved ones or from life.

Another possible sign of trauma is when one experiences dreams, intrusive thoughts, or even flashbacks from the experience. These can be deeply upsetting, making it feel like you’re experiencing it all over again.

Spiritual signs Trauma can manifest as a feeling of being distant from God or as though He has abandoned you. Struggling to pray or read Scripture, as well as intensely questioning and wrestling with God’s protection or goodness, may also point to trauma.

These various responses to a difficult experience may begin to hinder daily functioning. When they persist or intensify, it begins to suggest that the experience was more than simply upsetting; it has become traumatic.

Recovering from Trauma and Moving Toward Healing

Why is it that some people will experience a traumatic event, but they won’t necessarily be traumatized? People process and recover from challenging circumstances and experiences differently, and certain factors can render trauma more likely. Getting a handle on these can be a help in mitigating the impact of traumatic experiences and in building greater resilience.

Trauma is often more likely when one is exposed repeatedly or over a long time to dangerous or harmful situations and experiences. An example is when a person is repeatedly abused, or a second responder who finds their life under threat on multiple occasions. Trauma may also result when the event itself is sudden, deeply shocking, or involves being helpless. A deadly natural disaster is an example of this sort of event.

Other things that can make trauma more likely are when the individual feels like they are alone and without emotional support. We all need people around us to care for us and to be sounding boards for us when we go through crises. Ecclesiastes 4:9-10 states, “Two are better than one . . . if either of them falls down, one can help the other up.”

Being alone strips you of additional capacity to deal with difficult circumstances. Lastly, experiences that shake your core beliefs about your safety or your trust in God’s presence can also result in trauma.

Recovering from trauma is a journey. You can’t get there all at once, but it’s possible to heal and find yourself as well as your sense of safety and meaning again. Some steps that may be helpful along this journey include:

Naming the pain It’s important to acknowledge what you’ve gone through, and to name it for what it is. Be honest with the Lord and with yourself about what you’ve gone through. He knows you and loves you, through and through (Psalm 139), and He can meet you in your pain.

Pray and lament You can bring the pain, insecurity, loss of meaning, and everything else the traumatic experience has robbed you of or brought into your life and take it to the Lord in prayer. There are many Psalms of lament, like Psalm 6, 13, or 22, that can help you to give utterance to your confusion, grief, and fear even as you lean into God’s unfailing love. Take the time to reflect on what Scripture says about God’s character and faithful presence.

Gentle self-care Traumatic experiences and trauma wrench you out of what you know into new and painful territory. Instead of leaning into self-destructive behaviors to self-soothe or silence the pain, opt for gentle self-care. Rest, eat healthy and nourishing food, and get some exercise. Connect with other people. Small and consistent steps add up, and maintaining healthy rhythms can help you heal and regain a sense of safety and normalcy.

Get professional help In addition to seeking safe and wise support from loved ones who can help bear your burden and struggle, you can get professional help. A trauma-informed therapist can help you by offering practical tools as well as working with you through therapies to recover from trauma. They can guide you toward healing while integrating your faith as part of the process of recovery.

Seeking Help After a Traumatic Experience

Trauma isn’t the final word after a traumatic experience, and it isn’t a sign of weak faith. Instead, seeking help when dealing with trauma is a courageous and wise step. Healing, hope, and redemption are possible.

2 Corinthians 12:9 states, “Strength is made perfect in weakness.”

If you are feeling overwhelmed or unsafe after a traumatic experience, reach out to our office and speak to a representative today. They can schedule an appointment with a Christian counselor or therapist near you.

Photo:
“Road in the Field”, Courtesy of Annie Spratt, Unsplash.com, Unsplash+ License

The post Have I Just Had a Traumatic Experience? Signs and Ways to Recover from Trauma appeared first on Texas Christian Counseling.

item.title: 12 Ways to Make Your Marriage Christ-centered
item.description:
Whether you and your spouse are new Christians or have followed Christ for many years, it can still be unclear what a Christ-centered marriage looks like. Having a Christ-centered marriage goes deeper than believing in God. It requires more than simply believing and showing up. To make your relationship Christ-centered, follow these steps.

Commit today to place Christ first in your relationship

Regardless of how you have centered your relationship in the past, begin today by focusing on Christ. This commitment is for both of you individually and together as a couple. In every decision, obstacle, joy, and struggle, look to Christ for direction. Then remember the line from the movie “Facing the Giants”:

If we win, we praise Him. And if we lose, we praise Him. Either way, we honor Him with our actions and our attitudes.”

I have always said, “It is easier to praise Him in the good times,” but the more I have thought about it, the more I realize it is just as difficult, because when things are going well, we tend to take the credit instead of giving it to God.

It is important to focus on Christ in both the good and the difficult times. If we only seek Him in the difficult times, is He really the center of our lives? We don’t talk to our best friends only in difficult times, so why should our relationship with our Creator and Heavenly Father be any different?

Be actively involved in a Christ-centered and biblically focused church body

Scripture calls us to “not forgo coming together.” Being involved in a church body is what God calls us to, and it gives us other believers to walk beside us through all seasons of life. I am thankful for technology, which allows me to watch a service when I am under the weather, but there is nothing like corporate worship and hearing God’s Word taught by the pastor behind the pulpit.

There is nothing like singing together as a body of believers that you can’t get in the comfort of your home. This gives us a glimpse of Heaven. Serving, giving, and worshipping together with your church “family” are a blessing. Being active isn’t just about showing up and sitting in the pew; it’s about finding ways to be involved in ministry, small groups, outreach and evangelism, bereavement, the food pantry, and youth or children’s ministry.

Be an example for your children by being involved and making it a household rule to attend and be involved. Take your children and youth to their age group events and Bible study groups. Statistics show that if a child is involved in the church before they are eighteen, they are more likely to continue after leaving the nest.

Pray

Prayer is not just talking to God but having a conversation that involves listening, not just asking. Pray for and with your spouse. Ask each other regularly how you can pray for them. This is a great way for them to open up their heart to you in a way they may not do if you just asked: “How are you?” Here are a few things to pray for.

  • Pray for health and protection
  • Pray for their salvation (if not already) and pray for God to use them in their “mission field”
  • Pray for focus at work and home
  • Pray for their relationships (coworkers, church, friends, and others they meet)
  • Pray for clear communication and understanding of each other
  • Pray for what stresses them and what is bothering them

Read Scripture together and/or talk about what you are reading and how God is working in your life

Be a family that reads Scripture, talks about it, and memorizes it. After church, talk about the lessons and sermons. What stood out to you? What did you feel God speaking and convicting you about? What did you learn?

Make decisions together with the priority of honoring God, being obedient to Him and His Word

Some decisions seem so simple we don’t need to pray about them. All decisions need prayer. When we make big decisions like job changes and moves, we pray. What about where you will attend church, where your children will attend school, and what should your role in the church be?

Encourage each other to share your faith with others

When you are out together as a couple or family, do you find ways to share, pray, and help others? Do you see a need and meet it? We are not always able to help someone financially, but there are other ways to encourage and minister to others. Find ways to encourage, pray for, and serve others.

Hold each other accountable for your daily walk and growing in your faith

Periodically ask each other what God has been working on you about and/or teaching you. Hold each other accountable for daily reading, studying God’s Word, and prayer.

Find places of service together in your church and/or community

Minister together. It might be at your church, in your neighborhood, in your kids’ sports, or at their school. Find ways to support each other in ministry. You don’t have to be a paid staff member at a church to be ministering to others.

Your husband or wife may be coaching a community league; support them by building relationships with the players and their families. Host a Bible study from your church at your home together; invite someone who doesn’t have family close by to join your family for a holiday meal; or invite a couple or family over after church or to join you at a restaurant to get to know them better.

Prioritize your relationship in all aspects of life

Friendships of the same gender are important for mental health and, as Christians, for encouragement and challenge from the body of Christ. Time with friends should not take priority over time with your spouse. Communicate and plan for time together.

Christ-centered relationships are not perfect but should be an example to others about love, grace, forgiveness, and companionship

Would other couples see you as an example of love, grace, forgiveness, and respect? Find a younger couple, dating or engaged, that you and your spouse can meet with once a month to share life with and encourage in their relationship and faith.

Honor your vows

Here are the traditional vows,

“I, [Name], take you, [Name],
To be my wedded wife/husband,
To have and to hold,
From this day forward,
For better, for worse,
For richer, for poorer,
In sickness and in health,
To love and to cherish,
Till death us do part.”

When we recite these or something similar to each other on our wedding day, we really have little to no idea what this entails. It is a daily commitment. Our vows are not just for the hardest of days but for every day. It is not just for physical health but mental and emotional health as well.

Our vows are a commitment between a bride and groom and to God. Honoring the vows involves keeping the promise “to have and to hold,” “for better or for worse,” and “in sickness and in health.” Keep the vows not just when you feel like it, but whatever life brings you.

Serve one another

As Christians, we are called to serve, and that begins in the home. Seek out ways to serve each other on a daily basis. Be observant of each other’s stressors, struggles, and joys. Offer to take something off their plate or just do it. When they have had success or an accomplishment, celebrate it with them.

How can Christian counseling help couples put Christ at the center of their marriage?

Christian counseling can walk with couples as they work on these areas in their relationship. When couples address struggles like communication, work/life balance, finances, parenting, intimacy, and other daily stressors, counseling assists in the process of healing and helps them to focus their lives back on Christ.

“Support”, Courtesy of Getty Images, Unsplash.com, Unsplash+ License

The post 12 Ways to Make Your Marriage Christ-centered appeared first on Texas Christian Counseling.

item.title: What Is Avoidance Anxiety and How Do I Overcome It?
item.description:
It is in our nature to want to gravitate to the things that we enjoy, and to steer clear of those that we do not. We typically do not go out of our way to put ourselves in situations where we feel embarrassed, out of place, and not having a good time. The question is, when we experience these adverse situations, what do we do about them?

Sometimes, rather than face situations head-on or enter difficult situations more than once, we retreat from them and begin to avoid them. When a situation induces symptoms of anxiety, we can experience sweaty palms, increased heart rate, rapid breathing, and trouble concentrating, to name a few. We can choose to go through whatever is causing us feelings of anxiety, or we can shrink back from it.

When we retreat from these situations, we are engaging in avoidance. When we use that as a coping mechanism to deal with anxiety, it can often lead to anxiety feelings growing over time.

What Is Avoidance?

Avoidance is a term often used to describe a way of coping to protect us from real or perceived harm, and it is an effective survival mechanism. When something makes us feel anxious, we tend to avoid that thing. At first, we might feel less anxious as a result.  The issue is that after a while, the thing we are anxiously avoiding can seem harder to approach, and the problem seems much larger than before.

Avoiding fearful situations seems to make rational sense, but in truth, it actually increases and fortifies our fears. While this is the most common result of avoidance, there are some benefits to avoidance.

Not all avoidance is unnecessary. The nervous system does a good job of helping us avoid things that can truly harm us. It is when we associate harm with things that are not harmful that we experience difficulties. For instance, if you eat at a particular restaurant and get food poisoning more than once, steering clear of that restaurant may be a good idea.  However, if avoidance is used in situations that are not appropriate, it can backfire and enlarge our problems. Instead of teaching us to confront our fears and grow in our ability to tolerate adversity, avoidance encourages us to be wary of change and more risk averse.

It is common for conflict to cause a sense of anxiety. Initially, avoiding conflict by steering clear of conversations that could generate conflict might feel like you are making progress. However, when you avoid having difficult conversations, it can create room for the underlying problem to grow.

What may have been a small conflict can become larger because it was not handled early. When situations like this escalate, it reinforces the negative feelings toward conflict and encourages further avoidance. This can lead to the issue growing and can cause more relationship problems.

With those things that cause us to feel anxious, avoidance is an unhealthy (or maladaptive) way to cope because it merely causes that sense of anxiety to grow. You typically end up experiencing more of the very thing you were trying to avoid. The more you try to avoid, the more that builds negative sensory stimuli and associations related to what you are avoiding. This cycle makes it that much harder to overcome.

Although avoidance can lead to immediate relief from anxiety feelings, it can generate other unwanted emotions such as sadness, frustration, as well as guilt and shame.

Signs of Avoidance Anxiety

How can you tell if you are using avoidance as a coping mechanism? Below are a few things that can help you pinpoint unhealthy avoidance.

  • Your symptoms of anxiety causes you avoid certain situations, activities, locations, or people. If an occasion to encounter any of these comes up, you do everything possible to make sure you are not there, or that you are there for the shortest time possible.
  • You knowingly or unknowingly sabotage a task or situation in some way. Avoidance may push you to try to bury or forget the task. You may also employ tactics such as missing deadlines, forgetting to put the event on your calendar, creating a scheduling conflict, or deliberately missing your appointments.
  • Procrastination is also another way to avoid situations or things that make us anxious. This may look like doing something half-heartedly or distracting yourself with other tasks and forgetting your deadlines.
  • Failing or delaying to make a firm decision on something may be a sign of avoidance.
  • Avoidance can make one resort to people-pleasing to avoid conflict and stress in relationships.

Overcoming Avoidance Anxiety

Instead of avoiding the things that make us feel anxious, it is far better to begin confronting them so that you do not get stuck or allow anxiety to snowball into something much larger. It is important to learn how to cope with difficult things by approaching them head-on instead of avoiding them.  

Instead of taking the path-of-least-resistance and avoiding the things that cause you to experience anxiety, learning to confront your fears or aversion enables you to tolerate and face adversity. It can also teache you to adapt to difficult situations and overcome your feelings of anxiety. 

It’s important for you not only to recognize that avoidance does not always work, but also that avoidance comes with a cost. It impacts our health and relationships, not to mention our sense of competence, which can be undermined when we avoid doing difficult things. 

A few things you can do to overcome anxiety through addressing it and not through avoidance include: 

Identify your stressor or cause Know what initiates your feelings of anxiety by marking the symptoms and observing the negative thought processes and/or patterns that accompany certain situations. This deeper awareness can bring understanding about how these patterns reinforce defensive and avoidance behaviors. These include feeling victimized, procrastinating, checking your phone, using escape tactics to avoid people at social gatherings, or the inability to say no to people.

Learn to tolerate the uncomfortable In life, you will encounter many things that are not comfortable. Avoiding these means that there is a higher likelihood that you will do so the next time such situations are presented. When you can sit with difficult and uncomfortable feelings, you have more options available to you about how you want to face the problem. You can allow yourself to stay in the situation and experience those feelings until they pass. 

Use cognitive restructuring To confront your avoidant behaviors requires learning to recognize distorted thought patterns and not trusting or believing them. Cognitive restructuring is about challenging your belief system and negative patterns of thought by disrupting these and replacing them with observations and thought processes based on reality. Our fears often magnify situations and build them up to be more than they are, and these ideas need to be dismantled. 

Try exposure The other side of avoidance is exposure. This is a systematic process through which you gradually face your fears step-by-step. You repeatedly expose yourself to low levels of stress in the situation that you’re anxious to avoid. When you slowly teach your brain (specifically, your amygdala) to tolerate anxious feelings and begin to make positive associations with the object of your fears, that will gradually lessen that anxiety and fear. 

You can enter the situation you typically avoid by driving past a particular location, then practicing walking up to the entrance, then entering the place with a friend, then walking around alone, and so on, until your feelings of anxiety around the location or activity lessens and/or your ability to manage the feelings increases.

Develop a growth mindset Our anxious feelings are often centered on the possibility of rejection, failure, or the unknown. Rather than experience these, we opt to avoid the situation altogether. To overcome these, it requires that we teach ourselves that it is okay when things do not go okay or the way we envisioned they would go. We grow in our ability to adapt to situations by being willing to experiment, adjust, and learn through trial-and-error. 

Instead of looking at it through the lens of failure or success, a growth mindset promotes self-awareness and an open-minded curiosity about new situations. New situations can be looked at as challenges to be tackled and problems that require skill to be solved.

Get and stay healthy Eat and sleep well, avoiding caffeinated beverages, for instance, as they tend to increase feelings of anxiety. Exercise, whether that’s walking, running, swimming, kayaking, strength training, yoga, or cycling. Exercise can help you relax and get you prepared to face challenging situations with more emotional and physical capacity.

Exercise is great for using up nervous energy and elevating your mood through the release of endorphins. It is, however, important that you do not rely on exercise to avoid a situation that is causing you to feel anxious. Going for a run every morning is great for helping you release energy and get those “feel-good” hormones flowing through you so that you can tackle office interactions. But it can also be used to avoid situations. 

Going for a run every time something nerve-wracking comes up so you do not have to face it may just be an avoidance method. You can take on other practices that support your mental and emotional health, such as journaling and meditation. These are highly effective for managing emotional stress and helping you become more aware of your triggers.

Develop your skill set Part of why we often avoid the things that make us feel anxious is that we may not have the skills to deal with them. If you learned early on to avoid certain social situations, for example, that early learned behavior may mean that you never developed the skills to be in social situations. It gets harder and more awkward the older you get, thus increasing the possibility of turning to avoidance as a coping mechanism.

Similarly, if you are anxious about conflict, it may be that you do not have conflict resolution skills that will allow you to tackle conflict in a healthy way. Instead of avoidance, consider that it’s not too late to learn the skills you need to know how to navigate difficult situations.

Ask for Help It can be hard to make changes to your well-worn patterns of being that rely heavily on avoidance behaviors to deal with anxiety. You may find that you are not even sure where to begin with making necessary changes. If that is your situation, we have many counselors who are able to walk this journey with you. A counselor can help you develop the tools you need to replace old ways of thinking about and responding to symptoms of anxiety with more effective ones. To learn more about how a counselor can help, contact our reception team today. 

Photo:
“Sandy Coastline” courtesy of Rod Long, Unsplash.com, CCO License

The post What Is Avoidance Anxiety and How Do I Overcome It? appeared first on Texas Christian Counseling.

item.title: Compulsive Overeating Disorder: How You Can Learn to Control It
item.description:
Overeating is a common occurrence for many people around the holidays. We gather at our family’s home and enjoy Thanksgiving, Christmas, or Easter dinners a little too much, eating way beyond full and leaving uncomfortably full or falling asleep in front of the television.

But some people struggle with overeating regularly. They eat until they are in pain and may not know how much they have consumed. They consistently serve themselves too much, eat too fast, or graze throughout the day, consuming hundreds more calories than their body needs in a day.

The good news is that you can stop the madness of a compulsive overeating disorder.

How to Stop Compulsive Overeating

Stopping compulsive overeating requires breaking the pattern of bad habits and the vicious cycle between your negative thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. It takes time, so you may want to adopt a new change every week or month until you have changed your daily habits and routines.

For example, perhaps you should concentrate on sitting down at the table this week to enjoy your meals instead of eating in your car or at your desk. Next week, you can tackle adding more fiber-rich foods to your plate. You could work on changing your breakfasts one week, then your lunches the following week, slowly building on your new, healthy changes.

Take the time to sit down and eat Hectic schedules mean we are constantly on the go or trying to fit in more work during our downtime. As commendable as this work ethic may seem, staying too busy will affect your health. Slow down and serve yourself each meal at the kitchen or dining room table.

If you are at work, step away from your desk and find a table in the break room or a bench outside, where you can detach yourself from the day and concentrate on your meal. It is too easy to mindlessly consume food when you are distracted by the computer, television, phone, or driving to your next destination.

Try adding water-rich foods to fill you up The foods with a higher water content tend to fill you up without adding extra calories or fat. Think grapes,  apples, watermelon, salad greens, tomatoes, and broth-based soups. Try adding these at the beginning of a meal or as a snack if hungry.

Serve food on portion-controlled plates and bowls It is far easier to limit your portions if you do not eat straight out of a bag or container. Instead, find portion-sized plates and bowls. Serve your meals using these guidelines until you have confidence that you can eyeball an appropriate amount.

Eat fiber-rich foods Fiber fills you up and helps to keep your digestive system healthy. Unfortunately, most people do not eat enough fiber in their diets. The recommended amount of fiber is 25 grams for women and 35 grams for men. Try eating more fruits (leave the skin), beans, flax seeds, nuts, or whole grains or sprouted grains in your meals.

Add protein to every meal Protein promotes satiety. You are less likely to overeat a meal with boneless, skinless chicken breasts than a meal with simple carbohydrates like pasta. Just like with fiber, most people do not consume enough protein.

Check with your physician or a nutritionist about the appropriate amount of protein you should eat each day. As a rule of thumb, the more you exercise, the more protein your body will require for strength and recovery.

Consider low-glycemic foods to keep blood sugar stable Blood sugar plays a critical role in producing a constant level of energy. Suppose you consume too many simple carbohydrates (white bread, white flour, potatoes) and sugar (candy bars, pastries, processed foods, soda).

In that case, your blood sugar level will rise and fall dramatically, causing you to crash and bringing about fatigue, dizziness, and the inability to concentrate. Not maintaining a lower blood sugar level can also result in Type II diabetes. Try whole grain and sprouted bread, non-starchy vegetables, beans, oats, grapefruit, and Greek yogurt.

Add healthy fats to meals Healthy fats give you a sense of satiety while supporting your cells and giving your brain and body energy to do daily tasks. Add one teaspoonful to one tablespoonful of coconut oil to a protein shake or over vegetables. Toss a few nuts on a salad, or add flax seeds to oatmeal. You can add healthy fats as a topping or garnish to your regular foods.

Cut back on sugar intake An overabundance of sugar can lead to chronic conditions like Type II diabetes, heart disease, and inflammation. Sugar works in the brain like an addictive substance, making cravings stronger when you cut back on your sugar consumption.

Try out other sweeteners that will not spike your blood sugar in your coffee and baked goods. Depending on your sensitivity, you might be able to use small amounts of stevia, erythritol, or xylitol.

Identify your trigger foods Are there certain foods that you seem to lack control over? Many people find that certain foods trigger overeating. For example, fast food, chips, ice cream, candy, pretzels, cookies, or pizza. Figure out your trigger foods and cut back on how often you treat yourself to this food. When you do eat from this list, try limiting your portion.

Eat at regular meal times Grazing all day can lead to overeating and consuming too many extra calories, resulting in excess weight, more oversized clothes, and chronic health conditions. Use your schedule to assign meal times and optional times for snacking. For example, you may decide to eat every three to four hours, allowing yourself breakfast, morning snack, lunch, afternoon snack, and dinner.

Plan ahead When we do not plan for our meals, it is easier to make unhealthy choices when hungry. Decide on a day during the week (or on the weekend) to plan out dinners and other meals for you and your family.

Even if you are not ready to prep foods, such as cutting up fruits and vegetables for the week, you can ensure that you have ingredients on hand to make meals and give yourself time to thaw frozen foods.

Drink more water Water fills your stomach, especially if you drink some before  a meal. Giving your body plenty of hydration benefits your organs, brain, hair, skin, and nails. The body needs water to flush out toxins and flourish in every area. Make sure you get in at least eight cups of water each day, more if you exercise or live in a hotter climate.

Seek support and counseling We tend to live our lives like the five people we surround ourselves with. Are your friends and family supportive, or do they also compulsively overeat? It may be time to look for people who live the lifestyle you want: healthy and in control of their eating habits. If you do not know anyone who fits that description, reach out to us today. We offer group counseling for people experiencing overeating disorders and other eating disorders. Group counseling is a great place to share, learn new strategies, and hear from others how they have overcome eating disorders.

When You Need Help for Compulsive Overeating Disorder

The urge to eat can feel similar to the cravings and withdrawal symptoms that substance abusers experience when stopping an addiction. The draw toward more food is strong, and it does take time to train your body to accept smaller portions of healthier foods during mealtimes.

The Bible states, “No discipline is enjoyable while it is happening – it’s painful! But afterward there will be a peaceful harvest of right living for those who are trained in this way.” (Hebrews 12:11 NLT)

If you are struggling to beat an overeating disorder, reach out to one of our professional counselors today. We personalize a plan to help you meet your goals while helping you grow spiritually in your relationship with God. Contact us today, and let’s take the first step toward freedom.

“Encouraging Sign,” courtesy of Nik, Unsplash.com, CCO license

item.title: Bible Verses for Overeating Disorder
item.description:
Is overeating a struggle for you? Many of us face this struggle daily in our abundant culture, where food is tempting and readily available. However, the Bible can help you have better health by reminding you to curb your overeating habits.

When you use specific verses of God’s Word to prepare yourself, you can fight back with confidence when you are tempted to overeat. Jesus used Scripture to fight temptation at a time when he was very hungry (Matt. 4:1-11). If he did this to overcome Satan, we can do the same thing to gain spiritual victory.

The following verses are powerful weapons for you to fight temptation. Meditate on them, memorize them, write them down, post them where you see them often, and save them to your phone. The more ways you hide God’s Word in your heart, the more easily you will remember it when you are tempted to overeat. You can ask the Holy Spirit to bring them to mind when you need accountability in your eating habits.

The Best Bible Verses for Overeating Disorder

You can turn each of the following verses into a prayer in times of temptation. God will meet you right in those moments and give you the strength to overcome. He promises to deliver you from whatever temptation you face, and he will empower you to make better choices for your health.

…the rules of the Lord are true, and righteous altogether. More to be desired are they than gold, even much fine gold; sweeter also than honey and drippings of the honeycomb. – Psalm 19:9b-10

God considers his laws to be more desirable than the sweetest food available during Bible times – honey. His laws are more desirable than the finest gold, or perhaps your food craving of choice: chips, French fries, doughnuts, ice cream, pizza, or whatever tempts you most.

Remember that when you follow God’s laws, you will be blessed with a clean conscience. You won’t be riddled with guilt and shame like you may be when you overeat. God will help you make wise eating choices so you can live a disciplined life for his Kingdom work. His laws lead to life, while our poor choices lead to destruction, so remember this verse when you are tempted.

So I will bless you as long as I live; in your name I will lift up my hands. My soul will be satisfied as with fat and rich food, and my mouth will praise you with joyful lips. – Psalm 63:4-5

What are the richest foods you have tasted? Steak, lobster, cheesecake, or something else? Are you honestly as satisfied with God as you are when you eat these rich foods? You can learn to be more satisfied with God’s presence than you are with food, though this will take discipline.

The peace you find in God’s presence lasts much longer than the pleasure you get from eating rich food. When you learn to gain your true satisfaction from God, your faith will be grounded even while food looks tempting to you.

Delight yourself in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart. – Psalm 37:4

What are the desires of your heart when you are tempted to overeat? It’s probably not to simply feel full or enjoy the taste and texture of food. Most of us overeat to soothe our emotions and fill a place inside that feels empty. Often people with overeating disorders deal with loneliness, rejection, anxiety, depression, and other problems.

A caring Christian counselor can help you get to the roots of why you overeat. You can learn that taking delight in the Lord is much more satisfying than overeating, and you can trust him with the deepest desires of your heart.

How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth! – Psalm 119:103

God’s Word will become sweeter to you the more you meditate on it, study it, and apply it to your life. The Bible has healing properties, just like real honey does. But God’s Word heals you with God’s love, comfort, encouragement, protection, and joy as you learn to relax in his presence and enjoy time with him. Each day, meet with God for a few minutes, asking him to make his words sweeter than honey to you and healing for your soul.

Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth; keep watch over the door of my lips! Do not let my heart incline to any evil, to busy myself with wicked deeds in company with men who work iniquity, and let me not eat of their delicacies! – Psalm 141:3-4

These verses address the issue of controlling what we say. But they can also apply to what food passes over our lips. We can ask God to stand guard over our lips when we are faced with a tempting situation.

He will help you stop putting things into your mouth that aren’t good for you. You can ask God to keep you from drifting toward evil choices and help you avoid the wrong kinds of delicacies. The next time you are tempted, simply pray “Guard my lips,” and God will be right beside you.

I cry to you, O Lord; I say, “You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living.” – Psalm 142:5

When you feel like you want that third piece of cake or fourth slice of pizza, you can pray this verse. You can say, “Lord, I think I want this food right now. But I know my true craving should be for you because you alone can satisfy me.” Then walk away from the temptation, drink a glass of water, and engage in a different activity. God will be your refuge in that moment, a haven where you can find comfort that lasts longer than the food you are craving.

If you have found honey, eat only enough for you, lest you have your fill of it and vomit it. – Proverbs 25:16

The Bible is eminently practical. Any food, even healthy food like honey, can make you sick if you overeat. Choose to eat a balanced diet of nourishing foods to protect your health and feel your best. When you are tempted to overeat in certain food categories, remember this verse and don’t succumb to temptation.

Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” – Matthew 26:41

Our minds and spirits may be willing to make wise food choices, but the sinful nature of our flesh is vulnerable to temptation. All of us face this scenario at one time or another, particularly when we are stressed. But God will help you in the very moment of temptation if you cry out to him. Admit to him that your flesh is weak, and ask him to deliver you from the temptation to overeat.

No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation, he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it. – 1 Corinthians 10:13

This verse can be a practical comfort to you in times of temptation. Ask God to provide you a way out when you are about to overeat. He might instruct you to remove tempting foods from your pantry or eat a mini-meal before going to a restaurant. You can form more practical strategies to serve as escape routes with a qualified Christian counselor.

Christian Counseling for Overeating

The roots of overeating run deep for most people. You may need help from a Christian counselor to overcome overeating disorder. A counselor will offer Bible-based care with compassion and understanding. Your counselor will encourage you with principles that can keep you on track for a healthier lifestyle.

“Plate with Cake”, Courtesy of Olivie Strauss, Unsplash.com, CC0 License

The post Bible Verses for Overeating Disorder appeared first on Mill Creek Christian Counseling.

You can turn each of the following verses into a prayer in times of temptation. God will meet you right in those moments and give you the strength to overcome. He promises to deliver you from whatever temptation you face, and he will empower you to make better choices for your health.

…the rules of the Lord are true, and righteous altogether. More to be desired are they than gold, even much fine gold; sweeter also than honey and drippings of the honeycomb. – Psalm 19:9b-10

God considers his laws to be more desirable than the sweetest food available during Bible times – honey. His laws are more desirable than the finest gold, or perhaps your food craving of choice: chips, French fries, doughnuts, ice cream, pizza, or whatever tempts you most.

Remember that when you follow God’s laws, you will be blessed with a clean conscience. You won’t be riddled with guilt and shame like you may be when you overeat. God will help you make wise eating choices so you can live a disciplined life for his Kingdom work. His laws lead to life, while our poor choices lead to destruction, so remember this verse when you are tempted.

So I will bless you as long as I live; in your name I will lift up my hands. My soul will be satisfied as with fat and rich food, and my mouth will praise you with joyful lips. – Psalm 63:4-5

What are the richest foods you have tasted? Steak, lobster, cheesecake, or something else? Are you honestly as satisfied with God as you are when you eat these rich foods? You can learn to be more satisfied with God’s presence than you are with food, though this will take discipline.

The peace you find in God’s presence lasts much longer than the pleasure you get from eating rich food. When you learn to gain your true satisfaction from God, your faith will be grounded even while food looks tempting to you.

Delight yourself in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart. – Psalm 37:4

What are the desires of your heart when you are tempted to overeat? It’s probably not to simply feel full or enjoy the taste and texture of food. Most of us overeat to soothe our emotions and fill a place inside that feels empty. Often people with overeating disorders deal with loneliness, rejection, anxiety, depression, and other problems.

A caring Christian counselor can help you get to the roots of why you overeat. You can learn that taking delight in the Lord is much more satisfying than overeating, and you can trust him with the deepest desires of your heart.

How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth! – Psalm 119:103

God’s Word will become sweeter to you the more you meditate on it, study it, and apply it to your life. The Bible has healing properties, just like real honey does. But God’s Word heals you with God’s love, comfort, encouragement, protection, and joy as you learn to relax in his presence and enjoy time with him. Each day, meet with God for a few minutes, asking him to make his words sweeter than honey to you and healing for your soul.

Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth; keep watch over the door of my lips! Do not let my heart incline to any evil, to busy myself with wicked deeds in company with men who work iniquity, and let me not eat of their delicacies! – Psalm 141:3-4

These verses address the issue of controlling what we say. But they can also apply to what food passes over our lips. We can ask God to stand guard over our lips when we are faced with a tempting situation.

He will help you stop putting things into your mouth that aren’t good for you. You can ask God to keep you from drifting toward evil choices and help you avoid the wrong kinds of delicacies. The next time you are tempted, simply pray “Guard my lips,” and God will be right beside you.

I cry to you, O Lord; I say, “You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living.” – Psalm 142:5

When you feel like you want that third piece of cake or fourth slice of pizza, you can pray this verse. You can say, “Lord, I think I want this food right now. But I know my true craving should be for you because you alone can satisfy me.” Then walk away from the temptation, drink a glass of water, and engage in a different activity. God will be your refuge in that moment, a haven where you can find comfort that lasts longer than the food you are craving.

If you have found honey, eat only enough for you, lest you have your fill of it and vomit it. – Proverbs 25:16

The Bible is eminently practical. Any food, even healthy food like honey, can make you sick if you overeat. Choose to eat a balanced diet of nourishing foods to protect your health and feel your best. When you are tempted to overeat in certain food categories, remember this verse and don’t succumb to temptation.

Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” – Matthew 26:41

Our minds and spirits may be willing to make wise food choices, but the sinful nature of our flesh is vulnerable to temptation. All of us face this scenario at one time or another, particularly when we are stressed. But God will help you in the very moment of temptation if you cry out to him. Admit to him that your flesh is weak, and ask him to deliver you from the temptation to overeat.

No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation, he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it. – 1 Corinthians 10:13

This verse can be a practical comfort to you in times of temptation. Ask God to provide you a way out when you are about to overeat. He might instruct you to remove tempting foods from your pantry or eat a mini-meal before going to a restaurant. You can form more practical strategies to serve as escape routes with a qualified Christian counselor.

Christian Counseling for Overeating

The roots of overeating run deep for most people. You may need help from a Christian counselor to overcome overeating disorder. A counselor will offer Bible-based care with compassion and understanding. Your counselor will encourage you with principles that can keep you on track for a healthier lifestyle.

item.title: What is OCD and Do I Have It?
item.description:
Have you ever wondered, “What is OCD and do I have it?” Perhaps thoughts like these sound familiar: “Did I turn the stove off before I left for work?” “I need to make sure the locks are secure one last time or something bad will happen to my family.” “My hands feel dirty even after five times washing.” “If I don’t follow through with [this compulsion], I may be responsible for a loved one’s death.”

Do these or similar thoughts occupy your mind each day? Do you find yourself spending too much time ruminating on thoughts you didn’t choose to reflect on; thoughts you can’t seem to get out of your head? Are those thoughts often accompanied by behaviors others might consider bizarre or confusing?

These are just a few examples of the unsettling reality that obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) sufferers battle every day. This article will explore facts vs. common myths related to OCD, the different variations of this unique disorder, and what we can do about it.

What is OCD?

OCD is a unique disorder that has origins in anxiety but is given its own category due to its complex profile. OCD is often chronic, meaning managing it will likely be a constant battle, but with help and treatment, symptoms can decrease significantly, and sufferers can find hope!

As the name suggests, it is characterized by both obsessions and compulsions. The obsessions take the form of intrusive, unwanted, and disturbing thoughts that cause significant anxiety for the sufferer. Compulsions are then used to find temporary relief from these thoughts, offering the sufferer the feeling of control.

Unfortunately, when compulsions are carried out, this only increases the likelihood of intrusive thoughts recurring and strengthens the association between the thoughts, anxiety, and relief found in the behaviors. As with any uncomfortable feeling or situation, when avoidance strategies are employed, we only strengthen our brain’s association with the feared object, convincing our brain that it must be truly dangerous.

This creates a strong feedback loop, causing our brains to obsess over the anxiety-producing thought or event to keep us safe. Although the brain is doing its job, these obsessions can cause suffering, and so the brain finds ways to avoid the painful feelings through compulsive behaviors. Remember – avoidance increases anxiety symptoms. The most helpful way to reduce these uncomfortable experiences is to face them with the help of a trained professional.

Obsessions vs. Compulsions

Obsessions are preliminary to the compulsive behaviors individuals employ to alleviate discomfort. The person begins to ruminate on the intrusive thoughts, and significant amounts of time are spent worrying about the obsessions and practicing compulsions. Compulsions always come out of obsessions as a response to the discomfort they cause, though the link may appear subtle at times.

One thing to note about obsessions is they almost always manifest as an attack on something we deeply care about. This may be a faith belief, part of your character, someone you love, your health, and even your worth. These disturbing intrusive thoughts carry so much powerful weight because they strike to the heart of your deepest values and hidden fears.

Doubt is a common byproduct of the OCD experience, partly because these obsessions can lead you to doubt your morals, beliefs, reality, and even your humanity. But remember, the key thing to understand about obsessions is that they are intrusive – meaning unwanted. They are not a description of who you are or what you believe.

When intrusive thoughts wage war against your mind, the doubt and distress you have are evidence that these thoughts do not come from your character. They are not true beliefs or true moral dilemmas.

If we were to externalize intrusive thoughts and imagine them as a person, they would be manipulative, using your deepest-held values to create false allegations against you, using lies to confuse you and make you wonder whether your character ever had morals or integrity in the first place. And they would be doing all these things in the shadows, making you feel isolated and alone.

Hold on to your values and remember that intrusive thoughts are lies and they function like a bully. They don’t get to tell you who you are, and although at times it may not feel like it, they only hold as much power as you allow.

Common OCD Misconceptions

As with many mental health conditions, popular culture has created stereotypes that can increase confusion between the facts and the myths surrounding OCD. Many people will use the phrase “I’m so OCD” or “you are being OCD” to describe someone who tends toward perfectionism, values organization, or has challenges related to hypochondriasis or germophobia.

There is confusion about what OCD truly is, how the symptoms can present, and the severity of symptoms that lead to a diagnosis. Phrases and stereotypes like these can have a minimizing effect for those truly suffering with the condition.

The obsessional theme of organization and sanitization has gained popularity in recent years, leading many people to understand OCD from this one-dimensional frame. However, there are several different categories of obsessions, some of which may be surprising. If you wonder about OCD but don’t obsess about germs or organization, this list may interest you.

Common Obsessional Themes and Related Compulsions

This is a list of common OCD themes found in the DSM. This list is not exhaustive and, as with all mental health topics, everyone will experience the condition differently. Someone may only have one type of OCD; another person may struggle with several of these. These themes can change over time, and you may develop away from one obsession into new ones. There are also varying levels of severity that may change in different seasons of life.

Often, during high-stress seasons, OCD symptoms may flare, a common phenomenon shared by many disorders. Some themes of OCD obsessions include contamination, sexual, harm/violence, scrupulosity (religious), sensorimotor, and responsibility. Here we will provide a quick overview of each theme listed, but more information is available on trusted websites, such as the International OCD Foundation, for those who are interested in a deeper dive.

Contamination OCD is one of the more widely known subtypes because of its exposure in popular culture. People with this subtype of obsession are preoccupied with cleanliness and sanitation and excessively worry about becoming contaminated with illness or germs. A person may feel “dirty” until they can sanitize to a satisfactory level, sometimes at the risk of skin harm from excessive washing.

Some people may need to wash a certain number of times or practice compulsions until they “feel right.” Another common compulsion related to contamination OCD is rigid behavior around eating, and a highly controlled environment to avoid feeling contaminated.

Sexual OCD involves distressing thoughts related to sexual orientation or unwanted images. People with this subtype may experience shame related to mental images of performing inappropriate sexual acts or participating in sexual ways not acceptable to the individual. Another common theme in this subtype includes doubt about sexual orientation.

An individual may have doubts about their identity and where the thoughts and feelings come from. Common compulsions related to this subtype include reassurance seeking, mental avoidance of unwanted images and thoughts, or monitoring their reactions to the thoughts.

People experiencing Harm/Violence OCD often experience disturbing thoughts and images related to harming themself or a loved one. Additionally, thoughts related to fear of loved ones being hurt if compulsions are not performed are common.

Compulsions related to harm OCD include mental efforts to avoid distressing material, avoiding triggers, avoiding objects that could be used to cause harm, seeking reassurance, and mental checking of one’s character or morals. Sometimes, seemingly unrelated compulsions may include ensuring the right outfit is picked out, or other elements of the environment are under control to prevent the terrible end of a loved one that day.

Scrupulosity is a form of OCD that focuses on faith and religion. The scrupulous individual is consumed by the fear of offending God, sinning, or morally compromising their beliefs. Disturbing images related to sinful acts commonly coincide with this subtype.

Individuals may perform compulsions through ritualistic patterns, such as saying the “right” prayers, repeatedly asking for forgiveness, mental assessments of one’s character and morals, reassurance seeking, mental rationalizing to “argue” with the thoughts, and repeating Scripture a preset number of times, or until it “feels right.”

Elements of prayer, scripture memorization, and repentance can look like regular behaviors for someone practicing faith, but they become compulsions when they are done ritualistically in an effort to offset the discomfort from obsessions, rather than stemming from devoted practice. The individual may also practice their faith alongside the ritualistic compulsions. The difference is subtle, but important to recognize.

Sensorimotor (somatic) OCD includes obsessions related to bodily functions and feelings. Individuals may become hyper-aware of automatic body processes such as blinking, heartbeat, and breathing, and compulsions may include trying to take control over blinking and breathing through patterns and rigid rules related to the number of blinks or breaths in a given amount of time.

Individuals may spend large amounts of time monitoring somatic processes, avoiding situations that trigger hyper-awareness, and seeking reassurance and validation through research and questioning others’ experiences.

Responsibility OCD involves feelings of being responsible to prevent bad things from happening, or fears and doubts related to your behaviors causing a negative event. Those suffering from this subtype often feel responsible for the emotions of those around them and try to control the environment to prevent a negative outcome.

Though their intentions are noble, symptoms of responsibility OCD can quickly become consuming, causing significant distress to the sufferer and tension in social relationships. Efforts to control the environment can overtake an individual’s time and energy, leaving little left over for necessary tasks, such as taking care of health, housekeeping, work, and social spheres.

Responsibility OCD can also coincide with memory OCD, where an individual may doubt their memories or believe they have forgotten something important. Those suffering from this subtype may believe they hit someone with their car or were responsible for a negative situation although there is no proof of it ever occurring. These individuals seek reassurance and compulsively check for evidence to relieve the doubts about their memories.

How do I know if it’s an obsession?

We all have intrusive thoughts sometimes – those thought darts that seem to come out of nowhere and attack our innermost value systems. The experience can be alarming, but individuals without OCD can move on and not become consumed by the thought. OCD obsessions are different because they become consuming. They are distressing, often disturbing thoughts that feel like an onslaught the sufferer cannot prevent.

Obsessions take up time and mental space, and lead to compulsions to alleviate the pain these intrusive thoughts are causing. Although compulsions can be ritualistic, time-consuming, and energy-draining, many individuals battling OCD find comfort in the control that compulsions offer, and in the temporary relief from anxiety. Unfortunately, the anxiety comes back quickly when the intrusive thoughts return, making the association with fear stronger.

The Reassurance Feedback Loop

Seeking and receiving reassurance from anxiety can be a helpful way to connect with a trusted friend, validate your feelings, or gain a new perspective. However, reassurance seeking can become a compulsion when it is done continually and with an attempt to relieve anxieties and doubts generated from OCD obsessions.

Just like with any other compulsion, the association between relief from anxiety and reassurance seeking can be powerful, leading to a rigid pattern of behavior. Seeking reassurance can become a trap when an individual can no longer trust their own thoughts and may even feel like they cannot trust their reality without the input of another.

It can become a form of dependence when we continually seek validation from others to find relief. It is important to learn tools that bolster your inner strengths and aid in overcoming doubts without needing reassurance from others. Freedom from the reassurance feedback loop can increase autonomy and the quality of your relationships.

Put your mind at ease

Remember, OCD obsessions often target our most cherished beliefs and values. If you are having uncomfortable intrusive thoughts and are wondering whether they inform your character, remind yourself that these thoughts are unwanted and direct contradictions to your inner value set.

They do not come from a hidden desire, and your feelings of anxiety or disgust related to these thoughts are evidence of this discrepancy. Don’t let OCD’s manipulations fool you. If you are distressed by the obsessions trying to take over your mind, you can find comfort remembering these intrusive thoughts are evidence of the very values they are trying to attack.

Consider counseling

In counseling, you can explore OCD symptoms and how they affect your life. Your counselor will help you add tools that can equip you for battling and overcoming obsessions and compulsions. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and Behavioral Therapy are two of the most common treatments that offer relief from OCD symptoms.

Many individuals also find relief through medication. Through counseling, you can find the support and training needed to find freedom from compulsions and minimize the impact of obsessions on your life. Suffering in silence can increase OCD’s power.

Although it can be uncomfortable or feel embarrassing to openly discuss and dissect OCD obsessions and compulsions with someone, you can find significant relief in shifting the power dynamic away from the OCD.

Conclusion

Obsessive-compulsive disorder is an exhausting condition that causes great distress and can become debilitating when left untreated. Individuals may feel trapped by OCD obsessions and compulsions and consumed by the amount of time and mental effort exerted through simply trying to make it through the day.

Unfortunately, most of the time, compulsive efforts to relieve the discomfort created by OCD obsessions only reinforce the cycle and can make the distress and obsessions stronger.
