item.title: What is OCD and Do I Have It?
item.description:
Have you ever wondered, “What is OCD and do I have it?” Perhaps thoughts like these sound familiar: “Did I turn the stove off before I left for work?” “I need to make sure the locks are secure one last time or something bad will happen to my family.” “My hands feel dirty even after five times washing.” “If I don’t follow through with [this compulsion], I may be responsible for a loved one’s death.”

Do these or similar thoughts occupy your mind each day? Do you find yourself spending too much time ruminating on thoughts you didn’t choose to reflect on; thoughts you can’t seem to get out of your head? Are those thoughts often accompanied by behaviors others might consider bizarre or confusing?

These are just a few examples of the unsettling reality that obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) sufferers battle every day. This article will explore facts vs. common myths related to OCD, the different variations of this unique disorder, and what we can do about it.

What is OCD?

OCD is a unique disorder that has origins in anxiety but is given its own category due to its complex profile. OCD is often chronic, meaning managing it will likely be a constant battle, but with help and treatment, symptoms can decrease significantly, and sufferers can find hope!

As the name suggests, it is characterized by both obsessions and compulsions. The obsessions take the form of intrusive, unwanted, and disturbing thoughts that cause significant anxiety for the sufferer. Compulsions are then used to find temporary relief from these thoughts, offering the sufferer the feeling of control.

Unfortunately, when compulsions are carried out, this only increases the likelihood of intrusive thoughts recurring and strengthens the association between the thoughts, anxiety, and relief found in the behaviors. As with any uncomfortable feeling or situation, when avoidance strategies are employed, we only strengthen our brain’s association with the feared object, convincing our brain that it must be truly dangerous.

This creates a strong feedback loop, causing our brains to obsess over the anxiety-producing thought or event to keep us safe. Although the brain is doing its job, these obsessions can cause suffering, and so the brain finds ways to avoid the painful feelings through compulsive behaviors. Remember – avoidance increases anxiety symptoms. The most helpful way to reduce these uncomfortable experiences is to face them with the help of a trained professional.

Obsessions vs. Compulsions

Obsessions are preliminary to the compulsive behaviors individuals employ to alleviate discomfort. The person begins to ruminate on the intrusive thoughts, and significant amounts of time are spent worrying about the obsessions and practicing compulsions. Compulsions always come out of obsessions as a response to the discomfort they cause, though the link may appear subtle at times.

One thing to note about obsessions is they almost always manifest as an attack on something we deeply care about. This may be a faith belief, part of your character, someone you love, your health, and even your worth. These disturbing intrusive thoughts carry so much powerful weight because they strike to the heart of your deepest values and hidden fears.

Doubt is a common byproduct of the OCD experience, partly because these obsessions can lead you to doubt your morals, beliefs, reality, and even your humanity. But remember, the key thing to understand about obsessions is that they are intrusive – meaning unwanted. They are not a description of who you are or what you believe.

When intrusive thoughts wage war against your mind, the doubt and distress you have are evidence that these thoughts do not come from your character. They are not true beliefs or true moral dilemmas.

If we were to externalize intrusive thoughts and imagine them as a person, they would be manipulative, using your deepest-held values to create false allegations against you, using lies to confuse you and make you wonder whether your character ever had morals or integrity in the first place. And they would be doing all these things in the shadows, making you feel isolated and alone.

Hold on to your values and remember that intrusive thoughts are lies and they function like a bully. They don’t get to tell you who you are, and although at times it may not feel like it, they only hold as much power as you allow.

Common OCD Misconceptions

As with many mental health conditions, popular culture has created stereotypes that can increase confusion between the facts and the myths surrounding OCD. Many people will use the phrase “I’m so OCD” or “you are being OCD” to describe someone who tends toward perfectionism, values organization, or has challenges related to hypochondriasis or germophobia.

There is confusion about what OCD truly is, how the symptoms can present, and the severity of symptoms that lead to a diagnosis. Phrases and stereotypes like these can have a minimizing effect for those truly suffering with the condition.

The obsessional theme of organization and sanitization has gained popularity in recent years, leading many people to understand OCD from this one-dimensional frame. However, there are several different categories of obsessions, some of which may be surprising. If you wonder about OCD but don’t obsess about germs or organization, this list may interest you.

Common Obsessional Themes and Related Compulsions

This is a list of common OCD themes found in the DSM. This list is not exhaustive and, as with all mental health topics, everyone will experience the condition differently. Someone may only have one type of OCD; another person may struggle with several of these. These themes can change over time, and you may develop away from one obsession into new ones. There are also varying levels of severity that may change in different seasons of life.

Often, during high-stress seasons, OCD symptoms may flare, a common phenomenon shared by many disorders. Some themes of OCD obsessions include contamination, sexual, harm/violence, scrupulosity (religious), sensorimotor, and responsibility. Here we will provide a quick overview of each theme listed, but more information is available on trusted websites, such as the International OCD Foundation, for those who are interested in a deeper dive.

Contamination OCD is one of the more widely known subtypes because of its exposure in popular culture. People with this subtype of obsession are preoccupied with cleanliness and sanitation and excessively worry about becoming contaminated with illness or germs. A person may feel “dirty” until they can sanitize to a satisfactory level, sometimes at the risk of skin harm from excessive washing.

Some people may need to wash a certain number of times or practice compulsions until they “feel right.” Another common compulsion related to contamination OCD is rigid behavior around eating, and a highly controlled environment to avoid feeling contaminated.

Sexual OCD involves distressing thoughts related to sexual orientation or unwanted images. People with this subtype may experience shame related to mental images of performing inappropriate sexual acts or participating in sexual ways not acceptable to the individual. Another common theme in this subtype includes doubt about sexual orientation.

An individual may have doubts about their identity and where the thoughts and feelings come from. Common compulsions related to this subtype include reassurance seeking, mental avoidance of unwanted images and thoughts, or monitoring their reactions to the thoughts.

People experiencing Harm/Violence OCD often experience disturbing thoughts and images related to harming themself or a loved one. Additionally, thoughts related to fear of loved ones being hurt if compulsions are not performed are common.

Compulsions related to harm OCD include mental efforts to avoid distressing material, avoiding triggers, avoiding objects that could be used to cause harm, seeking reassurance, and mental checking of one’s character or morals. Sometimes, seemingly unrelated compulsions may include ensuring the right outfit is picked out, or other elements of the environment are under control to prevent the terrible end of a loved one that day.

Scrupulosity is a form of OCD that focuses on faith and religion. The scrupulous individual is consumed by the fear of offending God, sinning, or morally compromising their beliefs. Disturbing images related to sinful acts commonly coincide with this subtype.

Individuals may perform compulsions through ritualistic patterns, such as saying the “right” prayers, repeatedly asking for forgiveness, mental assessments of one’s character and morals, reassurance seeking, mental rationalizing to “argue” with the thoughts, and repeating Scripture a preset number of times, or until it “feels right.”

Elements of prayer, scripture memorization, and repentance can look like regular behaviors for someone practicing faith, but they become compulsions when they are done ritualistically in an effort to offset the discomfort from obsessions, rather than stemming from devoted practice. The individual may also practice their faith alongside the ritualistic compulsions. The difference is subtle, but important to recognize.

Sensorimotor (somatic) OCD includes obsessions related to bodily functions and feelings. Individuals may become hyper-aware of automatic body processes such as blinking, heartbeat, and breathing, and compulsions may include trying to take control over blinking and breathing through patterns and rigid rules related to the number of blinks or breaths in a given amount of time.

Individuals may spend large amounts of time monitoring somatic processes, avoiding situations that trigger hyper-awareness, and seeking reassurance and validation through research and questioning others’ experiences.

Responsibility OCD involves feelings of being responsible to prevent bad things from happening, or fears and doubts related to your behaviors causing a negative event. Those suffering from this subtype often feel responsible for the emotions of those around them and try to control the environment to prevent a negative outcome.

Though their intentions are noble, symptoms of responsibility OCD can quickly become consuming, causing significant distress to the sufferer and tension in social relationships. Efforts to control the environment can overtake an individual’s time and energy, leaving little left over for necessary tasks, such as taking care of health, housekeeping, work, and social spheres.

Responsibility OCD can also coincide with memory OCD, where an individual may doubt their memories or believe they have forgotten something important. Those suffering from this subtype may believe they hit someone with their car or were responsible for a negative situation although there is no proof of it ever occurring. These individuals seek reassurance and compulsively check for evidence to relieve the doubts about their memories.

How do I know if it’s an obsession?

We all have intrusive thoughts sometimes – those thought darts that seem to come out of nowhere and attack our innermost value systems. The experience can be alarming, but individuals without OCD can move on and not become consumed by the thought. OCD obsessions are different because they become consuming. They are distressing, often disturbing thoughts that feel like an onslaught the sufferer cannot prevent.

Obsessions take up time and mental space, and lead to compulsions to alleviate the pain these intrusive thoughts are causing. Although compulsions can be ritualistic, time-consuming, and energy-draining, many individuals battling OCD find comfort in the control that compulsions offer, and in the temporary relief from anxiety. Unfortunately, the anxiety comes back quickly when the intrusive thoughts return, making the association with fear stronger.

The Reassurance Feedback Loop

Seeking and receiving reassurance from anxiety can be a helpful way to connect with a trusted friend, validate your feelings, or gain a new perspective. However, reassurance seeking can become a compulsion when it is done continually and with an attempt to relieve anxieties and doubts generated from OCD obsessions.

Just like with any other compulsion, the association between relief from anxiety and reassurance seeking can be powerful, leading to a rigid pattern of behavior. Seeking reassurance can become a trap when an individual can no longer trust their own thoughts and may even feel like they cannot trust their reality without the input of another.

It can become a form of dependence when we continually seek validation from others to find relief. It is important to learn tools that bolster your inner strengths and aid in overcoming doubts without needing reassurance from others. Freedom from the reassurance feedback loop can increase autonomy and the quality of your relationships.

Put your mind at ease

Remember, OCD obsessions often target our most cherished beliefs and values. If you are having uncomfortable intrusive thoughts and are wondering whether they inform your character, remind yourself that these thoughts are unwanted and direct contradictions to your inner value set.

They do not come from a hidden desire, and your feelings of anxiety or disgust related to these thoughts are evidence of this discrepancy. Don’t let OCD’s manipulations fool you. If you are distressed by the obsessions trying to take over your mind, you can find comfort remembering these intrusive thoughts are evidence of the very values they are trying to attack.

Consider counseling

In counseling, you can explore OCD symptoms and how they affect your life. Your counselor will help you add tools that can equip you for battling and overcoming obsessions and compulsions. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and Behavioral Therapy are two of the most common treatments that offer relief from OCD symptoms.

Many individuals also find relief through medication. Through counseling, you can find the support and training needed to find freedom from compulsions and minimize the impact of obsessions on your life. Suffering in silence can increase OCD’s power.

Although it can be uncomfortable or feel embarrassing to openly discuss and dissect OCD obsessions and compulsions with someone, you can find significant relief in shifting the power dynamic away from the OCD.

Conclusion

Obsessive-compulsive disorder is an exhausting condition that causes great distress and can become debilitating when left untreated. Individuals may feel trapped by OCD obsessions and compulsions and consumed by the amount of time and mental effort exerted through simply trying to make it through the day.

Unfortunately, most of the time, compulsive efforts to relieve the discomfort created by OCD obsessions only reinforce the cycle and can make the distress and obsessions stronger. Counseling can help sufferers find relief, valuable education, and new tools to manage OCD symptoms and reduce their impact on your life.

Although OCD is most often a chronic condition, you can find great relief by developing insight and skills to battle obsessions and compulsions. Consider reaching out to our team today to find a counselor and begin your journey of discovery and renewed freedom.

And always remember – self-compassion goes a long way when learning new skills! No one is going to get it perfect, and that is okay. It is important to offer yourself grace when working toward new goals.

Someone may only have one type of OCD; another person may struggle with several of these. These themes can change over time, and you may develop away from one obsession into new ones. There are also varying levels of severity that may change in different seasons of life.

Often, during high-stress seasons, OCD symptoms may flare, a common phenomenon shared by many disorders. Some themes of OCD obsessions include contamination, sexual, harm/violence, scrupulosity (religious), sensorimotor, and responsibility. Here we will provide a quick overview of each theme listed, but more information is available on trusted websites, such as the International OCD Foundation, for those who are interested in a deeper dive.

Contamination OCD is one of the more widely known subtypes because of its exposure in popular culture. People with this subtype of obsession are preoccupied with cleanliness and sanitation and excessively worry about becoming contaminated with illness or germs. A person may feel “dirty” until they can sanitize to a satisfactory level, sometimes at the risk of skin harm from excessive washing.

Some people may need to wash a certain number of times or practice compulsions until they “feel right.” Another common compulsion related to contamination OCD is rigid behavior around eating, and a highly controlled environment to avoid feeling contaminated.

Sexual OCD involves distressing thoughts related to sexual orientation or unwanted images. People with this subtype may experience shame related to mental images of performing inappropriate sexual acts or participating in sexual ways not acceptable to the individual. Another common theme in this subtype includes doubt about sexual orientation.

An individual may have doubts about their identity and where the thoughts and feelings come from. Common compulsions related to this subtype include reassurance seeking, mental avoidance of unwanted images and thoughts, or monitoring their reactions to the thoughts.

People experiencing Harm/Violence OCD often experience disturbing thoughts and images related to harming themself or a loved one. Additionally, thoughts related to fear of loved ones being hurt if compulsions are not performed are common.

Compulsions related to harm OCD include mental efforts to avoid distressing material, avoiding triggers, avoiding objects that could be used to cause harm, seeking reassurance, and mental checking of one’s character or morals. Sometimes, seemingly unrelated compulsions may include ensuring the right outfit is picked out, or other elements of the environment are under control to prevent the terrible end of a loved one that day.

Scrupulosity is a form of OCD that focuses on faith and religion. The scrupulous individual is consumed by the fear of offending God, sinning, or morally compromising their beliefs. Disturbing images related to sinful acts commonly coincide with this subtype.

Individuals may perform compulsions through ritualistic patterns, such as saying the “right” prayers, repeatedly asking for forgiveness, mental assessments of one’s character and morals, reassurance seeking, mental rationalizing to “argue” with the thoughts, and repeating Scripture a preset number of times, or until it “feels right.”

Elements of prayer, scripture memorization, and repentance can look like regular behaviors for someone practicing faith, but they become compulsions when they are done ritualistically in an effort to offset the discomfort from obsessions, rather than stemming from devoted practice. The individual may also practice their faith alongside the ritualistic compulsions. The difference is subtle, but important to recognize.

Sensorimotor (somatic) OCD includes obsessions related to bodily functions and feelings. Individuals may become hyper-aware of automatic body processes such as blinking, heartbeat, and breathing, and compulsions may include trying to take control over blinking and breathing through patterns and rigid rules related to the number of blinks or breaths in a given amount of time.

Individuals may spend large amounts of time monitoring somatic processes, avoiding situations that trigger hyper-awareness, and seeking reassurance and validation through research and questioning others’ experiences.

Responsibility OCD involves feelings of being responsible to prevent bad things from happening, or fears and doubts related to your behaviors causing a negative event. Those suffering from this subtype often feel responsible for the emotions of those around them and try to control the environment to prevent a negative outcome.

Though their intentions are noble, symptoms of responsibility OCD can quickly become consuming, causing significant distress to the sufferer and tension in social relationships. Efforts to control the environment can overtake an individual’s time and energy, leaving little left over for necessary tasks, such as taking care of health, housekeeping, work, and social spheres.

Responsibility OCD can also coincide with memory OCD, where an individual may doubt their memories or believe they have forgotten something important. Those suffering from this subtype may believe they hit someone with their car or were responsible for a negative situation although there is no proof of it ever occurring. These individuals seek reassurance and compulsively check for evidence to relieve the doubts about their memories.

How do I know if it’s an obsession?

We all have intrusive thoughts sometimes – those thought darts that seem to come out of nowhere and attack our innermost value systems. The experience can be alarming, but individuals without OCD can move on and not become consumed by the thought. OCD obsessions are different because they become consuming. They are distressing, often disturbing thoughts that feel like an onslaught the sufferer cannot prevent.

Obsessions take up time and mental space, and lead to compulsions to alleviate the pain these intrusive thoughts are causing. Although compulsions can be ritualistic, time-consuming, and energy-draining, many individuals battling OCD find comfort in the control that compulsions offer, and in the temporary relief from anxiety. Unfortunately, the anxiety comes back quickly when the intrusive thoughts return, making the association with fear stronger.

The Reassurance Feedback Loop

Seeking and receiving reassurance from anxiety can be a helpful way to connect with a trusted friend, validate your feelings, or gain a new perspective. However, reassurance seeking can become a compulsion when it is done continually and with an attempt to relieve anxieties and doubts generated from OCD obsessions.

Just like with any other compulsion, the association between relief from anxiety and reassurance seeking can be powerful, leading to a rigid pattern of behavior. Seeking reassurance can become a trap when an individual can no longer trust their own thoughts and may even feel like they cannot trust their reality without the input of another.

It can become a form of dependence when we continually seek validation from others to find relief. It is important to learn tools that bolster your inner strengths and aid in overcoming doubts without needing reassurance from others. Freedom from the reassurance feedback loop can increase autonomy and the quality of your relationships.

Put your mind at ease

Remember, OCD obsessions often target our most cherished beliefs and values. If you are having uncomfortable intrusive thoughts and are wondering whether they inform your character, remind yourself that these thoughts are unwanted and direct contradictions to your inner value set.

They do not come from a hidden desire, and your feelings of anxiety or disgust related to these thoughts are evidence of this discrepancy. Don’t let OCD’s manipulations fool you. If you are distressed by the obsessions trying to take over your mind, you can find comfort remembering these intrusive thoughts are evidence of the very values they are trying to attack.

Consider counseling

In counseling, you can explore OCD symptoms and how they affect your life. Your counselor will help you add tools that can equip you for battling and overcoming obsessions and compulsions. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and Behavioral Therapy are two of the most common treatments that offer relief from OCD symptoms.

Many individuals also find relief through medication. Through counseling, you can find the support and training needed to find freedom from compulsions and minimize the impact of obsessions on your life. Suffering in silence can increase OCD’s power.

Although it can be uncomfortable or feel embarrassing to openly discuss and dissect OCD obsessions and compulsions with someone, you can find significant relief in shifting the power dynamic away from the OCD.

Conclusion

Obsessive-compulsive disorder is an exhausting condition that causes great distress and can become debilitating when left untreated. Individuals may feel trapped by OCD obsessions and compulsions and consumed by the amount of time and mental effort exerted through simply trying to make it through the day.

Unfortunately, most of the time, compulsive efforts to relieve the discomfort created by OCD obsessions only reinforce the cycle and can make the distress and obsessions stronger. Counseling can help sufferers find relief, valuable education, and new tools to manage OCD symptoms and reduce their impact on your life.

Although OCD is most often a chronic condition, you can find great relief by developing insight and skills to battle obsessions and compulsions. Consider reaching out to our team today to find a counselor and begin your journey of discovery and renewed freedom.

And always remember – self-compassion goes a long way when learning new skills! No one is going to get it perfect, and that is okay. It is important to offer yourself grace when working toward new goals.

item.title: What is OCD and Do I Have It?
item.description:
Have you ever wondered, “What is OCD and do I have it?” Perhaps thoughts like these sound familiar: “Did I turn the stove off before I left for work?” “I need to make sure the locks are secure one last time or something bad will happen to my family.” “My hands feel dirty even after five times washing.” “If I don’t follow through with [this compulsion], I may be responsible for a loved one’s death.”

Do these or similar thoughts occupy your mind each day? Do you find yourself spending too much time ruminating on thoughts you didn’t choose to reflect on; thoughts you can’t seem to get out of your head? Are those thoughts often accompanied by behaviors others might consider bizarre or confusing?

What is OCD?

OCD is a unique disorder that has origins in anxiety but is given its own category due to its complex profile. OCD is often chronic, meaning managing it will likely be a constant battle, but with help and treatment, symptoms can decrease significantly, and sufferers can find hope!

As the name suggests, it is characterized by both obsessions and compulsions. The obsessions take the form of intrusive, unwanted, and disturbing thoughts that cause significant anxiety for the sufferer. Compulsions are then used to find temporary relief from these thoughts, offering the sufferer the feeling of control.

Unfortunately, when compulsions are carried out, this only increases the likelihood of intrusive thoughts recurring and strengthens the association between the thoughts, anxiety, and relief found in the behaviors. As with any uncomfortable feeling or situation, when avoidance strategies are employed, we only strengthen our brain’s association with the feared object, convincing our brain that it must be truly dangerous.

This creates a strong feedback loop, causing our brains to obsess over the anxiety-producing thought or event to keep us safe. Although the brain is doing its job, these obsessions can cause suffering, and so the brain finds ways to avoid the painful feelings through compulsive behaviors. Remember – avoidance increases anxiety symptoms. The most helpful way to reduce these uncomfortable experiences is to face them with the help of a trained professional.

The person begins to ruminate on the intrusive thoughts, and significant amounts of time are spent worrying about the obsessions and practicing compulsions. Doubt is a common byproduct of the OCD experience, partly because these obsessions can lead you to doubt your morals, beliefs, reality, and even your humanity. But remember, the key thing to understand about obsessions is that they are intrusive – meaning unwanted. They are not a description of who you are or what you believe.

When intrusive thoughts wage war against your mind, the doubt and distress you have are evidence that these thoughts do not come from your character. They are not true beliefs or true moral dilemmas.

If we were to externalize intrusive thoughts and imagine them as a person, they would be manipulative, using your deepest-held values to create false allegations against you, using lies to confuse you and make you wonder whether your character ever had morals or integrity in the first place. And they would be doing all these things in the shadows, making you feel isolated and alone.

Hold on to your values and remember that intrusive thoughts are lies and they function like a bully. They don’t get to tell you who you are, and although at times it may not feel like it, they only hold as much power as you allow.

They do not come from a hidden desire, and your feelings of anxiety or disgust related to these thoughts are evidence of this discrepancy. Don’t let OCD’s manipulations fool you. If you are distressed by the obsessions trying to take over your mind, you can find comfort remembering these intrusive thoughts are evidence of the very values they are trying to attack.

Consider counseling

In counseling, you can explore OCD symptoms and how they affect your life. Your counselor will help you add tools that can equip you for battling and overcoming obsessions and compulsions. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and Behavioral Therapy are two of the most common treatments that offer relief from OCD symptoms.

Many individuals also find relief through medication. Through counseling, you can find the support and training needed to find freedom from compulsions and minimize the impact of obsessions on your life. Suffering in silence can increase OCD’s power.

Although it can be uncomfortable or feel embarrassing to openly discuss and dissect OCD obsessions and compulsions with someone, you can find significant relief in shifting the power dynamic away from the OCD.

Conclusion

Obsessive-compulsive disorder is an exhausting condition that causes great distress and can become debilitating when left untreated. Individuals may feel trapped by OCD obsessions and compulsions and consumed by the amount of time and mental effort exerted through simply trying to make it through the day.

Unfortunately, most of the time, compulsive efforts to relieve the discomfort created by OCD obsessions only reinforce the cycle and can make the distress and obsessions stronger. Counseling can help sufferers find relief, valuable education, and new tools to manage OCD symptoms and reduce their impact on your life.

Although OCD is most often a chronic condition, you can find great relief by developing insight and skills to battle obsessions and compulsions. Consider reaching out to our team today to find a counselor and begin your journey of discovery and renewed freedom.

And always remember – self-compassion goes a long way when learning new skills! No one is going to get it perfect, and that is okay. It is important to offer yourself grace when working toward new goals.

item.title: What is OCD and Do I Have It?
item.description:
Have you ever wondered, “What is OCD and do I have it?” Perhaps thoughts like these sound familiar: “Did I turn the stove off before I left for work?” “I need to make sure the locks are secure one last time or something bad will happen to my family.” “My hands feel dirty even after five times washing.” “If I don’t follow through with [this compulsion], I may be responsible for a loved one’s death.”

Do these or similar thoughts occupy your mind each day? Do you find yourself spending too much time ruminating on thoughts you didn’t choose to reflect on; thoughts you can’t seem to get out of your head? Are those thoughts often accompanied by behaviors others might consider bizarre or confusing?

These are just a few examples of the unsettling reality that obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) sufferers battle every day. This article will explore facts vs. common myths related to OCD, the different variations of this unique disorder, and what we can do about it.

What is OCD?

OCD is a unique disorder that has origins in anxiety but is given its own category due to its complex profile. OCD is often chronic, meaning managing it will likely be a constant battle, but with help and treatment, symptoms can decrease significantly, and sufferers can find hope!

As the name suggests, it is characterized by both obsessions and compulsions. The obsessions take the form of intrusive, unwanted, and disturbing thoughts that cause significant anxiety for the sufferer. Compulsions are then used to find temporary relief from these thoughts, offering the sufferer the feeling of control.

Unfortunately, when compulsions are carried out, this only increases the likelihood of intrusive thoughts recurring and strengthens the association between the thoughts, anxiety, and relief found in the behaviors. As with any uncomfortable feeling or situation, when avoidance strategies are employed, we only strengthen our brain’s association with the feared object, convincing our brain that it must be truly dangerous.

This creates a strong feedback loop, causing our brains to obsess over the anxiety-producing thought or event to keep us safe. Although the brain is doing its job, these obsessions can cause suffering, and so the brain finds ways to avoid the painful feelings through compulsive behaviors. Remember – avoidance increases anxiety symptoms. The most helpful way to reduce these uncomfortable experiences is to face them with the help of a trained professional.

Obsessions vs. Compulsions

Obsessions are preliminary to the compulsive behaviors individuals employ to alleviate discomfort. The person begins to ruminate on the intrusive thoughts, and significant amounts of time are spent worrying about the obsessions and practicing compulsions. Compulsions always come out of obsessions as a response to the discomfort they cause, though the link may appear subtle at times.

One thing to note about obsessions is they almost always manifest as an attack on something we deeply care about. This may be a faith belief, part of your character, someone you love, your health, and even your worth. These disturbing intrusive thoughts carry so much powerful weight because they strike to the heart of your deepest values and hidden fears.

Doubt is a common byproduct of the OCD experience, partly because these obsessions can lead you to doubt your morals, beliefs, reality, and even your humanity. But remember, the key thing to understand about obsessions is that they are intrusive – meaning unwanted. They are not a description of who you are or what you believe.

When intrusive thoughts wage war against your mind, the doubt and distress you have are evidence that these thoughts do not come from your character. They are not true beliefs or true moral dilemmas.

If we were to externalize intrusive thoughts and imagine them as a person, they would be manipulative, using your deepest-held values to create false allegations against you, using lies to confuse you and make you wonder whether your character ever had morals or integrity in the first place. And they would be doing all these things in the shadows, making you feel isolated and alone.

Hold on to your values and remember that intrusive thoughts are lies and they function like a bully. They don’t get to tell you who you are, and although at times it may not feel like it, they only hold as much power as you allow.

Common OCD Misconceptions

As with many mental health conditions, popular culture has created stereotypes that can increase confusion between the facts and the myths surrounding OCD. Many people will use the phrase “I’m so OCD” or “you are being OCD” to describe someone who tends toward perfectionism, values organization, or has challenges related to hypochondriasis or germophobia.

There is confusion about what OCD truly is, how the symptoms can present, and the severity of symptoms that lead to a diagnosis. Phrases and stereotypes like these can have a minimizing effect for those truly suffering with the condition.

The obsessional theme of organization and sanitization has gained popularity in recent years, leading many people to understand OCD from this one-dimensional frame. However, there are several different categories of obsessions, some of which may be surprising. If you wonder about OCD but don’t obsess about germs or organization, this list may interest you.

Common Obsessional Themes and Related Compulsions

This is a list of common OCD themes found in the DSM. This list is not exhaustive and, as with all mental health topics, everyone will experience the condition differently. Someone may only have one type of OCD; another person may struggle with several of these. These themes can change over time, and you may develop away from one obsession into new ones. There are also varying levels of severity that may change in different seasons of life.

Often, during high-stress seasons, OCD symptoms may flare, a common phenomenon shared by many disorders. Some themes of OCD obsessions include contamination, sexual, harm/violence, scrupulosity (religious), sensorimotor, and responsibility. Here we will provide a quick overview of each theme listed, but more information is available on trusted websites, such as the International OCD Foundation, for those who are interested in a deeper dive.

Contamination OCD is one of the more widely known subtypes because of its exposure in popular culture. People with this subtype of obsession are preoccupied with cleanliness and sanitation and excessively worry about becoming contaminated with illness or germs. A person may feel “dirty” until they can sanitize to a satisfactory level, sometimes at the risk of skin harm from excessive washing.

Some people may need to wash a certain number of times or practice compulsions until they “feel right.” Another common compulsion related to contamination OCD is rigid behavior around eating, and a highly controlled environment to avoid feeling contaminated.

Sexual OCD involves distressing thoughts related to sexual orientation or unwanted images. People with this subtype may experience shame related to mental images of performing inappropriate sexual acts or participating in sexual ways not acceptable to the individual. Another common theme in this subtype includes doubt about sexual orientation.

An individual may have doubts about their identity and where the thoughts and feelings come from. Common compulsions related to this subtype include reassurance seeking, mental avoidance of unwanted images and thoughts, or monitoring their reactions to the thoughts.

People experiencing Harm/Violence OCD often experience disturbing thoughts and images related to harming themself or a loved one. Additionally, thoughts related to fear of loved ones being hurt if compulsions are not performed are common.

Compulsions related to harm OCD include mental efforts to avoid distressing material, avoiding triggers, avoiding objects that could be used to cause harm, seeking reassurance, and mental checking of one’s character or morals. Sometimes, seemingly unrelated compulsions may include ensuring the right outfit is picked out, or other elements of the environment are under control to prevent the terrible end of a loved one that day.

Scrupulosity is a form of OCD that focuses on faith and religion. The scrupulous individual is consumed by the fear of offending God, sinning, or morally compromising their beliefs. Disturbing images related to sinful acts commonly coincide with this subtype.

Individuals may perform compulsions through ritualistic patterns, such as saying the “right” prayers, repeatedly asking for forgiveness, mental assessments of one’s character and morals, reassurance seeking, mental rationalizing to “argue” with the thoughts, and repeating Scripture a preset number of times, or until it “feels right.”

Elements of prayer, scripture memorization, and repentance can look like regular behaviors for someone practicing faith, but they become compulsions when they are done ritualistically in an effort to offset the discomfort from obsessions, rather than stemming from devoted practice. The individual may also practice their faith alongside the ritualistic compulsions. The difference is subtle, but important to recognize.

Sensorimotor (somatic) OCD includes obsessions related to bodily functions and feelings. Individuals may become hyper-aware of automatic body processes such as blinking, heartbeat, and breathing, and compulsions may include trying to take control over blinking and breathing through patterns and rigid rules related to the number of blinks or breaths in a given amount of time.

Individuals may spend large amounts of time monitoring somatic processes, avoiding situations that trigger hyper-awareness, and seeking reassurance and validation through research and questioning others’ experiences.

Responsibility OCD involves feelings of being responsible to prevent bad things from happening, or fears and doubts related to your behaviors causing a negative event. Those suffering from this subtype often feel responsible for the emotions of those around them and try to control the environment to prevent a negative outcome.

Though their intentions are noble, symptoms of responsibility OCD can quickly become consuming, causing significant distress to the sufferer and tension in social relationships. Efforts to control the environment can overtake an individual’s time and energy, leaving little left over for necessary tasks, such as taking care of health, housekeeping, work, and social spheres.

Responsibility OCD can also coincide with memory OCD, where an individual may doubt their memories or believe they have forgotten something important. Those suffering from this subtype may believe they hit someone with their car or were responsible for a negative situation although there is no proof of it ever occurring. These individuals seek reassurance and compulsively check for evidence to relieve the doubts about their memories.

How do I know if it’s an obsession?

We all have intrusive thoughts sometimes – those thought darts that seem to come out of nowhere and attack our innermost value systems. The experience can be alarming, but individuals without OCD can move on and not become consumed by the thought. OCD obsessions are different because they become consuming. They are distressing, often disturbing thoughts that feel like an onslaught the sufferer cannot prevent.

Obsessions take up time and mental space, and lead to compulsions to alleviate the pain these intrusive thoughts are causing. Although compulsions can be ritualistic, time-consuming, and energy-draining, many individuals battling OCD find comfort in the control that compulsions offer, and in the temporary relief from anxiety. Unfortunately, the anxiety comes back quickly when the intrusive thoughts return, making the association with fear stronger.

The Reassurance Feedback Loop

Seeking and receiving reassurance from anxiety can be a helpful way to connect with a trusted friend, validate your feelings, or gain a new perspective. However, reassurance seeking can become a compulsion when it is done continually and with an attempt to relieve anxieties and doubts generated from OCD obsessions.

Just like with any other compulsion, the association between relief from anxiety and reassurance seeking can be powerful, leading to a rigid pattern of behavior. Seeking reassurance can become a trap when an individual can no longer trust their own thoughts and may even feel like they cannot trust their reality without the input of another.

It can become a form of dependence when we continually seek validation from others to find relief. It is important to learn tools that bolster your inner strengths and aid in overcoming doubts without needing reassurance from others. Freedom from the reassurance feedback loop can increase autonomy and the quality of your relationships.

Put your mind at ease

Remember, OCD obsessions often target our most cherished beliefs and values. If you are having uncomfortable intrusive thoughts and are wondering whether they inform your character, remind yourself that these thoughts are unwanted and direct contradictions to your inner value set.

They do not come from a hidden desire, and your feelings of anxiety or disgust related to these thoughts are evidence of this discrepancy. Don’t let OCD’s manipulations fool you. If you are distressed by the obsessions trying to take over your mind, you can find comfort remembering these intrusive thoughts are evidence of the very values they are trying to attack.

Consider counseling

In counseling, you can explore OCD symptoms and how they affect your life. Your counselor will help you add tools that can equip you for battling and overcoming obsessions and compulsions. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and Behavioral Therapy are two of the most common treatments that offer relief from OCD symptoms.

Many individuals also find relief through medication. Through counseling, you can find the support and training needed to find freedom from compulsions and minimize the impact of obsessions on your life. Suffering in silence can increase OCD’s power.

Although it can be uncomfortable or feel embarrassing to openly discuss and dissect OCD obsessions and compulsions with someone, you can find significant relief in shifting the power dynamic away from the OCD.

Conclusion

Obsessive-compulsive disorder is an exhausting condition that causes great distress and can become debilitating when left untreated. Individuals may feel trapped by OCD obsessions and compulsions and consumed by the amount of time and mental effort exerted through simply trying to make it through the day.

Unfortunately, most of the time, compulsive efforts to relieve the discomfort created by OCD obsessions only reinforce the cycle and can make the distress and obsessions stronger. Counseling can help sufferers find relief, valuable education, and new tools to manage OCD symptoms and reduce their impact on your life.

Although OCD is most often a chronic condition, you can find great relief by developing insight and skills to battle obsessions and compulsions. Consider reaching out to our team today to find a counselor and begin your journey of discovery and renewed freedom.

And always remember – self-compassion goes a long way when learning new skills! No one is going to get it perfect, and that is okay. It is important to offer yourself grace when working toward new goals.

item.title: Feeling Lonely: Practical Ways to Build Real Friendships
item.description:
In elementary school, you could walk up to someone on the playground and ask, “Do you want to play?” and by the time the bell rang, you’d have a new friend. In college, proximity did most of the work for you. Because you lived, went to school with, and sometimes worked alongside people on campus, you naturally grew into friendship with them without much effort.

But there comes a point in adulthood when you realize that friendships don’t come as automatically as they used to. And if you’re a busy woman with a job or a family, you know that making friendships can be difficult.

So how do you build real friendships as a busy adult? Here’s where to start.

Start with who you are

One of the biggest obstacles to true friendship is the need for performance. You may not even realize you’re doing it, but many people try to be what they think they should be rather than who they are.

They might want to have the label of the easy, strong, or funny one. So, they curate their behaviors to support these labels to attract and impress others. And while it’s good to be easy-going, strong, and humorous authentically, real friendships aren’t built on false performances.

If you don’t know who you truly are, you will unconsciously shape yourself to fit whomever you’re around. You will become whatever they want or expect you to be, not who you are, or who God wants you to be. And that creates only surface-level connections, not deep and meaningful relationships.

Figuring out who you really are might not be as easy as it sounds. You must first remove yourself from the voices and influences around you to decide what you actually value. What’s important to you? What do you actually enjoy doing? What drains you? Where do you feel most like yourself?

It might seem odd that you have to think about who the real you is because you live with yourself every day. But when you separate your true identity from the influences around you, you might be surprised that your true identity is but a shadow of your public persona.

And when you develop a strong sense of self, you will naturally attract people who connect to the real you.

Learn safe vulnerability

There’s a fine line when it comes to emotional risk, but to thrive in friendships, you must learn how to be vulnerable while mitigating that risk.

Vulnerability is sometimes mistaken for trauma dumping on someone you just met. While this is usually not a successful way to build a bond with others, you don’t build intimacy by staying surface-level friends forever, either.

Healthy vulnerability forms when you share small personal truths or allow someone to see your authentic emotions, rather than the mask you usually wear. This transparency allows people to connect with the real you, and that not only builds true friendship but also confidence. As people accept you in your vulnerability, you are reinforcing to yourself that you’re worthy of love.

If you struggle with this, you’ve likely experienced past rejection or abandonment. Sometimes you learn early in childhood that being honest and authentic can result in negative consequences.

Be the Friend You’re Praying For

If you are lonely and want to attract a good, honest, fun-loving person who loves to watch action films, then be that person. People with like-mindedness will be attracted to you because they will see similarities in themselves.

God created Eve when Adam was busy going about his Father’s business. When you are busy being your authentic self, the one God wants you to be, He will guide and direct you into relationships that will benefit your work and enhance your life.

And once you meet someone with potential friend qualities, model what you want the next step to look like. Follow up with people after you meet them. Initiate plans. Friendships require time, effort, and initiative, and in order to reap the reward, you have to be willing to put in the effort.

Look in all the right places

Where you look for friendships matters more than you might think. Friendships tend to grow where people already share something in common, such as values, interests, or life stages.

If your faith is important to you and you’re hoping to build a friendship with other Christians who will not only share your values but also encourage your faith, the bar is probably not the most effective place to look. While it’s certainly possible to meet good, compatible people anywhere, you’re much more likely to find someone spiritually minded in places where faith is valued.

Many friendships end or never get started because the people involved are vastly different in their values. Of course, there are exceptions to this rule, and deep friendships can form out of respectful disagreement. These relationships can even make you grow in your beliefs and tolerance, but most friendships are built on some commonality.

If you’ve been discriminated against, made fun of, or dismissed because of your beliefs, your lifestyle, or hobbies, consider going to places where like-minded people naturally congregate. Maybe you’re considered “unconventional” by some. But instead of allowing your uniqueness to be a liability, find a community that will celebrate you and your unique qualities.

Be patient and consistent

One of the most discouraging things about adult friendships is that they often take longer to develop than friendships among young people. Childhood friendships are formed quickly because you spend hours together in a classroom. As adults, life is much busier, and relationships take more time to develop.

It can take several attempts before you find people who truly click with you. But consistency is key. Many adult friendships develop because you see the same people regularly. You might meet someone once and enjoy talking with them, but it is likely to take several conversations before you begin to feel comfortable with each other.

Real friendships grow naturally through a culmination of small moments. Research suggests that it takes roughly fifty hours of shared time together to move past the polite phase into a true friendship, so consider joining groups that meet weekly, such as a Bible study or social club.

Patience is also required when a text goes unanswered or an invitation isn’t accepted. In those moments that seem discouraging, try not to take it personally. Adult schedules are complex, and a “no” isn’t always a reflection of someone’s feelings toward you but more of their current lifestyle.

Loneliness can be deeply rooted

Sometimes the struggle to form friendships can’t be fixed with logistics and strategy. Sometimes the root of this lonely feeling is something that’s inside of you, such as a fear of commitment or a reflection of past wounds. It might be a culmination of years of insecurities or a coping skills deficit.

If your lack of community is due to deeper reasons than just being “new in town”, remember that God sees you fully and He loves you completely. He knows your faults, weird habits, fears, and attachment style. He knows your hurts and the reasons you can’t commit. And the best news is that He is your friend.

He loves you just as you are, in your raw, unfiltered form. He can help you to work through those other things. Those obstacles that hold you back from authentic connections here on Earth.

Therapy

If this is where you find yourself, feeling stuck in loneliness despite wanting meaningful friendships, therapy can help.

Your therapist can guide you as you explore the experiences that shaped your view of relationships and the obstacles that might be interfering with genuine connections. Therapy can help you to heal past attachment wounds and work through social anxiety.

Call our offices today if you’re feeling lonely. You can learn more about how a therapist can help you become a better friend and find meaningful and healthy relationships.

Resources:
“How many hours does it take to make a friend?” https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/0265407518761225

item.title: Strangely Specific Signs of Social Anxiety
item.description:
There comes a time in everyone’s life when they must confront the thing that makes them most anxious. This might be traveling by airplane, having to address a room of hundreds of people, or, for those with social anxiety, it might be something as simple as answering the phone. The signs of social anxiety can be so unexpected that it’s easy to be dismissive of someone’s struggle.

People with social anxiety frequently think of themselves as introverted or even quirky because they haven’t found a sufficient explanation for their anxieties. Whatever is happening beneath the surface, it is something that can be resolved. It may feel debilitating now, but it doesn’t have to stay that way.

Imperfect Comparisons

How often do we look at our peers and marvel at their confidence, tenacity, or success? We might envy their communication skills or their ability to hold the attention of the entire room when they speak. We can’t see their anxiety each time they speak, or the long road they have taken to find success.

It’s fine to compare ourselves to others if it inspires us to improve certain things. However, comparison so often makes us feel worse about ourselves, even when we can’t see things like hidden social anxiety.

Outwardly, a person might not display any signs of social anxiety, but just because we cannot see it does not mean it isn’t there. Perhaps they spent decades confronting their fears before they reached the point where they could confidently communicate with crowds. It’s not a bad idea to aspire to have someone else’s levels of confidence or communication skills. Keep in mind, though, that people are like icebergs; only a small part of them is visible.

Filling in the Gaps

Our brains have a wonderful ability to fill in the gaps when it comes to things we don’t understand or can’t fully see. This is how we make assumptions about others: our brain takes the information presented to it and guesses the rest.

Sometimes we are correct in our assumptions. It’s safe to assume that the person who is the life and soul of a party simply loves the limelight. However, what if that person is deeply depressed and doing an excellent job of covering up? Sometimes the root of our social anxiety lies in the mistaken assumptions our brains have made about ourselves and others.

For example, on a date, there are awkward moments of silence. This is normal and doesn’t necessarily mean anything bad. However, your brain might convince you that your date is quiet because he finds you boring. The truth is likely that they are quiet because they are also making assumptions about you.

In psychology, this is called a cognitive distortion. It is when a person’s brain habitually fills in the gaps in faulty ways. There are different kinds of cognitive distortions, but almost all of them are related to social anxiety.

When we assume that we know what others think about us, that is a cognitive distortion known as mind-reading. Expecting the worst possible outcome to every situation is a cognitive distortion known as catastrophizing, and taking the blame for things that couldn’t possibly be our fault is personalization.

Treating Social Anxiety

Social anxiety is more complicated than other forms of anxiety because of the cognitive distortions that are layered into it. We experience the physical effects of general anxiety, like the elevated heartbeat, sweaty hands and back, and shallow breathing.

We also experience emotional turmoil related to cognitive distortions, like having low self-worth, being easily embarrassed, and feeling exposed and insecure. This means that each person with social anxiety has any number of cognitive distortions fueling their fears. To treat the anxiety, you must get to the root of each distortion and challenge it.

Unfortunately, many people instinctively treat their social anxiety through avoidance, by rehearsing conversations before having them, or by ruminating on events once they are passed. Avoiding a party, for example, is another way of saying, “I’m not going because I know I would be judged by everyone there.”

Cognitive distortions sound so confident and assured, and avoidance behaviors, or ruminating and rehearsing behaviors, give the distortions too much weight. If you had confronted your thinking and attended the party, you would have given your brain the chance to calm down and prove to it that there was no real threat. It’s a complicated process to treat social anxiety, but perhaps the place to start is learning to recognize it.

Noticing the Signs of Social Anxiety

The majority of people who classify themselves as shy or introverted actually have untreated social anxiety. When we begin to see the signs of social anxiety in ourselves, we can begin to challenge the cognitive distortions behind them. The signs of social anxiety are often a combination of a cognitive distortion and an anxious action.

For example, people with social anxiety frequently cancel their plans at the last moment. This is avoidance behavior that usually stems from overthinking. The person wants to make their friends happy, so they initially agree to any and every suggestion. Meanwhile, they start catastrophizing or feeling the pressure to be perfect in a social situation, and they can’t face the pressure.

Just like with general anxiety, one of the clear signs of social anxiety is nervous fidgeting. The person gets a build-up of nervous energy and needs to discharge it with physical activity. There is no cognitive distortion attached to this behavior; it is simply a form of self-soothing.

Social anxiety is almost always visible in a person’s body language or speech, but most frequently it shows up as uncontrollable blushing. Whenever the person feels the spotlight on them, even by way of ordinary eye contact or polite interest, blood rushes to their face, and they can’t help but blush. Others might find it endearing, but for the person who can’t control their blushing, it is a physical nightmare.

One of the most common cognitive distortions related to social anxiety is the unshakable belief that others find you awkward or dull. Once again, this is mind-reading: you believe you know exactly what others think of you. Unfortunately, when you believe others find you awkward or uninteresting, your body language begins to stiffen, you avoid eye contact, and you forget how to interact naturally, making you come across as strange or cold.

On the topic of body language, people with social anxiety are usually found huddling on the outskirts of the group, with their shoulders hunched and jaws clenched. They are literally trying to shrink down their presence to avoid being noticed. There could be any number of cognitive distortions behind thinking like this, but it is almost certain that some kind of wrong thinking is inflating their social anxiety.

Lastly, one of the most common signs of social anxiety is that people stay on the move. They go from one group to the next, never staying long enough to be drawn into a conversation, and always hanging on the outskirts. They make sure that they never settle because their instinct is to escape the situation. Much like fidgeting, they are turning their nervous energy into motion and movement.

Truth and Freedom

Social anxiety is complex, but it is treatable. Our cognitive distortions might inflate the perceived threats in our heads, but it is possible to confront these thoughts and challenge them. When we do that, we begin to see and understand things as they truly are, not as we believed them to be. As the Scripture confirms, when we know the truth, it will set us free. (John 8:32) You are only as restricted by social anxiety as you allow yourself to be; freedom is waiting for you.

It’s not always easy to recognize the signs of social anxiety, much less confront the beliefs behind it. If you would like support navigating these challenges, I invite you to contact my office to schedule a session with me, Joseph Bennett, MAMFC, MARE, LPC. My team is warm, welcoming, and happy to make the process feel easy and comfortable from the first conversation.

Photos:
“Anxiety”, Courtesy of Markus Winkler, Unsplash.com, CC0 License; “Scrambled Thoughts”, Courtesy of Zyanya Citlalli, Unsplash.com, Unsplash+ License

The post Strangely Specific Signs of Social Anxiety appeared first on Texas Christian Counseling.

item.title: When to Seek Binge-Eating Treatment
item.description:
Binge-eating disorder is a serious mental health condition that typically requires professional counseling to work through, but it is possible to overcome the eating disorder. However, people often miss the signs or wait too long to seek binge-eating treatment.

Know the signs of binge-eating disorder, take your treatment seriously, and lean on your faith in God and His Son, Jesus Christ, and you will take your life back.

What are the signs of binge-eating disorder?

Sometimes the line between overeating (which many people do throughout the year) and binge-eating becomes blurred. Overeating may or may not be intentional and is typically contained in a single meal.

Binge-eating, however, can happen during a span of two hours. During a binge, you may consume hundreds or thousands of calories with no sensation of your stomach being full. Worse, you may zone out during the binge and suddenly realize what you have done hours later.

Do any of these signs of binge-eating disorder sound familiar?

  • Do you binge on food in a short period of time?
  • Do you keep your binges a secret?
  • Do you feel sick, ashamed, guilty, or distressed after a binge?
  • Do you frequently zone out during a binge?
  • Do you binge often?

If you answered yes to most of these questions, it might be time to seek treatment.

Do I need treatment?

The best indicator of whether you need treatment is your emotions after a binge. Do you feel ashamed or guilty? Are you depressed and feel like your life is out of control? These are the mental aspects of an eating disorder.

What about the physical complications from bingeing? Your primary care physician will complete bloodwork and a physical exam to rule out any medical conditions related to the bingeing behavior before diagnosing. Bingeing can lead to obesity, joint pain, digestive issues, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and other grave conditions.

Once you know that you need treatment, you can begin to proactively make lifestyle changes even before your first appointment with a specialist. The following is a list of some of our top tips:

Be mindful of hunger An episode of binge-eating may or may not happen when you are hungry. However, being aware of your hunger cues can help you be mindful of when you are reaching the point when your stomach is full.

Has it been a few hours since you last ate? Is your stomach growling or feeling empty? If your last meal consisted of unhealthy junk foods, your blood sugar might crash, leaving you dizzy, lightheaded, and faint. This can set you up for a binge to counteract the effects of low blood sugar.

Know your trigger foods and emotions If your emotions are running high, they can trigger a binge. Feeling stressed, overwhelmed, lonely, sad, hurt, or angry can leave you wanting something to take away the emotion.

You are looking for a way to fill your heart, but instead of turning to God and his word, you reach (sometimes unconsciously) for comfort food. If you find yourself bingeing on the same foods every time, consider removing those foods from your home until you feel confident in your treatment and more in control.

Slow down and focus When you catch yourself in the pantry, refrigerator, or car looking for a place to grab a quick bite, stop and consider your surroundings and mood. Are you actually hungry, or are you trying to avoid a particular emotion?

When you sit down to eat, eliminate all distractions to avoid zoning out during the meal. Turn off your phone, television, and other screens and focus on the portion in front of you. If you must eat in the car, pack your meal in a portion-controlled container.

Journal your food intake Sometimes change is preceded by an “ah-ha” moment, the moment you realize that you must change or else. There is something powerful in the “ah-ha” moment. It propels you to make better choices, learn new things, and stop making excuses.

Journaling your daily meals and snacks could be your “ah-ha” moment. Forcing yourself to write down every bite during a binge could be the eye-opener you need to make a change. Jot down your mood when the binge began and how you felt afterward. Analyzing your emotions can lead to a breakthrough.

Plan your meals Bingeing leaves you feeling out of control. If you sit down once a week and plan out your meals and snacks (leaving it flexible), you are more likely to stick to the plan, even on the busiest days. Knowing you have something good to look forward to every few hours may head off a binge. Plan to eat every three to four hours to keep your blood sugar constant.

Train your body When you exercise, your appetite decreases as hunger hormones shift. If the word exercise gives you images of leotard-clad women bouncing around to aerobics music, then think of it as training your body.

God wants us to train both our physical body to keep it fit and ready for His service, and our spiritual body. “Physical training is good, but training for godliness is much better, promising benefits in this life and in the life to come.” (1 Timothy 4:8 NLT)

These are a few activities you can try before and during binge-eating treatment. But once you agree to an appointment with an eating disorder therapist, what can you expect during your sessions?

What can I expect from binge-eating treatment?

Each client is unique, and we tailor our treatment plans to meet your needs. Some of the therapies listed below will not pertain to your treatment plan, but others will become the foundation of your recovery with Jesus Christ as the cornerstone.

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) – CBT has been proven to be beneficial in helping people with mental conditions across the board, from anxiety and depression to Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder to eating disorders.

CBT works with the negative thoughts that run through our minds before a binge. It teaches us how to catch those thoughts and change the verbiage, thus changing the resulting behavioral pattern. Since bingeing is, in part, a condition based on the behavior, changing the thoughts preceding the binge should change the binge-eating behavior.

Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) – DBT works to make the client aware of the present moment and stop zoning out, particularly during a binge. The therapy also uses the client’s tolerance by slowly increasing it, so they learn to face their emotions head-on instead of escaping from them. DBT is used to teach clients communication skills for conflict resolution.

Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT) – IPT focuses on the communication and relationship issues that may be affecting the client and possibly at the root of the eating disorder. When we have problems in our relationships, it can result in psychological problems and negative behaviors. IPT gets to the origin of these issues and uses new problem-solving skills to strengthen relationships and resolve conflicts.

Group Counseling – Group counseling provides support, advice, encouragement, and psychological techniques. Clients feel safe in smaller groups to share with others dealing with binge-eating and various eating disorders. Each session is confidential and hosted by a licensed counselor.

Each of our counselors treats binge-eating disorder in their own way and personalizes their treatments to the client. However, you always have a say in how you feel about a particular treatment strategy.

When You Need Treatment

The first step to overcoming binge-eating is realizing you need help. The second step is seeking assistance in breaking the cycle of this severe eating disorder before it leads to physical and mental illnesses.

Reach out to one of our counselors today to discuss diagnosis and treatment options. Even if you have tried counseling before, give us a call. We customize your treatment plan while helping you grow in your faith and relationship with Jesus. Together, we can beat binge-eating disorder.

item.title: Self-Growth and Mental Health in Teen Girls: Finding Strength in the Journey
item.description:
Teen girls are navigating a world that sends competing messages about who they should be and what they should look like. This shows up in their mental health, and they often spiral downward when it becomes overwhelming. Self-growth during the teenage years is a process filled with questions, setbacks, and moments of unexpected clarity.

When mental health challenges present themselves beneath the surface, getting through the day can feel discouraging. The expectation of growing, healing, and becoming takes on a different weight when emotional resources are already running thin. Adults who love and support teen girls can help them move forward with intention and hope by understanding the connection between mental wellness and personal development.

The Mental Health Landscape for Teen Girls Today

Anxiety, depression, and emotional distress have been on the rise among teen girls over the past decade. These challenges stem from social media exposure, academic pressure, and relational instability, all of which play significant roles in a teen girl’s life. Each of these pressures shapes a girl’s sense of identity before she has had the chance to develop fully.

Teen girls can find themselves putting on a confident front on the outside and quietly falling apart on the inside. Sometimes they measure their words against someone else’s highlight reel and feel as though they have come up short. The attitudes that teen girls absorb about appearance, achievement, and likability set impossible standards that no person can consistently meet. These leave young women feeling unseen and exhausted in equal measure.

Christian counselors try to recognize this pattern and understand that healing must address the emotional and spiritual roots of these pressures. Reaching out for support is not a detour away from development – it is where the true work begins.

What makes this so difficult is that many teen girls do not yet have the language for what they are experiencing. They know something feels off, but putting words to it takes time, safety, and the presence of someone willing to listen without rushing them toward an answer. With support, teen girls can be reminded that they are known and wonderfully made by God.

For You formed my inward parts; You wove me in my mother’s womb. I will give thanks to You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made; Wonderful are Your works, And my soul knows it very well. – Psalm 139:13-14, NASB

What Self-Growth Actually Looks Like for Teen Girls

Any discussions about personal development often bring to mind a picture of dramatic, sudden transformation. This picture shows a clear before-and-after and a polished version of something that was once broken. For teen girls, this growth doesn’t look that simple. It’s experienced in the quieter, more ordinary moments, such as:

  • Speaking honestly instead of staying silent to keep the peace.
  • The willingness to sit with discomfort rather than numbing it.
  • The decision to reach out to a trusted adult when isolation would be easier.

None of these moments will make the highlight reel. They are small, quiet, and easily overlooked. But they are the things that build a young woman from the inside out. Over time, they add up to something that pressure and outside opinions cannot easily take away.

At this stage of life, progress is learning to recognize one’s own emotional patterns and to build the ability to manage them more skillfully. This forms a sense of self that does not collapse under outside pressure. Self-growth is not a fast process, and it doesn’t always feel like there’s any real movement forward. It requires navigating uncertainty, experiencing failure, and choosing to keep going anyway. This kind of perseverance is its own form of strength.

The Connection Between Self-Growth and Mental Health Healing

Understanding that addressing her mental health and doing the inner work of becoming are not two separate journeys is an important realization that will shift everything for teen girls. Anxiety, depression, and emotional dysregulation that go unaddressed become roadblocks on the path to confidence and healthy relationships. These challenges can quietly erode a young girl’s sense of identity as well.

When a teen girl begins to invest in herself by understanding her patterns, naming her emotions, and learning her values, her mental health begins to stabilize. The process of connecting self-growth and mental health centers on strengthening what is already present and building the inner resources that carry her through each season.

This kind of internal investment does not happen all at once. It is built slowly, through repeated choices to stay curious about herself rather than critical, and to reach toward healing even when it feels out of reach.

Christian counselors are trained to lead teen girls in an integrative way by looking at the whole person rather than treating each challenge as a separate problem. They understand that this journey for teen girls is deeply personal, but can be guided with genuine compassion and grounded in faith. Then they can experience the joy and peace described in Romans:

Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you will abound in hope by the power of the Holy Spirit. – Romans 15:13, NASB

How Adults Can Walk Alongside Teen Girls in This Season

Parents and mentors can play a significant role in a teen girl’s mental health and development, even though it may not appear that way from the outside. Adolescence is a season for teen girls where connections are craved and rejected at the same time. She may push away the relationship she needs as she tries to form her own identity by testing the strength of the ones she already has.

When adults remain steady and emotionally present for these girls, it builds the kind of safety that allows real growth to take root over time. The goal is to stay close without trying to solve her problems or manage her experience.

This balance is easier to describe than it is to practice. Christian counselors work with teen girls and their families to develop communication skills and create an environment where a young girl feels heard, steady, and free to grow at her own pace.

Support for Teen Girls

The teenage years are not meant to be easy, but they shouldn’t be survived in isolation. Teen girls who wrestle with their mental health while navigating toward becoming who they are meant to be face a layered and demanding process. The important part is that these young girls are not navigating this process alone.

Support from trusted adults, a community of faith, and professionals who understand these challenges can help them learn to work through the hard moments and develop tools to carry them forward.

Scripture reminds us that God is not absent from the hard and confusing season of growing up. He meets these girls exactly where they are and can walk them through every part of the process, whether it is a setback or a breakthrough.

Faith does not remove the hard parts of adolescence, but it does mean that no girl has to face them without a God who sees her fully and walks with her completely. “The Lord is the one who goes ahead of you; He will be with you. He will not fail you or forsake you. Do not fear or be dismayed.” (Deuteronomy 31:8, NASB) That kind of presence changes everything about how the hard work gets done.

One of the most important decisions a teen girl can make on the road toward growth is reaching out. If your teen girl is wrestling with self-growth issues, contact our reception team today and learn how we can help.
