Even if you do not arrive together or sit together, your children will see that you both still support them in their endeavors. Decide on a reward system at your home and give your children your expectations of their behavior, but also be aware of your ex’s rules at their home.

Consider a mediator if you find it challenging to agree with the other parent. You may need someone else to help with exchanging the children temporarily until the newness of the separation and divorce is less emotionally charged and raw.

Keep schedules consistent

Children need routine to feel secure and stable in their environment and in relationships. Try to keep their daily and weekly schedules consistent, so they know what to expect.

For example, if you choose a coparenting schedule where the parents alternate weeks, keep that schedule. If something changes, inform your children about the change and whether it is temporary (for example, a parent has to travel for work and cannot take them that week) or permanent (the new schedule will be split into Sunday through Wednesday with Mom and Thursday through Sunday afternoon with Dad).

For teen children, consider asking them about what works better for them. It may be that walking home to Mom’s house after school is easier than waiting for the school bus to get dropped off at Dad’s home. Although you want to keep schedules consistent, both parents should remain flexible and be willing to change to make things smoother for the family.

Serve as a family

Family can be more than blood-related individuals. During and after a divorce is a good time to lean further into your church family.

Take your children to church and serve as a family in various ministries in and outside of the church. Your children learn to think about others, empathize, and see how they can be the hands and feet of Jesus to a hurting world. Schedule volunteer opportunities into your calendar and hang them up where the children can see.

Give them as much importance as you do doctor appointments or school. When children grow up doing good and showing Christ’s kindness to others in a family where religious beliefs are deemed necessary, the children are at a decreased risk of developing suicidal ideation or attempts, according to a study published in 2019 in Ethics Med Public Health.

Ask your church or local community center about volunteer opportunities. If you do not have a home church, ask friends and family about their churches or visit churches in your area that preach the Word of God and have a thriving children’s ministry.

Seek help as a family

Although it can be challenging, consider family counseling during or after divorce to help make coparenting smoother. Both parents can attend a few sessions with their children and work with a counselor to agree on schedules and expectations. After a divorce, as parents begin to date others and possibly remarry, family counseling can help in the introduction of new people into the children’s lives and blended family scenarios.

By seeking help as a family, you are reassuring your children that you want what is best for them and are willing to admit when you need help. Children learn life skills that will help them build emotional resilience.

Christian Counseling During and After Divorce

Children of divorce can struggle with the transition. Depending on the circumstances, these children may blame themselves, feel unseen, or even be angry. It’s okay to seek help from an unbiased third party at this time. A Christian counselor can help the whole family in the transition during and after divorce.

Contact our facility today to schedule a session with a counselor specializing in divorce and family counseling.

Resources:
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7430948/

item.title: Emotional Self Regulation: Refreshing Habits for a Challenging Year
item.description:
The year 2026 has already proven to be a year when so many things are changing, not only here in the United States, but globally. It seems now more than ever that everything is revolving around being digital-first and being prepared for the most unexpected things to change anytime.

As you fight daily to stay afloat, balancing work, friendships, and the endless stream of online content that never seems to pause, you need some kind of grounding technique to keep you balanced.

In this environment, emotional self-regulation is more important than ever. It is the skill of managing your feelings in ways that help you stay grounded, make better decisions, and protect your mental health.

This year calls for habits that feel fresh, practical, and suited to modern life. Here are a few helpful ideas to get you started:

Start with a Digital Detox Minute

Instead of long breaks from technology, try one minute each day where you completely disconnect. No phone, no music, no scrolling. Just sixty seconds of silence. This short pause helps reset your brain and gives you space to notice how you are feeling. It is surprising how much clarity comes from such a small habit.

Practice Micro Gratitude

Gratitude lists have been around for years, but in 2026, the trend is micro-gratitude. Instead of writing down three big things, focus on one tiny detail each day. It could be the taste of your morning coffee, the way sunlight hits your desk, or a funny text from a friend.

Use Mood Pairing with Music

Music has always been a powerful tool, but this year, many young people are experimenting with mood pairing. Instead of only listening to upbeat songs when you feel low, try matching your playlist to your current mood first. If you feel sad, play a slow track that reflects that emotion. Then gradually move to more uplifting songs. This will help you process emotions instead of forcing them away.

Try Movement Snacks

Exercise is known to support mental health, but long workouts are not always realistic. Movement snacks are short bursts of activity spread throughout the day. Stretching for two minutes between classes, dancing to one song before bed, or walking around the block after lunch. These small actions regulate stress hormones and improve emotional self-regulation by keeping your body and mind connected.

Practice Reverse Journaling

Instead of writing about your day, write about what you want tomorrow to feel like. This habit sets an emotional intention and helps you prepare mentally. For example, you might write, “Tomorrow I want to feel calm during my presentation.” This practice trains your brain to focus on emotional goals, not just tasks.

Support for Emotional Self-Regulation

The pace of life has accelerated, and young people are exposed to more information, opinions, and pressures than any generation before. Social media trends change daily, global events reach us instantly, and personal expectations are higher than ever. Without emotional self-regulation, it is easy to feel drained or disconnected.

Developing these habits now is not just about surviving the year. It is about building resilience for the future. Emotional self-regulation helps you respond thoughtfully instead of reacting impulsively. It strengthens relationships, improves focus, and protects mental health in a world that rarely slows down.

Trying new habits is a great start, but sometimes professional guidance is the best way to build lasting skills. If you feel ready to set mental health goals and want support to get started, help is available right here. Professionals are ready to work with you in person or virtually, giving you the tools to make emotional self-regulation part of your daily life.

2026 is a year of change, but it can also be a year of growth. By experimenting with fresh habits like digital detox minutes, micro gratitude, mood pairing, movement snacks, and reverse journaling, you give yourself the chance to thrive. And if you need extra support, know that expert help is only a call away on this site. Contact our representatives today to learn more.

item.title: What to Do When Your Partner Is Showing Signs of Abandonment Issues
item.description:
Relationships can be tricky even at the best of times. This is true for romantic, platonic, or family relationships. Many of the most frustrating behaviors in relationships can be signs of abandonment issues, and signals that the person you’re trying to love has past hurt inside of them. If you can find the balance of giving grace to people while building healthier boundaries, even the most insecure of relationships will have a fighting chance to flourish.

The Pattern of Abandonment

Maybe your new relationship started great, but now they’re acting weird, and you’re wondering what shifted. Perhaps that new friend with whom you clicked so well at first has recently started getting clingy and annoying. It has become an issue, and maybe you would cut them off if you didn’t feel so bad about doing that.

For example, maybe you want to build a healthier relationship with your mother, but you’ve realized that means you will have to call her out on a few things. It might help if you understood how her abandonment issues affected her parenting style, and by default, you.

Abandonment trauma breeds cycles of behavior where one damaged person neglects or rejects those closest to them. They, in turn, pass the damage onto others. This can lead to walking out on meaningful relationships without closure, or squeezing the life out of relationships because they’re afraid of being abandoned.

This pattern continues until someone sees the signs of abandonment issues and intervenes. No one is doomed to repeat the past or live as a victim of it. It takes work, gentleness, and wisdom to change course.

We can’t fix people, and we shouldn’t try. We can, however, be a better support for them, be patient with them, build better boundaries, and model healthier attachment in the way we treat them. In the process, we might realize signs of abandonment issues in our own lives and be forced to confront them. Sometimes, for us to love others better, we must work to resolve something in us that has been damaged for a long time.

Common Signs of Abandonment Issues in Relationships

Abandonment trauma and neglect go hand in hand. Many parents are loving and supportive only when they have time to be, but absent and emotionally distant the rest of the time. In this way, they are neglectful without realizing it, and cause abandonment trauma without meaning to.

This results in a person with abandonment trauma being constantly anxious about being left, ignored, or not cared for by the person they care for the most. This can lead to toxic behavior, and a lot of clear signs for those who can see them. Here are some signs to look for.

Things move quickly with them

You’ve just met them, and you don’t even know their middle name or birthday month, but they are already talking about the future. Not only is fast behavior like this disconcerting, but it is a sign of someone terrified of being forgotten and overlooked.

You might be guilty of this yourself. You may feel as if you are constantly holding yourself back from saying, “I love you,” or wanting to define the relationship. This is one of the clearest and most common signs of abandonment issues.

The person feeling this way needs to hear this: You have inherent worth and deserve to be seen, understood, and valued by others. Your experiences in the past of being overlooked and undervalued were unfair, and they caused significant damage. Now you must find your self-worth outside of the way that others treat you, whether they show you love or not.

You’re not “too much,” you’re not unlovable, and your desire to be loved is one of the most valid things. You must sit with these thoughts as often as possible, and let them into your soul as deeply as you can.

They panic over seemingly small things

People with abandonment trauma are overthinkers and worriers, sometimes to the extreme. A subtle shift in mood can cause them to panic, just as an unanswered text message can feel like a dreadful confirmation of someone’s disinterest.

Then they get stuck with another question: do they confront the issue even if it means they will come across as neurotic, or do they repress their anxiety even though it feels overwhelming? Either thing might result in being rejected and abandoned, just as they feared.

There are few things as painful as being undervalued, especially when it happens at a young age. People with abandonment trauma have determined that they are forgettable and that their needs are not a priority for anyone else. That’s an incredibly heavy thought. It’s no wonder that they are hyperaware of every shift and change in the relationship.

The way for them to break out of their anxiety and overthinking is to be reassured and to build their tolerance to discomfort. Be kind when they ask for reassurance because it probably took courage for them to speak up. Encourage them to sit with their discomfort as they wait for replies or question your mood, though. They need consistency and kindness, and they need to develop stronger methods of coping.

They’re either the first person to walk away or they remain in toxic relationships

One of the easiest ways to see signs of abandonment issues in people is to look at their previous relationships and identify any patterns of repeated behavior.

Perhaps they tend to stay in relationships where they are consistently treated poorly, used, and taken for granted. Maybe they always end the relationship before it’s had a chance to develop. The first person is more comfortable being alone, while the second is terrified of being alone, but both show clear signs of abandonment issues. Both of these people need to face their fears.

The person who is afraid of being alone needs to spend more time alone and to develop competence in caring for themselves. They need to find hobbies and interests outside of their relationships, and make friends with people who will be honest with them.

The person who struggles to commit must learn what rejection truly feels like, so they can stop doing it to others. They must also learn the joys, struggles, highs, and lows of being in a committed relationship, whether it’s romantic or not.

Healing Attachment Trauma

When you find yourself in a relationship with someone who has abandonment issues, you have a delicate role to play in their healing. You are not their healer, nor is the relationship. Your role is to provide healthy companionship and support. We all have some healing to do, and we all need company and compassion as we heal.

When you can see the signs of abandonment issues in your loved ones, you will begin to notice your own issues. Loving someone is like looking in the mirror: you see things you never realized were there, and some things you would rather ignore. This is what keeps us humble, grounded, kind, and intentional. No one is perfect, but we’re not meant to be. We’re all on a journey of getting better and loving better, and the rest we figure out as we go.

Confronting your abandonment issues is hard to do alone, and sometimes even harder to do in a relationship. This is where counseling comes in. It’s easier to examine the issue with someone who is not only trained to help but who doesn’t have an attachment to you beyond being compassionate and professional.

Please consult our online catalog of counselors to find someone suitable, or speak with our reception team, who can help.

item.title: Beyond Guilt and Shame: Christian Counseling for Externally Oriented Struggles
item.description:
Have you ever found yourself standing in the middle of your closet, surrounded by clothes with price tags still attached? Maybe you find yourself scrolling through social media and comparing your home to what you see in the photos. Materialism isn’t as simple as wanting nice things; consequently, the pursuit of material things often becomes a prison of guilt and shame. This prison is not how God designed us to live.

But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you – Matthew 6:33, ESV

Many Christians today struggle with the weight of materialism that previous generations had never encountered. Our culture today screams from every direction about how our worth is measured by what we own or don’t own.

From what we wear to the house we live in, we are under a constant barrage of temptations to compare. This message seeps into our thoughts and creates a battlefield between what we know is not true and what the world says is important.

The Spiritual Trap of Materialism

We often think of materialism in terms of someone greedy or obsessed with wealth. The truth is that materialism is much more subtle, especially for Christians, who seek to follow God’s heart.

Materialism isn’t just about having nice things. It is where we place our security, our hope, and our identity. It is how we often measure success in today’s world. This is how material possessions begin to fill spaces that were designed for God to occupy.

We don’t need to live in shame or feel guilty about the blessings that He gives to us. Scripture tells us that every good and perfect gift comes from Him. It is not in receiving these gifts that we become entangled in materialism, but rather when we make those gifts our god. When we place our happiness and security in what we can buy and acquire or display, we have shifted from spiritual to worldly living.

Once we are entangled in this, it becomes a vicious cycle. We find ways to convince ourselves that we need the things we see. And in that justification, we acquire it and feel satisfied for a fleeting moment. Then we become overwhelmed with guilt, asking ourselves, “Did I need this? Could the money have been spent better? What will people think?” That’s followed by the shame when we hear, “You’re not a good steward. “You’re selfish.”

Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. – Matthew 6:19-21, ESV

The Pattern of Guilt and Shame in Material Pursuit

To overcome the cycle associated with material pursuit, it is important to understand the difference between guilt and shame. We feel guilty about our purchasing desires or inability to be content. We then compare ourselves to others who seem to have less and feel guilty for wanting more.

This thought process leads us to look at credit card statements and feel guilty about our choices. Yet underneath all the guilt, shame is at work, whispering destructive lies about who we are.

Shame, on the other hand, tells us we’re greedy when we are simply human. Shame tells us we’re bad stewards when we are learning to navigate a chaotic and complex world. It then tells us we are failures as Christians because we struggle with contentment.

These thoughts trap us in a cycle and can lead to other issues, such as emotional issues, eating, shopping binges, and isolation.

Spiritually, the impact of guilt and shame cannot be understated. As we constantly battle these emotions, we find it harder to pray, read scripture, and believe that God delights in us. This leads to avoiding fellowship because we fear others will see through our disguise to the real image.

We may even stop tithing or giving because we are too guilty about our spending. This is where we find that the very relationship that could set us free has become clouded by the shame and guilt that we carry.

There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus – Romans 8:1, ESV

God Desires for Us to Be Free from Condemnation

God’s heart toward us is not one of disappointment regarding our struggle with materialism. He does not want to see us bound by guilt and shame. He is not sitting in judgment of a credit card statement or an Amazon cart. What He does see are His children, whom He adores, who are learning to navigate a world that consistently pulls them away from Him.

The difference between conviction and condemnation plays a crucial role in freedom from materialism. Conviction is when the Holy Spirit gently nudges and redirects us toward God’s desired plans for us. Condemnation is the harsh voice of the enemy that beats us down and leads us into hiding from God. Condemnation drives us away, but conviction draws us to God.

When we are feeling convicted about materialism, it is not to shame us; it is meant to set us free. God knows that when our hearts are tangled up in the pursuit of things, we miss out on His joy and peace.

He is not angry with the struggle we have, and He doesn’t show disappointment. He desires to see us walk in freedom from the vicious bondage of materialism. It is His love that compels Him to bring correction that will make changes in our lives.

God wants to provide not only our needs, but He also wants to bless us in abundance. It’s not that He doesn’t want us to have nice things. It’s that He wants us to have an identity in Him rather than belongings. When we are anchored in His love for us, we receive blessings with gratitude and hold them lightly because we know that our treasure is in heaven and not in the world.

The LORD your God is in your midst, a mighty one who will save; he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing. – Zephaniah 3:17, ESV

How Christian Counseling Provides a Healing Pathway

Anyone struggling with guilt and shame from materialistic patterns does not have to carry the burden alone. Christian Counseling can offer a path to healing that addresses not just the symptoms but the root causes of the struggle.

Secular counseling often focuses on behavior modification, but biblical counseling will recognize that material struggles are often symptoms of deeper emotional needs.

A Christian counselor can help with identifying the lies about worth, security, and identity that have been believed. Using Scripture, these counselors can guide us to discover God’s truth about our identity and how God sees us.

Using a faith-based plan, Christian counselors can help develop practical strategies for managing the triggers and making wise financial decisions. This will lead to contentment in building a relationship with God.

Some practical steps that may be included in faith-based Christian Counseling are:

  • Learning to pause before purchasing and ask God about the purchase.
  • Developing gratitude to shift focus from what you lack to your blessings.
  • Create accountability and relationships with other believers,
  • Establish financial boundaries that reflect values rather than impulses.

The goal of overcoming guilt and shame from materialism isn’t for us to live in deprivation. The main goal is freedom to make decisions from a place of peace rather than compulsion. This freedom allows us to enjoy God’s blessings without guilt and shame because we know our security is from Him.

Living in Freedom

God understands we live in a world where success is measured by one’s belongings. This is not how he intended for us to live. God’s plan has always included freedom and blessings of abundance. The mentality of guilt and shame comes from an enemy who wants to see us bound.

If you or someone you know is trapped in patterns of guilt and shame involving materialism, reach out to a local Christian counselor. Freedom can become a part of everyday life, replacing the shackles of guilt and shame.

item.title: 6 Premarital Counseling Questions to Consider Before Getting Married
item.description:
If you’re reading this, you’re probably thinking about marriage. You’re excited, nervous, maybe a little overwhelmed. That’s natural. And that’s exactly why premarital counseling is so important. It circumvents the blind trust and emotions that might cloud your judgment. While premarital counseling does discuss feelings, it’s definitely more about asking the right questions and seeing if you can live with the answers, all before you say, “I do.”

The truth is, love alone will not answer every question or solve every problem that you will encounter in your marriage. Love motivates, but preparation is what sustains a long-term relationship. And that, after all, is one of the goals of marriage, a lifelong partnership. Premarital counseling gives you the tools you need to explore your relationship honestly and safely at a deeper level.

6 Premarital Counseling Questions to Consider

Here are some important questions you and your partner are likely to explore in premarital counseling.

Communication and Conflict

“How do we handle disagreements after marriage?”

When you’re dating, conflict isn’t quite as threatening as it is during marriage. If you’re not fully committed before God and family or have legal ties to each other, you can simply walk away from a relationship when conflict gets heated or complicated. It might not be easy, but it certainly isn’t as difficult as it is when you’re spiritually and legally bound.

So how you communicate and resolve conflict in your marriage will not only look slightly different than it does now while dating or engaged, but really can make or break your relationship. When you’re dating, you can take time apart when conflict hits. You can go home to your own private space to think and regroup. When you’re living together, that option isn’t always available, nor is it always wise.

When you’re married, you have a greater obligation to resolve conflict in a way that honors the oath you took before God, and that strengthens your relationship. You have a greater motivation to avoid triggers that you know will hurt each other because you know they will only bring greater conflict and pain.

When you’re married, you are in a covenant, not just with that other person, but with God, so it’s important to figure out how to make things work even when you’re angry in the moment.

Finances

“How will we manage money as a couple?”

Finances are one of those important, touchy subjects that often wiggles its way in between couples, being a divisive force and causing strife. It’s important to discuss the difficult topics surrounding finances prior to marriage to help mitigate strife and potential financial disaster after.

If you haven’t already discussed each other’s financial history, premarital counseling is a great place to have that important talk. To seamlessly and effectively blend your lives, you will have to know about each other’s credit history, debt load, spending and saving habits, and financial goals and priorities.

When you’re single, your finances are more predictable because you know how much money you bring in and, conversely, how much you spend. But your partner might have very different spending habits that could not only disrupt your financial stability but could also cause major conflict in the process.

While these topics might be touchy and seem “private” now, you definitely don’t want to enter into a lifetime commitment, blending your finances and legal obligations with someone, without thoroughly exploring them.

Faith and Values

“Are we compatible in our faith and values?”

Perhaps the most important aspect of your life and future marriage is how God fits into it. If you want to have a fruitful, healthy, and fulfilling marriage, you have to have God at the center. When each of you, you and your future spouse, seeks God, rather than each other, you will find a life of fulfillment beyond the human experience.

God has instructed us not to marry someone who does not share our Christian faith. “Do not be yoked together with unbelievers. For what do righteousness and wickedness have in common? Or what fellowship can light have with darkness?” 2 Corinthians 6:14 (NIV). This means that you are not to tether yourself to someone who does not share your faith, values, and direction in life.

Like oxen that are yoked to an unequal partner, you too will never move forward, only around in circles, if you bond yourself to an unbeliever. Missionary dating can lead to an unequal partnership, so be honest with yourself when assessing how your partner’s spiritual beliefs shape their daily life.

In premarital counseling, you can explore questions that will help you evaluate the spiritual health of your relationship. Will they want to pray, worship, and serve with you? And if faith differences exist, how will you handle them going forward?

Family and Relationships

“What about the in-laws?”

When you marry your partner, you’re also likely to be marrying their family in a way. Their family has been with them through thick and thin, teaching, mentoring, and doing life together, so it is natural for them to want to keep them in their lives.

Genesis 2:24 gives us insights into God’s plan for marriage. The idea is repeated multiple times throughout Scripture (Matthew 19:5, Ephesians 5:31). God’s design dictates that marriage creates a new primary relationship. Your spouse is to become your closest human bond, and loyalty has to shift.

However, the idea of leaving and cleaving doesn’t mean that you will abandon your family or that they will abandon theirs. Your family and your new spouse’s family will be a part of your new union because they are a part of you and your partner’s history and lives.

Because of this, new boundaries and a new priority structure must be established prior to going to the altar. In premarital counseling, you will not only learn why prioritizing your closest covenant relationship is important, but also how to do it properly with decisiveness, respect, and reasonable expectations.

Intimacy and Physical Connection

“What will our sex life look like?”

Physical intimacy is often seen as the enemy in Christian relationships. But the truth is, the Bible is not prudish about sex. In fact, the entire book of the Song of Solomon celebrates romantic and physical love between a husband and wife. Sex is a gift from God. He created sexual desire on purpose to be a joyful bonding.

As a Christian couple, you probably already know how challenging it can be to abstain from sexual activity before marriage. But keeping your relationship fully within the boundaries of God’s blueprint will yield beautiful rewards.

Once you enter marriage, you can experience sex without guilt, fear, or shame because intimacy is no longer something you have to tiptoe around. It’s actually a sacred part of your covenant and a way to love and serve each other.

In premarital counseling, you will talk about expectations, comfort levels, past experiences, and any sexually related trauma that might impact your post-marriage intimacy. Unfortunately, sex doesn’t automatically become easier just because a ceremony takes place.

You’re two different people with histories, emotions, and vulnerabilities, all of which can impact your sexual relationship. Talking about intimacy during premarital counseling helps remove shame and confusion so you can have that joyful, healthy physical connection.

Goals and Future Plans

“What does our future look like?”

Along with all the emotional and spiritual foundations that help a marriage succeed, practical planning also deserves attention. While most couples know to plan for the first few months of their marriage by securing housing and having a temporary financial plan in place, many couples fail to ask deeper questions about their long-term future.

It’s important to know what your partner has in mind beyond the short term. You need to dive into their personal goals and career plans. You need to know where you are going to live because choosing a city or a neighborhood can impact lifestyle, family dynamics, financial expectations, and long-term dreams.

Premarital counseling will give you the platform, mediation, and tools you need to decide how you and your intended will approach career decisions and relocation. You can discuss whether your future plans include children, and if so, how many. How will you jointly handle parenting and discipline? These conversations involve not only hopes for the future, but fears and expectations. And because of this, it’s imperative to broach these topics prior to saying, “I do.”

Should We Do Premarital Counseling?

Marriage isn’t something that you just wander into, hoping everything will sort itself out. It’s far too precious and complex for that. And while some may tell you to follow your heart and do what “feels right”, Scripture and tried and true wisdom say to prepare, listen to counsel, and follow God.

While premarital counseling can’t prepare you for every one of life’s storms, it sure can help you go into the most important human covenant with eyes wide open. It can give you the tools you need to weather them together because there’s an interesting sense of peace that envelopes you when you and your partner come together and ask the hard questions and give the not-so-proud answers. From those uncomfortable moments comes trust and understanding and a firm foundation on which to build the rest of your lives.

Contact our office today to schedule an appointment with me or another qualified Christian counselor near you to begin your marriage with a strong foundation.

item.title: Generalized Anxiety Disorder: Common Symptoms and Treatment Options
item.description:
Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is a complex and often misunderstood mental health condition that extends far beyond ordinary worry or situational stress. While occasional anxiety is a normal part of life, GAD represents a persistent, excessive, and difficult-to-control pattern of worry that interferes with daily functioning.

For professionals and potential clients alike, understanding the symptoms of GAD is essential for early recognition, effective intervention, and long-term management.

According to the American Psychiatric Association, GAD is defined by excessive anxiety and worry occurring more days than not for at least six months, about a variety of events or activities. This chronic worry is accompanied by a constellation of cognitive, emotional, and physical symptoms that distinguish it from typical stress responses.

Cognitive Symptoms

Cognitive symptoms are among the most prominent features of GAD and are often the primary reason individuals seek help. These include:

Persistent Rumination

Individuals may find themselves stuck in repetitive thought patterns, analyzing past events or anticipating future problems. This rumination often lacks resolution and contributes to mental fatigue.

Difficulty Concentrating

GAD can significantly impair attention and focus. Clients may describe their minds as “cluttered” or report frequent distractions due to intrusive thoughts.

Indecisiveness

Even routine decisions can feel overwhelming. The fear of making the wrong choice often leads to avoidance or prolonged deliberation.

Catastrophic Thinking

A tendency to assume the worst possible outcome is common. Minor concerns may escalate into imagined disasters, reinforcing anxiety.

These cognitive patterns are not merely habits; they are deeply ingrained responses that often require structured therapeutic intervention, such as cognitive-behavioral approaches, to address effectively.

Emotional and Behavioral Symptoms

Beyond cognitive processes, GAD manifests in emotional and behavioral ways that can significantly affect interpersonal relationships and daily functioning.

Chronic Nervousness

A constant sense of unease or apprehension is typical. Even in the absence of immediate threats, individuals may feel “on edge.”

Irritability

Heightened emotional sensitivity can lead to frustration and irritability, sometimes affecting personal and professional relationships.

Avoidance Behaviors

To manage anxiety, individuals may avoid situations they perceive as stressful or uncertain. While avoidance can provide short-term relief, it often reinforces anxiety over time.

Reassurance-Seeking

Clients may frequently seek validation from others to alleviate their fears. While this can temporarily reduce anxiety, it may also create dependency and prevent the development of internal coping strategies.

Physical and Somatic Symptoms

GAD is not confined to the mind; it has significant physiological manifestations. These physical symptoms often result from prolonged activation of the body’s stress response system, commonly referred to as the fight-or-flight response.

Muscle Tension

Chronic tightness, particularly in the shoulders, neck, and jaw, is frequently reported. This can lead to discomfort and even pain over time.

Fatigue

Constant mental and physical arousal can be exhausting, leaving individuals feeling drained despite adequate rest.

Sleep Disturbances

Difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or experiencing restful sleep is a hallmark symptom. Worry often intensifies at night, making it hard to disengage from anxious thoughts.

Gastrointestinal Issues

Symptoms such as nausea, stomach pain, and irritable bowel patterns are common, reflecting the close connection between the brain and digestive system.

Cardiovascular Symptoms

Increased heart rate, palpitations, and occasional shortness of breath may occur, particularly during periods of heightened anxiety.

These somatic symptoms often lead individuals to seek medical evaluation before recognizing the psychological roots of their distress.

Diagnostic Criteria and Clinical Considerations

The formal criteria for diagnosing GAD are outlined in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5-TR). To meet the criteria, an individual must experience excessive anxiety and worry for at least six months, along with three or more associated symptoms such as restlessness, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, or sleep disturbance.

Additionally, the symptoms must cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. Clinicians must also rule out other conditions, including panic disorder and major depressive disorder, as well as medical causes or substance use.

From a professional standpoint, accurate diagnosis requires a comprehensive assessment that considers the client’s history, symptom duration, and functional impact.

This should be made clear to the client and the professional before making a clinical diagnosis. GAD is not just another “diagnosis” to tack onto a treatment plan but a clinical decision made based on the criteria above.

Functional Impact on Daily Life

GAD can have a pervasive impact on nearly every aspect of an individual’s life. In the workplace, excessive worry may impair productivity, decision-making, and interpersonal communication. Clients may struggle with deadlines, fear criticism, or avoid leadership roles due to self-doubt.

In personal relationships, chronic anxiety can create tension. Loved ones may find it difficult to understand the persistent worry, leading to frustration or miscommunication. Over time, this can contribute to social withdrawal or isolation.

Treatment is important to recognize early because of the impacts GAD can have on different aspects of daily functioning.

Evidence-Based Treatment Approaches

Effective treatment for GAD typically involves a combination of psychotherapy, lifestyle interventions, and, when appropriate, medication. The National Institute of Mental Health emphasizes that GAD is “highly treatable, especially when addressed early.”

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)

CBT is widely regarded as the gold standard for treating GAD. It helps clients identify and challenge distorted thinking patterns, develop healthier cognitive responses, and gradually reduce avoidance behaviors.

Pharmacological Interventions

Medications such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) may be prescribed to help regulate mood and reduce anxiety symptoms. These are typically used in conjunction with therapy.

Mindfulness and Relaxation Techniques

Practices such as deep breathing, meditation, and progressive muscle relaxation can help regulate the body’s stress response and improve emotional resilience.

Lifestyle Modifications

Regular exercise, balanced nutrition, and consistent sleep routines play a supportive role in managing anxiety symptoms.

The Role of Christian Counseling

While symptom management is important, addressing the underlying causes and maintaining long-term well-being often requires professional counseling. Counseling provides a structured and supportive environment in which individuals can explore the roots of their anxiety, develop coping strategies, and build resilience.

Christian counseling offers additional dimensions of support. By incorporating spiritual principles, scripture, and prayer, Christian counseling can help individuals reframe their anxiety in the context of their faith. Clients may find comfort in developing trust in God, surrendering control, and cultivating a sense of peace rooted in their beliefs.

For more information and to schedule an appointment with a Christian counselor near you, call us today.

References

National Institute of Mental Health. Generalized Anxiety Disorder.Photo:

item.title: Counseling for Children: “That’s Not Fair!”
item.description:
“That’s not fair!” If you’re a parent, you’ve probably heard that phrase many times, and recently. Children use it to plead their case when you make a decision that they disagree with. They might scream at you as they are carried away from the playground or mumble it as you unplug their favorite device.

Your child, of course, is using the phrase, “that’s not fair,” to express their feelings of disapproval and frustration in their lack of power. But what they aren’t doing is fully comprehending what the term means. That’s not too surprising, because a lot of people, even adults, don’t understand it. The phrase is often used to mean getting what you want, expecting equal outcomes, or expressing frustration, but that’s not what fairness is.

Is that distinction important? Especially at an early age? Yes. An early understanding of fairness shapes social skills, moral reasoning, and the ability and desire to follow rules. Misunderstanding the concept of fairness can lead to issues with entitlement or frustration.

How Fairness is Misunderstood

Many people, children and adults alike, confuse fairness with getting what they want. A child might argue that it’s not fair that their sibling gets more time online. But what they might not understand is that the older sibling’s privilege is often a fair outcome rooted in age appropriateness or their demonstrated effort in following household rules, rather than a mere arbitrary gift.

The word fair, as defined by Merriam-Webster, is: “marked by impartiality and honesty: free from self-interest, prejudice, or favoritism.”

Pause a moment on that phrase, “marked by impartiality and honesty: free from self-interest, prejudice or favoritism.” That means that for something to be fair, it must first be rooted in honesty and equality, not simply whether the outcome is what you wanted it to be or not.

Fairness considers each person’s intrinsic and inalienable rights. Those things they are entitled to, based on their position in life, honesty, responsibility, effort, and age appropriateness, are what determine what is fair.

Biblical Meaning

The dictionary definition of fairness aligns with what the Bible teaches. In James 3:17, it says, “But the wisdom that comes from heaven is first of all pure; then peace-loving, considerate, submissive, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial and sincere.” (NIV) Fairness, then, is directly connected to God’s wisdom. Fairness means treating people with honesty, kindness, and without favoritism, as God models and instructs.

The Bible also warns not to confuse fairness with favoritism and links a person’s actions to a just outcome without prejudice. In James 2:1-9, “My brothers and sisters, believers in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ must not show favoritism… If you really keep the royal law found in Scripture, ‘Love your neighbor as yourself,’ you are doing right. But if you show favoritism, you sin and are convicted by the law as lawbreakers.” (NIV)

This passage is powerful because it speaks of the core concept of true fairness, that outcomes are determined by outside factors, choices, and universal truths, not by self-interest or special treatment. It establishes an absolute, impartial rule. If a person does something wrong, they will be repaid for their wrong. Their repayment is the fair consequence or impartial results, but not necessarily pleasant.

Fairness is about honesty. God cares deeply that our actions and decisions reflect truth, not deception or manipulation. Proverbs 11:1(NIV) says: “The Lord detests dishonest scales, but accurate weights find favor with him.”

Applying that to the definition of fairness, being fair is not really about what you give or even receive, but it’s about the integrity behind your decision. Just like God measures things honestly, you too are called to be honest in how you treat others, even when it might be easier to favor one person over another.

How The Misconception Affects Children

Is establishing a true definition of fairness and instilling that in your children really that important? Yes, because a convoluted view of fairness can trickle down and affect every area of their life, from how they perceive the way others treat them to the consequences they expect and their work ethic.

Children need to realize that fairness is not a guarantee of happiness, but rather a reflection of justice. If your child is angry that you held to your word and gave them half an hour on the playground, they need to realize that their anger doesn’t make the decision unfair because they were given what they were promised. And if you decide to extend their time on the playground, that is not fairness, but generosity.

Consider a teenager who gets upset because you’ve limited them to one hour of screen time a day. They might insist that “it isn’t fair” and feel frustrated. However, the key to their understanding of the concept of fairness is recognizing the distinctions between rights and privileges. Fairness doesn’t apply to what was never guaranteed in the first place. By setting a limit, you are being generous in allowing the privilege at all, not unfair by restricting it.

And that brings us to the issue of entitlement. Just because you want something doesn’t mean you’re entitled to it. Fairness is about justice, integrity, and consistency, not just granting every desire. When children internalize this, they learn to appreciate boundaries, respect rules, and see that generosity is a gift, separate from what is deserved or owed.

Reframing Fairness

If your family is struggling with issues of entitlement or a misconception about fairness, consider seeking therapy. A therapist can work with your child to transition them from an outcome-based definition of fairness to an integrity-based definition. By showing them that fairness doesn’t mean that they get what they want, but rather what they deserve, they will learn about gratitude, hard work, and integrity.

A therapist can also help your child categorize things like food and safety as inalienable and guaranteed rights, and screen time or toys as privileges they either earn or are gifted. A therapist can also help link action to consequence through role-playing and help the child process feelings of frustration.

What many call “fair” is just a veneer for favoritism

The popular definition of fairness can often refer to favoritism or generosity. Favoritism subverts the essence of true fairness because it injects partiality into the outcome and removes reality and responsibility. It directly violates the core principles of the fairness you’re teaching your children because it introduces the idea of partiality and prejudice into the outcome.

Children, whether they’re expecting reward or leniency, need to learn that fairness, not favoritism, is based on integrity, inalienable rights, effort, responsibility, and other, more complicated factors, not just arbitrary preferences or instant gratification. In teaching your children the right mindset surrounding fairness, you’re also teaching them about graciousness and generosity.

Peppered among your hardline rules and consequences is a softer space reserved for grace. Because while consistent absolutes are important, it’s also valuable for children to see that kindness and fairness can coexist.

The message of salvation illustrates the ultimate example of fairness and generosity. We are sinners and deserve judgment. But God, in his unwavering and omnipotent love for us, gave the most generous sacrifice so we can live eternally. Not because we are worthy or because it’s our right, but because of His generosity and love.

God created a way for us to escape the punishment that was fair for us to receive and interrupted that with generosity. And that lesson of justice and generosity can lead your child closer to a life of integrity and a closer walk with God.

To learn more about teaching fairness and mercy to your children, contact our office today to schedule a meeting with me or one of the other Christian counselors in our online directory.

References:
https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/fair

item.title: How to Disclose Infidelity
item.description:
Across the world, emotional and sexual infidelity destroys relationships, leading to breakups or divorces. In the United States alone, it is estimated that 20-40% of relationships are affected by infidelity (Marín, Christensen, & Atkins, 2014). Emotional and sexual infidelity is damaging because it affects self-esteem, causes depression and anxiety, creates attachment injuries, and triggers suicidal ideation in hurt partners.

Frequently, infidelity in relationships leads to significant distress for both partners, especially in the brief period after disclosure or discovery. Hurt partners react in a variety of ways to discovering infidelity: initial shock, wanting to leave, time apart from the offending partner, feeling trapped with no option to leave, or staying and beginning the work to rebuild the relationship.

The Fact of Disclosure

While the consequences are the same for disclosing infidelity to a hurt partner or the hurt partner discovering infidelity, it seems that gentle and thoughtful disclosure is more likely to lead to repair, recovery, and reconciliation between the partners (Simonyi-Gindele & Simonyi-Gindele, 2020).

Involved partners often believe that disclosing infidelity is the harmful part. However, the infidelity itself does the real damage to the hurt partner (Simonyi-Gindele & Simonyi-Gindele). If the offending partner validates the hurt partner’s sense of reality, the disclosure will go more easily. As described above, the hurt partner will experience a gamut of emotions. Emotionally, hurt partners will feel like their entire world has collapsed around them.

There are a few exceptions to a gentle, thoughtful disclosure. The first exception is when the hurt partner has expressed an imminent, verifiable threat to harm the involved partner if he or she discloses infidelity.

In those special circumstances, preventive law enforcement intervention and involvement would be strongly advised before disclosure. The offending partner may choose to keep it secret or divorce the hurt partner as an alternative. Not disclosing infidelity in these cases leads to superficial emotional intimacy.

The second exception applies to individuals with a sex addiction. Since there are likely multiple sex partners and infidelities, the process is more complex than a simple thoughtful disclosure (Schneder et al., 1998). In addition, the hurt partner is likely aware of the involved partner’s dalliances (Schneder et al.). Individuals with a sex addiction may require advanced mental health care at an inpatient program specializing in sexual addiction and betrayal.

The Process of Disclosure

Schneder and associates concluded that disclosure is often a process, not a one-time event. However, disclosure should not be staggered. It is best to get everything in the open, as described below. Nevertheless, we are human and tend to forget some details, especially if we do not have support to remind us.

Second, they reminded us that the initial disclosure is usually the make-or-break point to healing the relationship in the long run, including all the major elements of the acting-out behaviors. Initial disclosure does not involve the “gory details.” The “gory details” are sexual positions used by the offending and affair partners and anything that enhanced the romance, i.e., perfume, adult toys, and lingerie, between them.

Third, they recommend that both partners need support from professionals and peers during the process of disclosure. When the involved partner chooses to disclose infidelity to his or her partner, it is advisable to gather all the information possible. Although heart-rending, disclosure is best when it delivers everything in one swift and painful blow.

The offending partner must have a support system in place. The support system will keep the involved partner from leaving out any details. Offending partners are often anxious when disclosing information to the hurt partner. For the hurt partner, a support system will help him or her sort his or her feelings objectively, weigh the pros and cons, give the hurt partner the pros and cons, and help guide the recovery process.

Disclosing Details of Infidelity

If details are left out, the disclosure becomes staggered disclosure. Staggered disclosure causes further injury because it rips the scab off a healing wound. Staggered disclosure requires as much work as discovery of infidelity to rebuild trust with the hurt partner. The hurt partner asks him or herself questions, such as “What is next?” “What did my partner leave out?” “Is my partner truly remorseful?” or “Is my partner trying to weasel out of natural and logical consequences?

In addition to a support system, the involved partners need to be prepared to answer all the hurt questions. The most important questions are:

  • who the affair partner was
  • when the affair began and ended
  • how many separate acts of infidelity occurred
  • what made the affair partner different than the hurt partner
  • whether there was safe sex
  • whether the offending partner was in love with the affair partner
  • whether the affair partner and the involved partner were treated for STDs
  • whether contact with the affair partner has ended
  • whether a child was conceived during the affair
  • why the offending partner is choosing to return to the hurt partner

This writer believes that two particular questions are strictly off-limits for the hurt partner to ask: 1) which sex positions were used during the affair, and 2) whether items were used to spice up the affair, i.e., lingerie, perfume, adult toys, etc. Both questions tend to retraumatize hurt partners as they visualize these acts or scenes repeatedly in their minds.

When disclosing infidelity, especially when done without a mental health professional present, disclosure needs to be slow and in bite-sized pieces. The hurt partner will likely be quite hurt and will need time to absorb everything.

Thus, it is advisable to allow a minimum of two to three hours to disclose the infidelity. Allowing plenty of time gives the hurt partner time to absorb the information emotionally and take appropriate breaks to prevent flooding of emotions. It is important to reveal everything in one session.

Considerations When Disclosing Infidelity

When disclosing infidelity, it is important to be empathetic toward the hurt partner. The involved partner must place him or herself in the shoes of the hurt partner. Second, the offending partner must not pass judgment on the hurt partner or minimize his or her actions. Third, the involved partner must recognize all the emotions the hurt partner is experiencing. Fourth, the offending partner must communicate the understanding of the hurt partner’s emotions by validating them.

It is guaranteed that the hurt partner will have some strong emotions. It is wise for the involved partner not to treat the hurt partner’s emotions as an overreaction. Likewise, it would be detrimental to tell the hurt partner how to feel. As described above, the hurt partner will feel blindsided, shocked, confused, grieved, and emotionally kicked in the stomach.

It is unrealistic to believe that forgiveness happens instantaneously, like taking a magic pill that erases all harm done. In cases of infidelity, the offending partner must apologize for the infidelity.

However, it is completely delusional to believe that forgiveness takes place immediately. When infidelity is disclosed, validating the hurt partner’s pain, accepting responsibility, laying out a recovery plan, seeking individual treatment beforehand, and taking steps before disclosing, i.e., switching jobs to move away from an affair partner/co-worker, goes a long way for the hurt partner.

In addition to the three requirements above, trust must be rebuilt. Trust involves honesty, transparency, reliability, and security. Security is the subjective quality of feeling safe. No objective standard can measure security. Reliability means being willing to be held liable again and again. An offending partner in infidelity says something and follows through with it.

Transparency means everything is visible and can be inspected by the hurt partner. The involved partner does not try to hide anything from the hurt partner. Honesty means being truthful, even when it hurts. Deception and manipulation of the hurt partner do not occur.

Regardless of whether the infidelity was disclosed or discovered, the reconciliation process will be excruciating for both partners. Infidelity recovery includes evaluating the damage to the relationship, rebuilding trust, reestablishing commitment between partners, creäting and maintaining accountability, learning to communicate more deeply, and developing true forgiveness (Fife et al., 2023).

Next Steps

Often, when rebuilding a relationship plagued by infidelity, couples require forgiveness and seek professional help. An educated, Christian counselor can teach clients how to forgive each other, help them manage painful and recurring memories, assist the couple with their changing couple-dynamics, and modify power dynamics within their relationship.

At Spokane Christian Counseling, we have many counselors who have walked alongside countless clients to restore relationships and help them start on the path of recovery and reconciliation.

Fife, S. T., Gossner, J. D., Theobald, A., Allen, E., Rivero, A., & Koehl, H. (2023). Couple healing from infidelity: A grounded theory study. Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 40(12), 3882-3905.

Marín, R. A., Christensen, A. & Atkins, D. C. (2014). Infidelity and behavioral couple therapy: Relationship outcomes over 5 years following therapy, Couple and Family Psychology: Research and Practice, 3 (1), 1-12.

Schneider, J. P., Corley, M. D., & Irons, R. K. (1998). Surviving disclosure of infidelity: Results of an international survey of 164 recovering sex addicts and partners. Sexual Addiction & Compulsivity, 5(3), 189–217. https://doi.org/10.1080/10720169808400162

Simonyi-Gindele, C. & Simonyi-Gindele, V. (25 Mar. 2020). Key things to include when disclosing infidelity (Episode 271). The Marriage Podcast for Smart People. Retrieved from Key Things to Include When Disclosing Infidelity – OnlyYouForever

item.title: Learning How to Forgive Yourself When It Feels Impossible
item.description:
It’s easy to hold a grudge against someone who wronged you, but it can also be relatively easy to forgive them. Learning to forgive yourself can be more challenging. Forgiving usually goes something like this:

You replay the offensive action as it unfolded in real-time in your head with a judgmental eye. You speculate about motives and judge them in all their faults and frailties and talk it over with your best friend, who will assure you that you were not at fault (because that’s what best friends do). Eventually, forgiveness and acceptance can come through an apology, bringing restoration to the relationship and satisfaction to your soul.

But when you’re holding resentment against yourself, the act of forgiveness can be more complicated and the process less straightforward. Do you want to confess and regurgitate your transgressions with someone else? And when you’re fighting with yourself, a healing apology may not be forthcoming.

Why It’s Important to Forgive Yourself

Sometimes we’re easy on ourselves, like the time you justified popping a few grapes at the grocery store just to test them. There are other times when we are our own harshest judges. Our self-serving bias may allow us to take credit for our successes (of course they’re a result of my abilities). When it comes to our failures, we may blame those on external factors such as someone else’s actions or even bad luck.

But when we judge our actions with the ferociousness of a chef judging a microwave dinner, we forget that we should also show ourselves grace. Holding yourself to a high standard is commendable, but so is forgiving yourself when you fall short of those goals. After all, even those award-winning chefs have off days and come home to microwave a TV dinner.

We’re allowed to learn and grow and to try again and again without the constraints of self-criticism holding us back.

Viewing yourself through the lens of your mistakes can weigh you down, making even your victories and moments of peace a little less meaningful. When you forgive yourself, you can let go of that weighty guilt and relentless regret. This means you can stop carrying around the weight of your mistakes. Because you know what? God has already promised to forgive you.

Learning to Accept Forgiveness

As a follower of Christ, you know you are called to forgive others, but that same grace and compassion should be extended to yourself. God has already made a way for your forgiveness by sending His only Son to die for your sins. Now, you just have to accept that gift and release yourself from the harshness of your regret.

That process isn’t always easy. In fact, forgiving yourself can be even more difficult than forgiving others and is a deeply personal process. We’ve all been told to “let it go!” But letting go is easier said than done.

Support as You Forgive Yourself

Thankfully, you don’t have to walk the path alone. A Bible-believing therapist can serve as an invaluable ally in this sometimes-tumultuous process. Your therapist can help you break free from the constricting chains of guilt and point you back into the loving and compassionate arms of the Lord. They can also help you uncover the root of your feelings, reframe your thinking, and empower you to move forward through healing and hope, so you don’t stumble back into self-deprecation.

Forgiving yourself means seeing yourself through the lens of God’s everlasting love, not the foggy and scratched lens of sin and regret. God’s grace is much bigger than your failures and much more everlasting than your sins. Regardless of your past failures and mistakes, you can walk in confidence knowing that you are loved and forgiven. Let the therapists at our location help you find that forgiveness. Give our office a call today.

item.title: Addressing Sexual Intimacy Issues in Marriage
item.description:
Sexual intimacy issues in marriage can stem from many factors. The good news is that it is never too late to rebuild emotional and physical intimacy through communication, reduced performance expectations, and counseling.

Common Sexual Intimacy Issues

Sexual intimacy issues can create a distance physically and emotionally in a marriage. It can lead to hurt, frustration, anger, and resentment. Keeping lines of communication open, being willing to be vulnerable, and seeking help when needed can strengthen the relationship.

The following are several common sexual intimacy issues couples face.

Hormonal Changes

Hormonal changes throughout life can lead to decreased libido or a mismatched libido between a couple. For example, a woman going through early menopause symptoms may have a lower libido as well as physical symptoms, such as vaginal dryness, that make sex painful. While her husband may have higher hormone levels, causing him to want to make love more often.

Hormonal changes are normal. If they become a problem where sexual intimacy is concerned, speak to your physician about the possibility of hormone therapy.

Lack of Emotional Intimacy

Expecting physical intimacy without emotional intimacy can lead to lulls in a marriage. The act of sex becomes more of a demand than a pleasure, losing the connection it once held. Emotional intimacy starts with non-sexual acts of love. For example, little acts like holding hands, brushing by the other, maintaining eye contact, and spending quality time together all build emotional intimacy.

Consider scheduling weekly or bi-weekly date nights and make it a priority to touch your spouse more. Put in the effort to serve and spoil your spouse in the little things. Open the line of communication by asking for the same in return.

After Effects of Infidelity

Infidelity can tear a relationship apart. If you are working on rebuilding your marriage after infidelity or an affair, know that it is possible with time, effort, forgiveness, and grace from the Lord. The after-effects of infidelity can make it more challenging for spouses to express themselves sexually as they have lost the trust and freedom that makes sexual intimacy safe in marriage.

Speak to a counselor about ways to rebuild your marriage after infidelity. Couples therapy is effective in getting spouses on the same page.

Medical Conditions

Certain medical conditions and side effects of medications can lead to sexual intimacy issues in marriage. For example, a man can experience erectile dysfunction at any age, while a woman may feel overwhelmed by family responsibilities while dealing with hormonal changes and anxiety. Combined, these issues can decrease libido.

Speak to your physician about medical conditions and medications hampering your sexual relationship and work on building and strengthening emotional intimacy during this season.

Meeting an “Obligation”

No one feels like having sex all the time, especially if you are tired, anxious, depressed, or ill. Often, spouses will participate to keep the peace, but it feels more like an obligation than a connection. This can lead to bitterness, resentment, and frustration.

If meeting an obligation has become more of the norm, speak to a counselor today about how to get both of you back on track and address the issues holding you back.

Christian Counseling for Sexual Intimacy Issues in Marriage

Christian counseling combines faith-based principles with evidence-based techniques to address the individual holistically. When it comes to sexual intimacy issues, your counselor will help you work on communication, build emotional intimacy, seek treatment for medical conditions, and learn to lean into each other in this season while drawing closer to God. Contact us today to get started.

item.title: Anxiety in the Bible: How to Move from Worry Toward Rest
item.description:
We often try to ground our sense of peace in things that can change in an instant. We look to our health, financial stability, our friendships and other relationships, our looks, and other areas for peace. These things can have benefits in their own way, but they ultimately form a poor foundation for life because they aren’t permanent.

If we want something that will stand the test of time, a foundation upon which to build our lives that will survive the fiercest assaults that life can launch against us, such a hope and such a foundation can only be found in Jesus. This has remarkable implications for our lives, including the sense of security we can have, knowing that we are safe in Christ, even when we go through tough times.

Anxiety is a normal reaction to stress as a potential danger. We need a way to protect ourselves against harm, and so our bodies have the remarkable ability to prepare for such instances. Our fight-or-flight response, which is triggered by stress and danger (whether real or imagined), prepares our body to respond appropriately to the situation. This could be a job interview, a first date, or a snake that just slithered across your path.

While feeling a bit of anxiety can be a normal response in stressful situations, such as a public speaking engagement or taking a test, those feelings of anxiety can also function as an indicator of something deeper. It’s important to notice when they become excessive, all-consuming, and begin interfering with your day-to-day life. In those cases, anxiety has become a disorder, and that is a condition diagnosable by a mental health professional.

If you find that your anxiety is out of control and undermining your well-being and daily functioning, you should consider going to a mental health professional for a proper diagnosis.

Thankfully, the Lord has not left us without wisdom and guidance regarding anxiety or any other part of our lives. Treatment for anxiety includes psychotherapy and medication. Part of what happens in psychotherapy is talking with your therapist. They can help you begin understanding the causes of anxiety, your triggers for anxiety, and any patterns of thought, behavior, and action that undermine your well-being.

These unhealthy and unhelpful patterns of behavior and thinking need to be understood and ultimately replaced by healthier ones. Part of how you can deal with everyday anxiety, as well as deeper anxiety disorders, is to speak God’s truths over yourself. You can begin to pattern your thinking and being in ways that align with God’s truth and ways.

Below are some Scriptures that can help us work through our anxiety and ground us in the hope, security, and freedom from fear that can only come through Jesus Christ.

Come and find rest

“Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” – Matthew 11:28–30, ESV

Jesus invites people to place their trust in him and place their lives in his hands. For those who are carrying the burden of religious legalism, Jesus invites you to set it down. Instead of being weighed down by the laws that seemed to multiply guilt without necessarily offering any relief, Jesus offers rest for our souls.

This means that He is offering freedom from the crushing burden of guilt of trying to earn salvation by good works to those who desire eternal rest and seek forgiveness of their sins.

Sometimes, we are anxious in life because we feel like we don’t measure up to a standard, whether it is that of the people around us or to God’s standards. Jesus frees us from that by offering us the lighter burden of being his disciples and finding rest through simple commitment to him.

We live for Him, and He loves, cares for, and accepts us already. We pursue our life in Him from the position of knowing we are already loved and accepted, and we don’t have to earn it because Jesus has done it for us on the cross.

When good things become ultimate things that take us off course, it can make us anxious as we try to keep it all together. In our culture, we are consumed by many anxieties and concerns, and these have become ultimate for many of us. When things like our safety, our personal health, or the environment and its viability become ultimate concerns, the enormity of the problems, coupled with our limited capacities, makes us feel endlessly fragile and anxious.

What we need is to bring things back into perspective and make God the center of our lives. That way, these other things begin to occupy their proper place. When we yield to Jesus and his yoke, it allows us to approach these good concerns with the resources and wisdom of God, and that can help us find peace and rest. We can trust that our work in the Lord will not be in vain (1 Corinthians 15: 58). We don’t need to feel anxious about our impact or how things will unfold.

Finding Peace in Hard Places

The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul. He leads me in paths of righteousness for his name’s sake. Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil,
for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me. – Psalm 23:1-4, ESV

Fear is probably the strongest human emotion, and we often agonize over all the challenging and dreadful things that could happen to us at any moment. This includes what might happen to our health and finances, losing our loved ones, failing at something important, or being rejected.

Life is often not safe, and we never know what we can find in the hard things we go through. Many things can bring suspense and danger in our lives. These verses from Psalm 23 are a good reminder that the people of God have assurance that God is with them in those times, and so they need not fear. God draws us to find rest and restoration when we follow and trust him.

Trusting In God’s Provision and Care

And he said to his disciples, “Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will put on. For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing.

“Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds! And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? If then you are not able to do as small a thing as that, why are you anxious about the rest?” –  Luke 12:22-26, ESV

There are many reasons why believers should not be anxious, and several of them are given in this passage from Luke. For one thing, our lives are more than what we eat; even our bodies are more than what we eat. We do need food and clothing, but these things enable us to focus on what life is really about: loving God and loving our neighbor. It’s challenging, but we can love God and our neighbor whether we are well-fed or not.

If our lives are preoccupied by the means and not the ends of our lives, we can be consumed by the pressure to gather the things that seemingly secure our existence, so much so that we miss the point. Believers also shouldn’t be anxious because they realize how much value they possess in God’s eyes. If he cares for birds, why wouldn’t he care for you?

Anxiety is also not in our best interests because none of us has enough control over our own life, even to add a single hour to our span of life. It’s quite counterintuitive, but striving and taking things into our own hands, and then getting anxious because life is not under our control, doesn’t help us. It is far better to surrender ourselves to the loving care of our heavenly Father, who does have everything under control.

Important Reminders

Psalm 56 reminds us that “When I am afraid, I put my trust in you.” (Psalm 56:3, NIV) We can try to put our trust elsewhere, but those things will ultimately fail and disappoint us. This will likely lead us into deeper anxiety and worry as we try to secure ourselves against the hardships we face in life.

Writing nearly seventeen centuries ago, in his long prayer called Confessions, Augustine wrote, “You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our hearts are restless until they rest in you.” (Augustine) Our restless and anxious hearts try to find peace and rest in many ways, but we can only find what we are looking for in the Lord. This is our deepest need.

To deal with our anxiety, we should be aware of this need and where to have it met. We can grow in our awareness of our unhealthy patterns of behavior and thought through therapy and with the assistance, when necessary, of medication to ease the symptoms of anxiety. This can help us function in life. If you’re ready to learn more about therapy for anxiety, contact this office for more information.
