item.title: 3 Life Stages When Female Friendships Are Essential
item.description:
Female friendships can be complicated to maintain, tough to build, and even more challenging to restore when there’s a break. It might feel frustrating or pointless to continue putting the work into these relationships. But as you grow and change through life’s seasons, your friends are the ones who sustain you and remind you of your purpose.

Here are five life stages when female friendships aren’t just nice to have but are empowering and essential.

Transitioning into Teen Years with Friendship

This life stage can be fraught with drama, disagreements, and simply changing your mind about so many topics. However, when transitioning from childhood and early adolescence to the teen years, having female friendships for support is integral to emotional and mental health.

When you were 12, 13, or 14, what were you most concerned with? Was it makeup, beauty products, clothing, shoes, or boys? If your answer is yes, you’re in like company. Many young women entering their teen years think about these, too. However, did you know that teen girls today also have deeper, heavier worries on their minds?

Recent research suggests that teen girls are also concerned about long-term decisions, such as where they’ll attend college, what career to pursue, how they’ll earn an income, and family conflict resolution. Just as with adult females, this life stage is one where, without supportive friends, a young teen may find it even more challenging to navigate than it already is.

So, how do teen girls form supportive, healthy female friendships? First, they look to their role models. Many teens learn how to treat friends by the way their parents treat others. If you’re the mother of a teen girl, remember that she’s watching and listening to how you talk to, treat, and talk about your own friends.

Second, pay attention to how your daughter talks about casual friends at school. If one day there’s a breakup, and the next day there’s a hookup between her bestie and her bestie’s boyfriend, it might mean her best girl is prone to drama, mixed signals, or a preoccupation with the things that aren’t lasting. Listening first and asking questions second about your daughter’s friends is one way to tiptoe into discovering what kinds of people she’s around most.

Most teens spend the majority of their time at school, so it’s normal to be lumped together with people you might not ordinarily choose. Much like an office setting where you can’t choose your co-workers, the same goes for school. That’s why asking questions is vital. Not every friend your daughter talks about is going to be her best one, or healthy, and that’s okay. It’s to be expected.

Letting your daughter in on some friendship secrets could help her as she searches for friends who will guard her vulnerability and add joy to her life rather than drama. Secrets you probably didn’t know you had tucked away might include the power of observation.

Talk to your daughter about things like observing how a friend talks about others and paying attention to her discussions around faith or morality. Also, note whether she’s inclined to persevere when something difficult happens or when she’s tasked with a group project. It’s even important to teach her to recognize if a friend asks for help from trustworthy adults if she’s struggling. Remind your daughter to look for good character in her friends.

Another secret you help her learn is to join teams and activities based on interest level and based on who’s involved. As your daughter decides what activities to pursue, remind her that an activity may not be worth pursuing if it means joining a group of girls who go out after a game to party or who talk about others in a demeaning way.

Sometimes teens need to learn the hard way who a good friend is and isn’t. Having an understanding, listening ear is always a gift to her during this season.

Friendships in Young Adulthood

Whether you see young adulthood as 18 or 25, having female friendships can buoy you during these transitional years.

Women face monumental decisions such as where to live, what career to pursue, and how to find a faith community and grow in their spiritual life. This is also the time when many young women start to reflect on their childhood, see some areas for improvement, and desire a closer relationship with family members.

It can be a terrific time to pursue counseling, too. If you or someone you know has been thinking or talking about family relationships or childhood wounds, our offices are widespread and staffed with credentialed, competent counselors, and we’ll match you with the right person to suit your needs.

Female friendships in your early to mid-20s can be tough to maintain when so many women are in life transitions. Whether they’re getting married, starting a career, pursuing a post-graduate degree, or having children, women during this life stage may find it hard to be consistent with their old friends and carve out time to make new ones.

Some tips we want to remind young women are that they have a unique personality and gifts to share. Old ways of connecting, like community service, are sometimes overlooked unless you’re heavily plugged into a service-oriented church.

Aside from contributing your time or talents to a cause you believe in, community service is also a wonderful way to form female friendships. Look for causes that matter to you, and you’ll likely find others who have at least one interest in common.

Another way to find or maintain female friendships at this stage is to develop a creative communication method that works most of the time. This isn’t the time to wish your friend a casual “let’s keep in touch” or “let’s get together next month.” If you want to maintain friendships, you’ll have to be direct, intentional, targeted, decisive, and a little creative.

Use apps like Marco Polo or WhatsApp to help you stay in touch with regular video chat exchanges or life update check-ins. Arrange to talk regularly and create a Zoom call where you can agree on a set time period (not to cut each other off but to respect each other’s time and commitments during this life stage).

Think about a friend who is getting married. Her life is changing radically, so she might not be able to predict what her everyday life will look like after marriage. But give her a month or so, and then try to connect at a time that works for her. You can mutually decide how often you want to call or text to check in and how you plan to maintain your friendship in a season where your lives may not align.

Consider all that you do have in common and don’t write her off simply because her life stage will shift. She’s going to need a friend who knew her before her marriage and can remind her who she is on tough days. And you’ll benefit from getting insider info on what it’s like to be married. Everything she goes through while adjusting is something you can file away and learn from in the future.

Friendships When Your Children Are Grown and on Their Own

You may be newly empty-nested or empty-nested for a decade, but somewhere in this life stage, friends are going to come in handy. Here’s why.

Being suddenly empty can shock our systems. For some of us, it’s an easy transition at first. But then, after years of watching our adult children make choices on career, life, and love, we may encounter a time when our needs fade into the background of their thriving, busy lives.

It’s not that you aren’t happy that they are doing so well (you are!), but when their lives get chaotic, fruitful, stressful, and full, it’s common for them to forget to include a parent in their world. That’s if you’re close geographically; it’s even harder when you live far away.

Friends can be the balm to your loneliness and feeling left out because they can help you find new interests, explore ideas you’ve never considered before, or take risks that you once would have balked at. Now you have the time, energy, and financial resources to pursue them.

They can also listen when you feel left out, give you a kick in the pants when you need to be reminded you’re not a victim, and help you learn how to be vulnerable when it’s the last thing you want to be.

If you’re newly empty-nested, a friend who stays beside you regardless of her life stage is a treasure. She may not be able to relate to what you are going through, but she can mirror what she sees in you and echo what she hears you say. Having female friendships where we’re heard, seen, and known can carry you through just about anything.

You can carry someone else through this life stage, too. Here’s how:

  • Call and invite her for coffee or a walk, even if she says no too many times. (Don’t give up.)
  • Show up at her house with a to-go coffee from her favorite cafe, chicken salad and croissants, or a puzzle you can work on together. It reminds her that she still has needs and interests outside of her children.
  • Engage in her stories about her children, even if you’ve heard similar ones. Listening to her is a way of holding space for her grief, joy, pain, and the immense transition she’s going through right now.
  • Ask her to try something new with you, somewhere new together. Trying something you’ve never done together builds camaraderie in a way that old hobbies can’t. You’ll probably have to be brave together, and it’ll elicit some laughs, giving your grieving friend a place to escape for a little while.
  • Encourage your friend to attend counseling. Even if it’s just a few sessions, seeing a counselor during seasons of transition can provide her with healthy tools and mindset shifts.

To schedule an appointment with me or one of the other counselors in our online directory, contact our reception team today at Vancouver Christian Counseling in Washington state.

item.title: Trauma Response: Is it Exhaustion or the Beginning of Faith?
item.description:
If you’ve been through a traumatic experience, you probably have also experienced the exhaustion that comes from the aftermath. Common trauma response symptoms include anxiety, depression, catastrophic thinking, anger, self-blame, hypervigilance, and dissociation, among others.

There comes a point when the burden gets too heavy, and you simply can’t carry it any longer. Some people view this “I just can’t do it anymore” pinnacle as a breaking point, but what if it is actually where your faith begins?

Common Trauma Response Symptoms

A person’s trauma response is experienced in various ways. Perhaps you’ve suffered through a prolonged illness, been a caregiver, gotten divorced, been laid off, or are/were the victim of abuse.

Your body and brain will take these trauma experiences and mull them over, and these significant events in your life will manifest in a variety of ways, depending on a lot of factors. This includes but is not limited to your personal history, the circumstances of the event, and your level of support.

No matter the trauma experience or the initial response, there’s no denying that going through a major life-altering event or taxing season will take its toll on you. Some people cycle through the stages of grief and their trauma response quickly, but for some, the weight of it all can drag them down for a long time.

When It’s Too Much

Dark response seasons can morph into your new normal. Your once trusting heart can suddenly become skeptical because of a betrayal. Your once carefree spirit might suddenly feel the weight of living within a tight budget, and as a result, can develop into a fear of homelessness or bankruptcy that can affect you even months, years, or decades after you’ve landed a new job and have found financial stability.

Trauma experiences change us. Sometimes for the worse, which are the effects that bother us the most and get the most attention. When something happens that not only changes our outlook but seems to rewrite our DNA, it is bound to get more attention than the joy of finding a new job or a compliment we receive.

These changes in our being can feel like protection. We might view our new conservative spending habits as being frugal or good stewards. We might find our caution in relationships as wisdom instead of a response to a toxic friendship. And sometimes we’re right. Sometimes trauma changes who we are and how we respond for the better, or at least not for the worse.

But sometimes, in the darkness of the night, as you struggle to find peace and quiet, even in the comfort of your bed, you can feel the weight of the trauma. Maybe you feel as if you’ve gotten over the original trauma, but those aftereffects, those changes in your thought patterns, or those new insecurities that have cropped up, can exhaust you.

In those moments, you might think to give up. You might just want it all to go away or to find a way to leave it all behind. You might long for that trusting, naïve version of yourself that was kidnapped and replaced with this new cynic. This new anxiety-ridden, socially awkward, and paralyzed shell may seem like an improved version of yourself, one that will protect itself with ten-foot-high brick walls and barbed wire.

But maybe, in those quiet, solitary, undistracted moments, you miss that confident person you used to be or the innocence that was stolen. And it is then that the trauma and consequences culminate and leave you confused, overwhelmed, and simply exhausted.

Is it exhaustion or faith?

Could it be both? When you finally reach your threshold, the pinnacle of the aftereffects, a new thing starts to happen. When you’re at your lowest, and you realize that you’ve hit rock bottom, something inside of you might start to change or emerge.

Amid those overwhelming feelings comes peace knowing you can’t fight anymore. Amidst the exhaustion comes the comforting thought that maybe the fight isn’t even worth it. And in those moments of sheer hopelessness comes the opportunity for faith.

The Bible says clearly, “And we know that in all things God works for the good of those who love Him, who have been called according to His purpose.” (Romans 8:28, NIV) This means that God can bring something meaningful, positive, or redemptive out of even the most painful experiences in your life, if you love Him and are called according to His plan.

God doesn’t waste our pain. Even in our deepest holes, darkest hours, and lowest valleys, God can transform those moments, and us, into something quite beautiful.

Surrender

If you really dissect what is going on, you might start to view your exhaustion and oppression as surrender, not the weakness that you’ve accused yourself of for so long. When you’re wringing your hands and listening to your heartbeat accelerate, maybe you’re finally ready to just give it over, everything, to God.

There is power in giving up your power. Releasing your illusion of control can afford you a great deal of freedom. Yes, you have free will, but as a Christ follower, you also have the vested interest of the Creator who not only can help you but wants to.

When you’ve come to the end of your strength, faith begins. In 2 Corinthians 12, we are given a glimpse into the Apostle Paul’s own suffering:

But He said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore, I will boast all the more gladly about my weakness so that Christ’s power may rest in me. That is why, for Christ’s sake, I delight in weakness, in insult, in hardships, in persecutions, in difficulties. For when I am weak, then I am strong. – 2 Corinthians 12:9-10, NIV

Your exhaustion, overload, and feeling fed up don’t preclude you from God’s grace. In fact, it can be the place where His strength can shine its brightest. It’s the origin of your acknowledgement of your human condition. It is the beginning of you being able to say, “I give up and give it to you, God.” And it’s the start of something amazing.

When your burden becomes knee-buckling, you start to see that your wisdom is finite, your body human, and your reasoning flawed. But it’s also the place where you can more clearly see that God’s wisdom is infinite, His strength enduring, and His reasoning omnipotent.

A Little Help from a Friend

While God can do miraculous healing in the heart and change circumstances to your favor, even in ways you hadn’t thought of yet, He often works through people. In this mindset, Christian therapy can be viewed as a vessel of God’s providential care.

Talking with a skilled Christian therapist can help you identify your trauma and responses. It can give you the chance to dwell in the areas that might be too prickly to dwell in alone. A therapist can also guide you through healthy coping skills and help you reframe your thoughts through a biblical lens. They can walk with you as you process the pain in a safe and supportive environment.

Christian therapy isn’t necessarily meant to fix you instantly, but instead to direct you by helping you understand your story. More importantly, it encourages you to invite God into every messy, complicated chapter.

If you’re exhausted from the aftereffects of trauma, God may be telling you it’s time He steps in and begins to renew your mind. Lean on the power of the Almighty, loving, living God. Consider every hard feeling you have as an arrow, pointing you to the rest, trust, and healing that can only be found in the arms of your loving Father. Are you ready to move from exhaustion to faith? Contact our reception team to schedule an appointment with me or to learn more.

The post Trauma Response: Is it Exhaustion or the Beginning of Faith? appeared first on San Diego Christian Counseling.

item.title: Ways Your Helicopter Mom Affected Your Mental Health
item.description:
Sometimes it is the best intentions that cause the most enduring damage. That certainly is the case for anyone who grew up being parented by a helicopter mom. This style of invasive parenting is not a recent phenomenon.

The term dates back to a phrase from a book on parenting that was published in 1969, where a teen describes his controlling mother as always hovering over him in the background. In the decades since 1990, the idea of helicopter parenting has become increasingly discussed, with many proudly self-identifying as helicopter parents.

When compared to neglectful parents, helicopter moms appear as attentive, engaged, and involved in their children’s lives. In truth, however, the average helicopter mom is causing layers of psychological and emotional damage to her children, often without meaning to.

It’s a complicated thing to realize as an adult that your parent did more harm than good. Some people are forever affected by their helicopter mom. It is only when they begin to confront their past and make changes in their present that they can undo some of the damage that was done.

The Defining Aspects of a Helicopter Mom

It’s important to accurately identify what a helicopter mom is and determine what sets them apart from a healthy, attentive parent. Currently, there are many parents who proudly wear the label of helicopter parent simply because they are intentional, involved, and engaged in their child’s life. There are, however, several important differences between nurturing parents and helicopter parents.

During infancy and early childhood, the idea of being a helicopter parent is acceptable, to a point. There are many ways a baby or a toddler can injure themselves, and many situations that require a parent to monitor their child carefully.

At a certain age, it is important to lengthen the strings that connect you to your child. You must allow them space to grow, make mistakes, and learn to make good choices. A helicopter parent does not adapt or adjust their parenting style as their child grows.

The helicopter mom remains overly involved in all aspects of their child’s life, often into teen years and sometimes adulthood. Under her anxious glare, the child cannot make any decisions without first consulting her.

They cannot develop individuality or form their own opinions. It is often difficult to perform vital but ordinary tasks, such as cooking, cleaning, or performing basic hygiene. The helicopter mom has inserted herself into so many aspects of her child’s life that she is the sun around which her child’s life orbits.

The Helicopter Mom: Intention Versus Impact

As the saying goes, the path to destruction is paved with good intentions. There are multiple reasons why someone becomes a controlling, invasive, anxious parent, but it is almost always done out of concern and with good intentions. As an adult sorting through the damage that was done in your childhood from a helicopter parent, it’s important to distinguish your parents’ intention from the impact they have had on your life.

For example, your helicopter mom might have tried to shield you from pain, disappointment, and failure. These are important aspects of life, though, and you will only develop and mature if you learn to face them.

If you were never permitted to fail, you will feel guilty and ashamed each time you do. If you were protected from discomfort, you would feel helpless in every challenge. If you were never allowed to make a choice, even the wrong one, you will never have confidence in your ability to move forward in life or adapt to difficult situations.

Without meaning to, helicopter moms ensure their kids enter adulthood as dependent, anxious, confused people, who often feel guilty, ashamed, or resentful, without even knowing where those feelings come from.

The Dark Turn

In some cases, helicopter parenting produces much darker results. Helicopter parents are micromanagers who constantly communicate that they mistrust their children. To a teen who is desperate for some space to develop their own identity, or an adult who craves the feeling of independence, this is insulting, frustrating, and stifling.

Sometimes the only way to fully experience freedom is rebellion. They might lash out in anger, build boundaries so high that the relationship becomes strained, or resort to burning bridges. When you strip back the layers of helicopter parenting, you expose anxiety, distrust, and a need for control. Treating someone this way, even under the guise of love, will result in nothing good.

At best, the child will grow into an insecure, fearful adult with no confidence or coping skills and a constant need for validation. At worst, they will be resentful, damaged, trapped, and eager to find a way out. This will come as a shock to the micromanaging parent, who has likely convinced themselves that everything they did came from the best intentions.

Finding Healing and Wholeness

Adults who were impacted by a helicopter mom have a difficult path ahead of them as they attempt to resolve their trauma from the past. Many people manage to maintain a close relationship with their controlling parent, despite realizing the damage that was done. Even when they can trace their current issues back to their experiences growing up, pinning all the blame on their parents doesn’t help them find peace.

The great trick of healing from trauma caused by a helicopter parent is in learning to give space to feeling mixed emotions. You can be both grateful for your mother’s involvement and concern in your life, while also being frustrated by her dominance and control.

You can love her, but also reduce her impact in your life by setting up boundaries. You can be angry about the way she instilled anxiety and fear into your life, but recognize that she has the same struggles without anyone helping her.

One of the most important things you can do for your healing is to identify specific behaviors that were shaped or inspired by your helicopter mom. Whether it is a feeling of general helplessness, guilt, anxiety, a fear of failure, or a constant need for validation, identify each one individually and call it out.

Acknowledge it is part of your psyche, that it impacts your life, and note where it came from. Expect to feel anxious in this process because you are confronting things that your nervous system has been trained to avoid.

An important part of this process is identifying your mother’s voice in your head. The helicopter mom voice often says things like, “Ask me before doing this,” or “You’ll only mess this up if you try it yourself.” If you were taught that failure is scary and that you can’t be trusted to try new things, you already know what you need to do. Hear that voice in your head, tell it to hush, and do it anyway.

Freedom

Helicopter parents position themselves to be the single most important resource in their child’s life, regardless of how old or in what stage of life their child is. This does not always come from a place of narcissism or self-importance, though sometimes it does. At the core of this parenting style is anxiety and fear disguised as love and concern.

Your helicopter mom might have reduced your confidence, heightened your anxiety, and diminished your identity. There is always time to address these things and start living your life free from the overbearing influence of a micromanaging parent. It is a difficult road to walk, and there might be a few fraught confrontations to initiate, but you have what it takes to do this.

You might need support as you venture forth in confronting your past. We suggest meeting with a counselor with whom you can share your journey. We hope that you can find someone suitable on our online catalog, or someone from our reception team can help you.

Photo:
“Helicopter Rescue”, Courtesy of Markus Spiske, Unsplash.com, CC0 License

The post Ways Your Helicopter Mom Affected Your Mental Health appeared first on Seattle Christian Counseling.

item.title: The Danger of Overstepping Boundaries and How to Find Support
item.description:
Boundaries are what keep us safe. They create a safe border around your life that aligns with what you believe and what is important to you. They also protect the particularly vulnerable areas and give others a clear understanding of how you expect to be treated.

Boundaries are clearly important and help to create structure and protection for you. When those emotional borders are breached, it can feel like a violation. You may feel violated when this happens. It can even open the door for manipulation, guilt, and frustration. These put a strain on your relationships. It can drain your resources like your finances and your energy. And when you don’t put a stop to it, it can cause you to be a target for others.

Understanding Boundaries

A boundary, by definition, is “something that indicates or fixes a limit or extent.” (Merriam-Webster Dictionary) In the context of personal boundaries, it’s a clear guide telling the world how you expect to be treated and how you will likewise treat others in return.

Boundaries tell others and, more importantly, remind you what you’re willing to give and what you’re not. These invisible fences protect your time, resources, energy, and even your emotional well-being. Without them, it’s easy to be swept away by the demands of others.

The reality is that boundaries make relationships healthier. They prevent awkward confrontations. They prevent resentment, and they ensure that both parties are being fairly treated. They create structure and allow relationships to grow without draining you.

Some may criticize your boundaries, saying they’re selfish. Those critics are usually the ones who want to push past your comfort zone for their own gain. Even with clearly set boundaries in place, not everyone will respect them.

Relationship Types

Most people agree that boundaries are important to set. But setting boundaries can be tricky, especially in relationships where there’s a perceived hierarchy, like a parent and child relationship or a boss and employee.

It’s common for one party to feel automatically subordinate, which makes it easy for the other person to take advantage of their position. If you’re the subordinate, you might feel guilty if you push back against things that violate your boundaries for fear of retaliation.

A child might find it difficult to say no to a parent, even if that child is an adult. In long-standing relationships, old patterns of obedience or people pleasing can make standing up for yourself feel impossible. If you’re an adult, you might find it difficult to say no to your parents, even if their requests are unreasonable. Younger children might feel like boundaries are punishments, but they’re tools that teach respect and structure.

At work, especially under a boss or supervisor, it’s easy to let your own time and energy be stretched too thin because you feel obligated or threatened into compliance. An employee might naturally surrender rights they shouldn’t out of fear of being fired.

Overstepping Boundaries

Overstepping happens when someone ignores or violates the lines that you’ve clearly drawn or when someone takes (or tries to take) more than you’re willing to give. If you haven’t been clear or decisive in communicating your boundaries, then the fault might land on you. It’s a sign that it’s time to be transparent and clear.

Most of these issues can be resolved with an honest conversation. But if someone oversteps a boundary that you’ve clearly laid or repeatedly pushes those limits, it’s likely their behavior is not a misunderstanding.

Overstepping boundaries is a sign of someone else’s neediness, not your failure. Read that again. Read it a dozen times if you need to. Because it’s the truth and it’s a fact that often gets clouded, forgotten, or manipulated.

When people don’t respect your boundaries, your generosity and kindness become a weapon. A weapon in the hands of those who are manipulating you can be dangerous. These manipulators employ guilt tactics and abuse your kindness, using the best part of you for their good and your detriment.

Repeated violations can lead to frustration and even resentment. They often create a cycle where you feel guilty for merely protecting yourself. But how do you protect yourself? Over time, this will undermine your self-esteem, may change the way you interact with people in the future, and will certainly damage your relationship with them.

When you start rearranging your life to manage someone else’s, you’re no longer operating out of a heart of love but from pressure. This isn’t loving for either one of you.

Spiritual Principle of Boundaries

God calls us to love others, but He doesn’t ask us to sacrifice our own well-being in the process. In Matthew 5:37, Jesus reminds us to let our yes be yes, and our no be no. God wants honesty in our interactions, and establishing boundaries is a way of thriving in the life that God has given you.

Well-meaning Christians often confuse the idea of setting boundaries with being selfish. They believe that being Christ-like is synonymous with being endlessly available and self-sacrificing. Of course, the idea of dying to self is a solid Christian principle, so it’s no wonder that there is confusion. But dying to self refers to surrendering sin and selfish ambition, not healthy boundaries that safeguard the life God entrusted to you.

Christ didn’t model boundary-less living. Jesus himself stepped away from crowds to rest. He withdrew to pray. He said no to certain demands so He could say yes to the mission the Father gave Him. Even Jesus, who was perfectly loving, did not allow people to dictate His time or derail His purpose.

God never intended for you to live exhausted, either. He doesn’t want you to be resentful or drained dry. Psalm 121 reminds us that God watches over our comings and goings. He cares about your daily life, not just the big Instagram-worthy events. You can do this in your day-to-day life by protecting your peace, health, and time. This is a form of stewardship that honors God.

Therapy for Help with Boundaries

Psychology echoes the Bible’s idea of boundaries. Therapists explain that boundaries are necessary for emotional safety and help you maintain a balanced life. When you don’t set or enforce them, you expose yourself to unnecessary stress and can burden yourself with more responsibility than necessary. Those burdens can cause a myriad of negative consequences.

If you have a difficult time creating, communicating, and enforcing boundaries, seek professional help from a licensed therapist. Your therapist can walk you through the steps of deciding how you want to be treated by the people in your life. They can also help you learn how to communicate those boundaries effectively and how to enforce them.

Therapists can also help you recognize when your boundaries have been violated and give you practical and reasonable responses to employ in those circumstances. You can find support in these delicate situations that helps you recognize problem areas and learn new ways to move forward.

Starting with a therapist doesn’t need to be intimidating. You can connect with a Christian therapist who will share the same spiritual foundation discussed in this article. That will help you start from a place of shared purpose and understanding. It will also give you a model for how to live life with healthy, Godly boundaries.

You can reach out to a therapist near you or someone on this site. Therapy can be in person or virtual, offering an array of options so it fits into your life. You don’t have to continue living by other people’s needs. You can learn to create and maintain boundaries that support you.

Call or fill out the contact form on this site to learn more about how to meet with a Christian therapist who can help.

https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/boundary

item.title: Common Signs of Codependency in Relationships
item.description:
Relationships work best when two people connect, sharing their needs, working together to resolve problems, and showing a mutual appreciation of the differences that make them unique. Healthy relationships can abide differences, and they nurture the pursuit of one’s best self as the Lord envisions it. At their best, relationships help us to be more fully human.

Just as relationships have their benefits, they can also have a dark side. How people conduct themselves in relationships, and the way others relate to them, may not be healthy. Some patterns of speech, behavior, and attitudes can be devastating, not just for the relationship itself, but for the individuals in that relationship. Being attentive to and discerning of these patterns can help you identify and avoid unhealthy relationships.

Codependency is just one of many different unhealthy patterns of relationships. You may find that one or more of your relationships has a codependent dynamic, and for your sake and the sake of others around you, it’s important that you pinpoint that dynamic and find ways to turn things around.

Codependency and Its Root Causes

The word ‘codependent’ is likely vaguely familiar to you. To begin with, there’s nothing wrong with two people being mutually dependent on one another. In fact, there’s something beautiful about the way the Lord designed us to thrive through relationships. We are meant to live in community with others, sharing the best of ourselves with them (1 Corinthians 12; Matthew 22:34-40; John 13:34-35).

While mutual dependence is one thing, codependence points to something else entirely. When a person is codependent, they rely excessively on another person for things such as their identity, sense of self-worth, or emotional support. They might feel lost without the other person, unable to forge a path for their own life or follow their own priorities.

At first glance, it can be hard to draw a firm line between healthy reliance and excessive reliance. Relationships differ, and life often has fluid circumstances that make it complex and difficult to pin down. A partner or spouse who’s struggling with physical or mental impairment due to illness may be entirely dependent on their counterpart, and rightly so, even if it’s just for a season. A child is also dependent on a parent.

Codependency shows up in those relationships and situations where a person can be reasonably expected to establish their own sense of self, and they can meet significant emotional needs without reference to others. The excesses of codependency will typically show up in unhealthy patterns of enabling behavior, sacrificing oneself to meet others’ needs, being controlling over others, ultimately to the detriment of one’s well-being.

When it comes to the roots of codependency, it often traces back to formative early life experiences. If a person grows up in an environment where abuse, neglect, or inconsistent caregiving are the norm, they may develop low self-esteem and deep-seated fears of abandonment. They may not trust that what is here today will be here tomorrow, and that can induce anxieties and fear about the permanence of relationships.

These early life experiences can result in a codependent dynamic. The individual learns to draw lines between their value and how well they either please or care for others. Their sense of identity becomes attached to what they do for others, and their sense of purpose is tied to caring for others, even when that care is detrimental to their own well-being.

Signs of Codependency in Relationships

How can you identify patterns of codependency in your relationships? One of the challenges with identifying codependency is that it can easily be mistaken for being a nice person who is deeply loving and self-sacrificial. Codependency can be praised because it can look like being a saint. Knowing some of the signs of codependency can help you identify these tendencies and distinguish them from healthy self-giving.

Some of the common signs of codependency include the following:

Poor boundaries A boundary is a limit that indicates what you feel comfortable or uncomfortable doing, or it can be thought of as a psychological demarcation that distinguishes one individual from another. A person with poor boundaries can struggle to say ‘no’ to others’ requests or impositions. They may also feel responsible for others’ feelings or problems.

People-pleasing Codependency can also involve being eager to please people. You may be afraid to offend others and go out of your way to be inoffensive. It is rooted in an overwhelming need to gain the approval of other people, even when it comes at great personal expense.

Control issues A potentially surprising sign of codependency is the desire to manage others’ lives to feel secure. A codependent person often swoops in to rescue others, which can easily and quickly look like controlling them, their lives, and their choices.

Low self-esteem In a real way, a codependent person has a poorly developed sense of self. The result is that they might go through life measuring their self-worth through others’ opinions of them or the relational status they have.

Caretaking Another sign of codependency is feeling compelled to “fix” others’ lives and problems, especially when it is accompanied by neglecting one’s own needs.

Fear of abandonment Codependency might also be indicated when a person stays in unhealthy relationships out of fear of being alone.

Resentment Willingly serving others is one thing, but codependency often results in feelings of resentment toward them. Codependence leads to joyless, nearly servile attempts at meeting the needs of others. Doing things you really don’t want to be doing to earn the approval of others can wear on your soul and result in deep resentment toward them, and yourself as well, for going along with it.

The Spiritual Dangers of Codependency

In a codependent dynamic, there’s the party who always swoops in to rescue the other individual who’s perpetually in trouble, whether it be addiction, money problems, or bad relationships. The enabler is more than happy to allow the rescuer to rescue them, and that dynamic can continue uninterrupted for long seasons and cycles in their lives. There are dangers with a codependent dynamic, and some of these are spiritual in nature.

Codependency can pose subtle yet profound spiritual dangers, whether related to people-pleasing, poor boundaries, resentment, or the source of one’s identity. There is, for instance, a possibility of wandering into idolatry when you elevate people to a position of influence and authority that rightly belongs to the Lord alone.

When you root your identity in anything other than Christ, the likely result is disappointment, hurt, and disillusionment. The identity that you form from relationships, and the self-worth that’s rooted there instead of in Christ, isn’t a stable one, particularly because people can be fickle. The price that’s exacted may lead you into ungodliness to retain those relationships.

Prioritizing others’ needs to the point of neglecting your own doesn’t mirror who God is. Jesus was the quintessential servant-leader, but He was able to assert His own boundaries, contradict what was untrue, and take time for Himself to rest and pray (Mark 1:35; Mark 10:45; Matthew 22:23-33). Prioritizing others’ needs above your own or the Lord’s purposes for your life may result in spiritual neglect and distancing yourself from God.

Recovery from Codependency

The path toward recovery from codependency is possible. While codependency is rooted in a poor sense of self, it is possible to begin rooting your identity in Christ, helping you to reorient your life and nurture healthier relationships with good boundaries that promote well-being.

Some steps you can take:

Acknowledge the issue Ask the Lord for discernment to identify unhealthy patterns in your life and relationships.

Seek the Lord Rebuild your identity in Christ, including your sense of self-worth. Hear what the Lord has to say about you throughout Scripture (Galatians 2:20; 2 Corinthians 5:17; Romans 8; Psalm 139).

Establish healthy boundaries Healthy boundaries are necessary and promote mutual respect. Learn to say “No” without feeling guilty about it.

Prioritize self-care Prioritize your emotional, physical, and spiritual well-being as part of what it means to be a good steward of all that the Lord has given you.

Seek support Mentorship, support groups, and professional Christian counseling can help you on your journey. Such relationships can foster healing and accountability as you grow healthier, less codependent relationships.

To learn more about the signs of codependency and to schedule a consultation with a local counselor or therapist, contact our office today.

Photo:
“Eye Contact”, Courtesy of Ryan Jacobson, Unsplash.com, CC0 License

The post Common Signs of Codependency in Relationships appeared first on Los Angeles Christian Counseling.

item.title: Helicopter Moms and the Anxiety Loop
item.description:
To the onlooker, a helicopter mom seems devoted, attentive, and deeply invested in her child’s well-being. Every quick rescue and even every reminder to “be careful” comes from a place of love. A helicopter mom might have wonderful intentions, devoting her life to her children because of the fierce and protective love she feels. That’s the way mothering should be, right?

The Bible even says that a friend is someone who will lay down their life for their friend (John 15:13). And if that’s God’s idea of true friendship, shouldn’t it be more so for parents? The Bible goes even deeper regarding parental love.

Biblical love for children requires guiding them with wisdom, compassion, and discipline while modeling God’s truth through your daily living example. Loving your children well, selflessly, and wholly is the will of God.

Yet, even the most loving intentions can sometimes go too far. When a parent’s protective love goes beyond healthy boundaries, it can be detrimental to the child. Love, vigilance, control, and devotion can turn into what has become popularly known as “helicopter parenting.”

Being a Helicopter Mom

While dads can step over the line of devotion to control, too, helicopter moms get all the publicity. Why? Because society expects mothers to be the primary caregivers. Their involvement is more visible, their worry more scrutinized, and their efforts more intensely judged because statistically, moms are the parent who are most involved in the daily operation of childcare.

Helicopter moms might also create an environment where dads can be more relaxed. If mom is being “overprotective”, then dad doesn’t have to. In fact, dads can then become the “chill” or “cool” parent because they know Mom is carefully monitoring their children.

Unfortunately, “chill” dads often push moms who are prone to hovering to become more vigilant because they feel the full weight of responsibility to protect and guide the children.

How did this happen?

Being a helicopter mom isn’t usually toxic from the start. It usually starts off with appropriate vigilance and devotion, and is often reinforced with compliments of superior parenting. “You’re such a devoted mom” is a nice compliment to hear when you’ve been up all night with a crying baby.

When your baby is born, it’s natural, healthy even, to devote the majority of your time to that new little life. They are helpless without assistance, and most moms revel in the honor of motherhood. Even the late-night feedings and dirty diapers can be thought of as undercover blessings when you see those innocent and dependent eyes staring back at you.

As children grow, their needs change, and the level of assistance they need also changes. But it’s sometimes difficult to relinquish the full control over their lives that you have had since their birth.

It might feel that as you let go, you’re also “slacking off” on your job as protector and guide. Your intentions to guide and protect may be entirely pure, selfless even, but the result might not be what you intended or healthy for your child.

Are you a helicopter mom?

You might not hear the “thwop, thwop, thwop” of the blades circling overhead, but you might have your suspicions. Maybe someone has even accused you of being one, or you’ve been labeled with similar adjectives like “overprotective” or have been told that you’re “too involved.” If you have, you’ve probably been offended and passionately defended yourself, explaining that you’re a good mom or that you just love your children.

It’s natural to defend yourself; after all, you love your children, and that’s a good thing. But sometimes actions that you are labeling as love are fueled not by devotion, but fear. The unfortunate byproduct is not necessarily protected children, but children who develop anxiety and lack independence.

The more a mother hovers, the more anxious both she and her child become. Children then begin to rely on constant guidance, doubting their own abilities to handle life’s challenges. Parents’ anxiety grows each time they feel the need to intervene, worrying that if they let go, even this one time, it might end in disaster.

Anxiety Transfer

What starts innocently as appropriate and normal devotion slowly becomes a feedback loop where parents’ worry triggers the child’s dependence, and the child’s dependence reinforces the parents’ worry. This loop is what psychologists call the anxiety transfer. The irony of it all is that in trying to protect their children from harm or failure, helicopter moms may inadvertently fuel the anxiety that they’re trying to prevent.

The effects of anxiety can actually shape a child’s view of the world, and more alarmingly, they can shape a child’s view of themselves. Children who grow up in an environment where constant oversight is the norm may internalize the belief that making mistakes is equal to failure.

Why? Because they aren’t allowed to fail. Mom steps in whenever she sees that her child is struggling instead of letting them experience failure. This lets the child know, even inadvertently, that mom doesn’t want them to fail.

This is a more dangerous message than failure itself because not only is failure impossible to avoid, it’s also a good learning tool. Failure teaches your children more about themselves. They learn their strengths and their weaknesses. They learn self-soothing and how to get back up when they’ve been knocked down. Intervening can take those valuable lessons away from them and replace them with self-doubt and fear.

Breaking the Loops

Even if your kids are grown, or maybe especially if they are, it’s important to break the cycle. If you’ve come to the realization that you’re a helicopter mom, that’s the first step in breaking the anxiety loop.

Recognizing that you might be hovering more closely out of fear rather than love allows you to pause and make intentional, healthy choices, not reactionary ones. Afraid of change? Well, the goal isn’t to stop loving your children, but to love them in healthy ways that help them grow, rather than holding them back or creating more anxiety.

Once you’ve realized that you might be a helicopter mom, it’s time to learn how to put more trust in God. Proverbs 3:5-6 reminds us to “Trust in the Lord with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding” (NIV). While this might be difficult to do if you’re in the habit of controlling your child’s life, it should come as a relief. God is not only inviting you to give your child to Him, but He’s also demanding it.

This relinquishment should bring you peace because you are no longer entirely responsible for every part of your child’s life. God can and will guide both you and your child through challenges in a way that you cannot do alone. How? Prayer and meditating on the Scriptures can calm your heart, redirect your fear, and give you insights as to how you should be parenting your child.

Therapy can also help you break helicopter tendencies. Speaking with a counselor can help you identify specific patterns of worry and dig to the root of your insecurities. They can also help you learn strategies for managing these worries.

They can help you recognize the difference between protective love and overbearing fear and build emotional tools for letting go in healthy ways. And these important skills will do more than just benefit you as a parent. They will also benefit your children as they witness patience, self-awareness, and strategic decision-making skills unfold in real life.

Bye-Bye Guilt

And bye-bye sole responsibility. You’re one person, not God. And while your intentions to control your children come from a place of love, they also come from a place of fear. Your fear of your children failing or your fear of them making a wrong choice may well be rooted in your own anxiety.

That’s where faith comes in. God loves your children, even more than you do, hard as that is to believe. And He wants them to learn to be strong, independent warriors for Christ, not adults who still live in their parents’ shadows. So, if you’re a helicopter mom, realize that your love for your children won’t go away when you let go. In fact, the act of “letting go and letting God” is in itself a selfless act of love.

To learn more and to make an appointment with a Christian therapist to learn how to break the anxiety loop, contact our office today.

item.title: Stress Eating: What Causes It and How to Overcome It
item.description:
Food, glorious food. The Lord has blessed us with many things, one of which is food. After blessing the first humans and commissioning them to be faithful stewards over His creation, the Lord instructed them on where to find food, a necessity for their survival (Genesis 1:28-30). Then we read, “God saw all that he had made, and it was very good” (Genesis 1:31, NIV). Food is a part of that “very good”.

However, it would be painting a skewed picture to leave matters at that. The Fall of humanity occurred, and our connection to the Lord, ourselves, each other, and between ourselves and the non-human created world was severely disrupted (Genesis 3). As Paul puts it, the creation is in “bondage to decay” (Romans 8:21, NIV). One implication is that our bodies and food may not naturally be in a harmonious relationship.

Stress eating is one of the ways we can relate to food and ourselves in an unhealthy and unbalanced way. Understanding what stress eating is, why we do it, how it affects us, and the ways to overcome it can help you manage life challenges more constructively.

Stress Eating in Brief

Commonly, we often talk about comfort eating, but it is also referred to as stress eating or emotional eating. One reason the term ‘emotional eating’ can be helpful is that it leaves room for the different emotional states that could be at the root of why we’re eating to satisfy something other than our hunger. A person can ‘eat’ their feelings, and that includes emotional states such as anxiety, sadness, or stress.

When a person eats to cope with their stress or other emotional states, that’s marked by a few characteristics. Typically, they will crave comfort foods. These are foods that are high in salt, fat, or sugar content. Stress eating is about using food as a coping mechanism, and often, the eating is not about satisfying hunger. Another characteristic is that there’s often a loss of control, making it hard to stop or limit one’s food intake.

As the eating isn’t strictly related to physical hunger, stress eating will often lead a person past satiation. This can cause significant health issues in the short term as well as down the line.

Why We Stress Eat

Stress eating can be a huge challenge, and to tackle it, you need to understand why we turn to food to relieve emotional distress. Several factors may be at play to explain why we stress eat. Stress eating is about using food to manage feelings of stress. In other words, food functions as a coping mechanism to manage the unpleasantness of stress, sadness, or anxiety.

Stress releases the hormone cortisol, and that hormonal response can increase one’s appetite and cravings for comfort food. Depending on the type and duration of stress, stress can activate the brain’s reward system, making you more sensitive to rewards like dopamine, which make comfort foods appealing. Stress eating feels good, providing temporary relief or comfort from stressors.

We also stress eat because it’s something we’ve learned to do. Foods high in sugar, fat, and salt activate the brain’s reward system, which releases dopamine, and then we begin to associate those foods with pleasure. These foods become associated with positive emotions and memories connected with relaxation, comfort, or feeling good. It increases the likelihood of stress eating at a future date.

Another factor that also makes it likely to stress eat is the lack of other, healthier coping mechanisms. If you don’t have other stress-management techniques handy, it may be easier to turn to food for a quick fix.

The combination of environmental, biological, and emotional factors may make it challenging to resist your cravings for comfort foods when you’re experiencing stress or other difficult emotional states. Though stress eating can provide you with temporary relief, ultimately, it may lead to negative consequences such as unplanned weight gain, feelings of guilt, or worsened mental health.

How Stress Eating Affects You

On that note, highlighting how stress eating affects you can provide you with important information about the cost of stress eating. Pointing out the negative effects of stress eating isn’t necessarily enough to turn things around, but it can be helpful. Naming these effects can, for instance, help you to identify and process your experiences after stress eating. Stress eating can affect you emotionally, mentally, physically, and relationally.

One of the ways that stress eating affects an individual includes impacting their physical health. It can lead to digestive issues, particularly when you eat beyond feeling full, and it can result in unplanned weight gain. With weight gain come other concerns, such as decreased mobility and an increased risk of chronic diseases such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and cardiac disease.

Stress eating can also affect your emotional well-being. When you stress-eat, the lack of control and sheer excess of it all can lead to feelings of guilt and shame. You may even become anxious about your eating habits and what they are doing to you. Stress eating can worsen conditions like anxiety and depression, impacting your mental health as well.

How you perceive yourself matters. Feelings of guilt or shame from stress eating may result in low confidence or a negative self-image. When your self-esteem takes a knock, that can affect how you perform and are in your relationships, at work, and in other contexts. This may, in turn, fuel further distress, which can turn into emotional eating to cope, feeding a seemingly endless cycle.

Another possible effect of stress eating is that it can affect your relationships. Dealing with conflict by stress eating won’t resolve matters; it may result in deepening the conflict. If a person hides their stress eating, that can also introduce strain into the relationship. The cycle of emotional distress that stress eating can create makes it harder to manage emotions and stress effectively. This can make conducting a healthy relationship more challenging.

Managing and Overcoming Stress Eating

When you recognize the impact of stress eating on your life, that could be a good first step toward seeking help and cultivating healthier coping mechanisms that won’t undermine your well-being. Some of the strategies that can effectively help you to manage and overcome stress eating include the following:

Identify triggers Whether through journaling or reflection, it’s possible to identify and learn to recognize the emotions, situations, events, or experiences that lead to stress eating. Perhaps for you it’s a hard workday, or it could be a relationship conflict that leads to stress eating. Maybe it’s having tight deadlines or struggling to connect with loved ones. Keeping a food diary may help you track your habits.

Eat regular, balanced meals When you eat regularly and your meals are balanced, this can help you reduce cravings and maintain relatively stable levels of energy. Good nutrition helps your emotional, mental, and physical well-being, which can all contribute to better emotional regulation. Doing this requires planning, including having healthy snacks and meals available to avoid eating impulsively.

Practice mindful eating Mindfulness is all about being fully present in whatever situation you’re in. When you’re mindful about your eating, you pay attention to cues such as whether you’re hungry or full, eat your food slowly instead of wolfing it down, and take the time to savor your food and the process of preparing it. These are small ways to build a healthy relationship with your food.

Develop self-care habits Making self-care a priority, whether that’s getting enough sleep, doing regular exercise, spending time with loved ones, doing hobbies, or taking time to rest and relax, all helps to reduce stress levels. The more you perform and enjoy these activities, the easier it’ll be to turn to them in times of stress instead of to food for comfort.

Challenge your thoughts There’s a place for challenging your negative thoughts, particularly the ones that can lead you toward food as a source of comfort. Whether it’s thoughts encouraging one more bite or thoughts that are self-disparaging, they can and should be challenged. Apply what you know is true to address your emotional eating patterns and nurture a healthy relationship with yourself and your food.

Seek support and professional help Don’t suffer in silence about stress or your eating habits. Embarrassment, guilt, or shame shouldn’t stand in the way of your seeking the help you need. Talk to wise and trusted loved ones about what you’re going through. You can also consult professionals, whether a registered dietitian or nutritionist, or a counselor who can give you guidance in addressing harmful thought patterns.

“So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all for the glory of God” (2 Corinthians 10:31, NIV). It’s possible to develop a healthier relationship with your food and to deal with stress and other emotions effectively without turning to food for comfort. Reach out for help from a professional to start that journey. Contact our office today to learn more.

The post Stress Eating: What Causes It and How to Overcome It appeared first on Spokane Christian Counseling.

item.title: When Information Becomes Mental Exhaustion: God’s Invitation to Rest
item.description:
When you wake up and check your phone before your feet hit the floor, your brain has already sprinted into the day. Notifications, emails, and breaking news flood your mind before you have even had time to get ready for the day. This leaves you tired and mentally exhausted before the day truly begins.

Constant information is normal in our world today. But this does not make it healthy. We were not designed to take in all the information at our fingertips. This leads to a constant state of mental exhaustion, and this can affect our joy, relationships, and our walk with God.

What is mental exhaustion?

Mental exhaustion is not just feeling a little bit tired. It is a state of deep cognitive and emotional fatigue stemming from prolonged stress and overstimulation. Some of the most common signs of mental exhaustion include:

  • Difficulty concentrating
  • Feeling emotionally numb
  • Struggling to make decisions
  • Increased anxiety or irritability
  • Trouble resting
  • Feeling disconnected from God, self, and others

When we are faced with constant input, such as news, social media, and text messages, our brains remain in a state of constant alert. Over time, this can result in chronic mental exhaustion, which directly impacts our mental health.

How Constant Information Input Fuels Mental Exhaustion

Our brains were not designed to process thousands of pieces of information every day. When we do not disconnect from this constant information, we are subject to various effects on our minds and mental health.

The brain stays in an always-on mode Every notification, headline, and message is a demand on your attention. Your brain treats these as micro-stressors because the content is most often either urgent, emotional, or negative.

Over time, this low-level stress can lead to difficulty relaxing, heightened anxiety, and chronic mental fatigue. We are reminded in Scripture that we are not meant to live in constant alarm, but peace is hard to experience when our minds never shut down.

Attention becomes fragmented Endless scrolling and rapid content consumption teach our brains to expect constant novelty. This results in us living in fragments, such as skimming instead of deeply reading, half-listening, and being distracted while praying. When we become this fragmented, our mental exhaustion is amplified as we try to hold onto too many pieces of information at once.

Emotional overload and numbness Each day, we are exposed to grief, outrage, disaster, rage, and comparison. The input we see is other people’s successes and highlight reels, the global crisis and tragedies, or public arguments and controversies. Each of these is more than what the human heart was designed to carry.

We are not expected to carry the emotional weight of the whole world. It ends up becoming too much for us to hold onto unless we give it to God. We either feel overwhelmed or shut down emotionally, and each of these results from mental exhaustion.

The Spiritual Dimension of Mental Exhaustion

Mental exhaustion is not just a psychological issue. It also has a spiritual dimension. When the noise is constant, we have a harder time hearing God’s voice, remembering His promises, being still, and discerning what truly matters. Scripture calls us to a different place and posture.

The Invitation of Jesus to the Exhausted: Jesus speaks directly to the weary when he tells us to come to him and that he will give us rest (Matthew 11:28-30). He doesn’t say to come to Him when life is quiet. He invites us in, already burdened, tired, and overloaded. This is a promise of rest for our souls that is not found on a screen.

God’s Design for Stillness: We are called to intentional stillness in a world of nonstop input. This is not just a physical stillness. It is a mental and spiritual stillness mentioned in Psalm 46:10. It is a choice to step away from noise and resentment, recognizing that God is God and we are not.

How Mental Exhaustion Affects Mental Health

Constant information doesn’t just make us tired; it also makes us feel anxious. It also contributes to broader mental health challenges. Continuous exposure to news and arguments can trigger chronic worrying and nervousness, leading to a more intense struggle with anxiety.

This mental exhaustion leads to hopelessness or disconnection, which aligns with the symptoms of depression. Late-night scrolling before bed makes it harder to fall asleep and stay asleep, which leads to even more exhaustion. The combination of responsibilities and constant digital input increases the risk of burnout.

Mental health struggles are complex and have many causes, but reducing constant input is a meaningful and often necessary step toward healing and overcoming mental exhaustion.

A Biblical Perspective on Limits and Rest

God built limits and rhythms of rest into human life from the beginning. If He modeled it, then we must understand that observing limits is not a weakness; it is wisdom. When we ignore our limits and push through serious mental exhaustion, this is not faithfulness. We are trying to be our own source and Savior.

When constant input results in an increase in anxiety, God invites us to do more than cope. He expects us to bring to Him our burdened minds and hearts. This includes the weight of everything we have consumed, such as news, conversations, pressures, and fears.

We cannot guard our minds on our own. If we choose to focus on God’s word, we find that His peace is how our minds are truly guarded. It doesn’t mean we’re ignoring the world’s pain or injustice, but it does lead us to understand that constant negativity and noise aren’t what we are meant to dwell on daily. We get to decide.

Practical Steps to Reduce Constant Input

The goal is not to escape the world, but to live wisely within it. There are some practical, grace-filled steps we can take to shift away from constant input and ease mental exhaustion.

Identify your sources of overload When you honestly identify what is feeding your mental exhaustion, you can see that it is not random and that it has patterns and inputs that can be changed. Ask yourself if you can do without so much social media, news, messages, or podcasts. Find and remove specific accounts or chat threads that leave you drained each day.

Create gentle boundaries around technology Consider making small, deliberate changes that can serve as boundaries to protect your mind from constant intrusion. Set specific times to check the news or social media, turn off non-essential notifications, and place your phone out of reach on the side of your bed at night.

Practice daily moments of digital sabbath Just because you cannot disappear for a weekend does not mean you cannot carve out consistent breaks. Make time throughout the day to get away from the constant source of input. Quiet time in the morning, a short walk without headphones, or a few minutes of breathing and prayer in between tasks can help you reset and create a digital Sabbath that helps your mental health.

Rebuild your thought life with Scripture We can change the type of input that we receive. This means we can choose to read God’s word throughout the day instead of using digital input. It can be a short passage or a simple verse. The goal is to reflect on phrases that will cause you to hear the voice of God’s truth in overcoming mental exhaustion.

Invite community and professional help We were never designed to carry burdens alone. Talking honestly with a trusted friend or mentor when symptoms of anxiety, depression, or burnout are intense is not a lack of faith. Choosing to connect with a Christian counselor is a sign of spiritual and mental wisdom that will help you understand God-given limits and navigate toward healing.

Overcoming Mental Exhaustion

We may not be able to completely escape constant information. But we do not have to live in its grip every day. We can take small steps to limit constant information and replace it with truth, to experience something the world cannot offer: a quiet mind and a steady heart, with a soul learning to rest. It is normal to feel like change is hard and almost impossible. What makes it possible is consistency, with one little step at a time to advance toward change.

Connecting with a local Christian counselor is one way to get started on learning how to reset your mind in a restless world. If you would like more information on this process or to set up an appointment, reach out to our office or browse our online counselor directory. You can find a Christian counselor who can help you on your pathway to overcoming mental exhaustion in a noisy world.
